THE DREAM. Last night it chanc'd I breathed her name For whom my widowed youth Mourns ever ;—in a dream she came To bless my spirit's truth; Time darted backward in his flight To bring again one summer night. Once more beside the stream she stood, The while a rapt surprise Of passion-crowned womanhood Brimm'd in her earnest eyes; Then softly spoke one whisper'd word, None but the listening streamlet heard. For me no word was needed then; Nor language could divine The rapture of that look, or when She rais'd her;f ace to mine, And, heart to heart, in one caress We tasted perfect blessedness. The patient stars gazed silently On valley, wood, and hill; The peaceful water rippled by, The very night stood still.; Only a far-off nightingale Sang from a hollow in the dale. Long did we stay in silence there Without the heart to speak— It was enough to feel her hair Against my brow and cheek; And once—ab, whither fled that gleam ? She smiled. (I kissed her in my dream.) But soon I felt her bosom swell, And, as in other years, The moon came from a cloud to tell Love's rosary on her tears; She was so close, I did not start To hear the beating of her heart. At last, with passion at its height, Even as she kiss'd me—lo, God called her: was it yesternight, Of ten dark years ago? Far off the brown bird learns his song' • But oh, my love, how long? how long? —Belgravia. MONTAGU SMITE.

Think nothing in conduct unimportant or indifferent. Try to see yourself through the eyes of those around

you. Par your debts while you have the money in your pocket. Avoid passion and excitement; a moment's anger may be fatal. Learn to say No; not snappishly, but firmly and respectfully. Trust no tecrets to a friend which, if reported, would make an enemy. Work to-day, for you know not how much you maybe hindered to-morrow. In private watch your thoughts: in the family watch your temper; in company watch your tongue. Carry sunshine in your own heart, and, like the per- ' fume of flowers, it will breathe a fragrance everywhere. A teacher questioning his class on Scripture history, asked a little boy who was the holiest man. "Moses, sir." said the little boy. "110 w do you know he was the holiest man ?" asked the teacher. " Because, sir," was the quirk response, "I often hear my fattier say 'Holy Moses.'" A little lawyer, giving evidence, was asked by a gigan- tic counsellor what was his profession. Be replied that he witS an attorney. "You a lawyer! Why, I could put you into my pocket !" "If you did," was the ready response, " you'd have more law in your pocket than in your head." CHINESE SOLOSCON.—Not long since a case was heard in a law court in Shanghai, which showed great skill and acuteness on the part of the judge. A man was accused of stealing a table, but denied the charge, on the ground tha" he was so weak that it was not Possible fcr him to carry off the article. The judge, listening to the story with a pitying ear, bade the man go home and get cured. At the same time, as he was so poor, lie gave him a bag containing 10,000 cash (equal to £2 is. 81.). The man thankfully placed the bag of coin across his shoulders. and left the court. In a few minutes he was again taken up, tried, and found guilty, the judge observing that a man who could walk off with a sack of cash (a small brass coin) could easily carry away a light table. —Little Folks Magazine.f,r September. WHO WAS NAPOLEON H ?—Never was a boy born into the world with more snlendid prospects than Napoleon Francis Charles Joseph, the only child of Napoleon I. and the Empress Maria Louisa, daughter of the Emperor Francis of Austria. He was heir to the thrones of France and Italy, and at his birth he was created King of ROMP. is father was master of half the continent of Europe. and three of his uncles were kings. Tue birth of a child whose destinies seemed so brilliant was announced to the people of Paris by a salute of a hundred and one of those cannon which had helped to win so many victories for his father; and the great bell of Notre Dame rang a triumphant peal. But when the young Napoleon was born, in 1811, his father's star was setting and his won- derful career drawing to its close. His first three ye ire were the happiest period of the young king's life. His disposition was affectionate and precocious; and it may well be true that the only real happiness., the ambitious father ever knew was found in romping with his child. The great Emperor would spend hours at a time playing with the child upon whom all his hopes rested. The little Napoleon was very much like other small boys of his age. One day, when his governess had promised him a reward for -doing some- thing which lie was not very fond of doing. he asked to be allowed to play with a group of dirty children whom he had seen in the road outside the Palace of St. Cloud delightfully employed in making mud-pies. On another occasion his governess shamed him out of crying and going into "tantrums" by closing the windows and fastening, the shutters, for fear people should discover that the future emperor had a bad temper. But if the little prince was ill-tempered sometimes, he was as kind- hearted as most children are. When he was barely I three, the widow of an officer who had been killed in one of Napoleon's battles waited for him, with her little boy, while he was walking in the park of St. Cloud, and the fatherless boy handed him a petition to the emperor, asking fora pension, for they were nearly destitute. The wondering little Icing probably understood no more than that the boy's fattier had been killed; but he gave the petition to the emperor, who granted the poor lady her pension.—From Little Folks Maga:ine for September. THE PURPLE AND THE PRIESTHOOD.—In the fourth ceptury we may see St. Ambrose, in the great basilca of Mflan, surrounded by his faithful people, gathered there day and night to protect him from the violence of the Arian Empress Justina ; and to dispel the weariness of that long watch we may see him teaching them the an- tiphonal singing and the Latin hymns, which have con- tinued to add for centuries to the joy of worship. Or we may see him, in the year 390, meetityg the great Emperor 'Theodosius at the door of the basilica, and refusing to admit him until he has openly expressed his penitence for the brutal massacre of Thessalonica. And when Theodosius is admitted we may see him lay aside his purple and his diadem, and lie prostrate on the ground in the sight of all his people, smiting upon his breast with tears, and crying. "My soul cleaveth to the dust: oh! God, quicken Thou me according to Thy word." How had Christianity grown before such a scene could have been possible! Theodosius was an irre- sponsible autocrat, invested with almost superhuman dignity, the foremost man in all the world; hut the Christian bishop stands undaunted before him as his per6onified conscience. The might of his unarmed weakness became irresistible, because it is clothed as with the thunders of Sinai,and the imperial hands which had reddened themselves with innocent blood are im- potent to strike. The Emperor was absolved; he mounted the chancel steps to offer his gift, and then Seated himself among the clergy in the chancel. In- stantly Ambrose sent a deacon to sav to him, "The purple robe makes emperors. not priests," and that his Seat of honour was below the chancel steps; and Theo- dosius rose to purer grandeur by at once, and humbly, taking the lower room. How often has the scene been repeated! When our Henry 11. suffered himself to be scourged by the monks of Canterbury before the shrine of St. Thomas it Becket; when Henry IV. of Germany stood shivering in the snow before the Castle-gate of Pope Gregory at Canossa; when at Venice BArbIIXOSea took his mantle off, And, kneeling, on his neck received the foot Of the proial pontiff. Yes; for did not He say—of whose words every jot and tittle must be fulfillA—" Ye shall stand before kings and Aiail not be ashametl."—Sam!av Magazine. div.head: GAS-BURNER MAN. BY SYGIL.
div.p: THE GAS-BURNER MAN. BY SYGIL.

I should think every business man and every trades- man knows him well. He is a familiar figure amongst us. As verdancy and flowers herald the advent of Spring, so the gas-burner man comes with the fall of the leaf. And year after year, with a guileless simplicity, we trust him and buy his burner, paying him from three hundred to a thousand per cent, more for it than we could get the identical burner for at the ironmongers; the iron- monger himself, getting generally, an enormous profit on that particular article. He is, almost alwais, an unedu- cated man, and he knows no more about light or burners than we do ourselves. But until we find him out we have an unquestioning faith in his assumed knowledge and veracity. And he descants upon the virtues of the par- ticular burner which he is vending with such versimili- tude that it doesn't take him long to make us decide that, with the assistance of his burners, we shall reduce , our gas bills to something like one half of what they have hitherto been. And they need reducing, don't they? Can we not always see, every one of us, that every bill we get is twice as big as it really ought to be? Why, certainly. But we don't reduce them worth an old broken knife. Oh, no; you cannot intimidate a good, moral and upright, sevenpence-halfpenny a quarter gas- meter in that underhanded fashion. There is nothing slothful about a real good grass-green painted, enamel dialed, corporation-furnished meter; it has never to apply for an extension of hours to get its work in. But it is the gas-meter's foe we are dealing with this round. After being imposed on a great number of years, I at last found him out, and then I declined to contribute any more to his welfare. After that, when any of him called, he generally felt hurt. He was also disappointed,because the unsophisticated look with which kind Nature has en- dowed me always led him, and still leads him, to think that I am one of his born friends and patrons. I was in the office of a friend some three years ago when, the door being closed, we heard a gentle knock at it. My fri nd called out," Como in." The door opened and a dapper little chap came in with a very small satchel in his hand. He was a gas-burner man, and a smart one, but was, as is usual, uneducated. He sailed in at once, and before anyone could say anything to him lie had lit the gas, drawn our attention to the meagreness of the light, turned it off, taken off the old burner, put a new one in its place and lit the gas again. He then appealed to us for an opinion. My friend, like myself, not re- membering his opening speech said," What advantage do you claim for your burner ?" "Every advantage, sir. In the first place you get a better light, and in the second you get perfect com- bustion." " Well," said my friend, " it seems to be a better light, but it may be a different number of burner." "Oh, no sir. If you will look you will see that it is a number 4;" and, taking the old one from the snantelshelf where he had placed it, he said, "You see this is a number 4 too." I saw that both burners were number 4's, and I also noticed that they were both made by the same maker— Bray, I think, was the maker's name. •Taking another burner out of his bag, he showed us the inside of it, where we could see a piece of gauze. That was the only apparent difference between the two burners. But his burner certainly gave a more brilliant light than the old one, and I, with my usual obtuseness, could not think how it was that it did so. My friend said, How do you get perfect combustion with your burner? I thought there was no such thing as perfect combustion." "People have always said so lip to now, but it has been proved by this burner that there is such a thing, ' and I believe, sir, that I can prove it to you." Taking a penny from his pocket, he drew our atten- tion to it, showing us that there was no smut on it. He passed it through the flame horizontally backwards and forwards, and to our surprise he showed us that the coin was just as clean and shiny as ever. That, he said, proved perfect combustion. He then turned off the gas, took off his burner, put the old one on, and lighted the gas again. Then taking up the genie penny, he passed it through the flame, and behold! it was quite smutty and black where it had come in contact with the flame. I don't think I was quite as much surprised as my friend was, for I had certainly found one thing out, and I thought I had detected something else. I now noticed that the old burner was giving off just as good alight as the new one had given. The true explanation flashed across my mind on the instant. He had, the first time he lighted the gas, only partly turned it on. We had never thought to notice whether it was turned on or not. P.esides, he had kept us busy looking at the light and listening to his talk. I drew his attention to the light now, but, as was to be expected, he denied that it was anything like equal to the one from his burner. My friend also thought the light was a deal better now than when he first lit it, but the other partly persuaded him that it was not so good as wherChis burner was on. I said to the burner man, "Now, will you just lend me that penny, and let me put it through the flame." Turning his back upon me, he said, directly addressing my friend, "It is one of the greatest improvements that has been made in burners for a great many years, and it is calculated that it will reduce the gas bills of everyone as uses 'ern from twenty-five to fifty per cent." I said, "Just lend me that penny, will you? I want to try the perfmt combustion trick." Without noticing me, he continued, "Of course, they cost you more nor the others, but they will pay for tbersels in a week." I said, "Here, old man, just let me have that penny for a minute while I try the perfect combustion trick, and I tapped him on the shoulder. Still ignoring me, he went on, " Now, if you take a quantity you get 'em cheaper, but you can have any number you think proper. If you take—" Having tried again to get the penny and failed, I took one from my own pocket. I passed it through the lower part of the flame, and then looked at it. It was just as clean and bright as before I put it in the flame. I now passed it across the upper part of the flame, and la ! it collected a layer of soot on its surface in an in- stant. (Let anyone try this who doubts it.) The burner man was watching may every movement, and, when he saw me smile, after passing the penny through the flame the second time, he knew that the jig was up. Smiling himself, he said, "Well, what do you think about it ?" I said, "It's a capital dodge, and no mistake." Be said, "It is so good a dodge that I have worked it on thousands of people for this last two years, and you are the first that has detected the trick." He admitted that his burners were just the same as my friend's, except that his had a bit of gauze in, wnich didn't make the slightest difference to the flame. With more candour than honesty, he admitti d that he graduated his prices according to the looks of his customer. The next conflict I had was with a gas-burner man at my brother's house. We were sitting talking over some business, when a knock came to the door. My brother attended to the door himself. I heard a voice ask if the master was in, and, the owner being answered in the affirmative and asked his business, he said, "I have brought you some gas-burners to look at." My brother, thinking somebody had sent him specially, invited him in. He was a long, lank, and somewhat grimy individual with a dirty grey beard. lie' had on a rusty billycock, an old greasy frock coat and a pair of boots which had apparently, in some 'by- gone age, taken a leading part in an earthquake. But he had an the effrontery of his race. Ile soon got to work, and then, from his trousers' packet, he produced a burner which was in two parts. The top part was an ordinary burner ; the bottom part was a small brass cup, into which the burner fitted. At the bottom of the cup was a small hole to admit the gas. Over this hole was a small leaden pellet, which was to effect a saving cf gas by checking it. The burner screwed into the cup, and the cup screwed into the bracket. I think that old chap will remember us the longest day he lives. If he had never heard a scientific or an un- scientific term before, be fetched up Vont day for all the time he had lost. After he had eased his mind of what he had to say, and had shown us his burner, I said," Now, before you put your burner on, allow me to ask you if you understand the anatomy and phy- siology of light, and can you show us the advantages of your burner upon scientific principles."
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 8, 1888.

tie said, "If I cannot, no one can." But he answered] in such a manner as led me to think that he thought he might be mistaken. "Very well, then," I said. "If you can do that, and can substantiate what you say, you may get an order worth having. Now, as you know, common gas is com- posed of carbon, hydro sulphide of chyle, chloride of sodium, and bichlorate of animalculx." yes." _

_ " And that a flame is composed of intransigeant polarizations of crystals of bi-metallic corruscations, acted upon by the atmosphere, which is composed of oxyhydrogen gas, pyroligneous acid, lirocone malachite, sulphuric ether, and a small quantity of bi-carbonate of proto-chloride of phosphorous." "Yes, that is so," said the old chap. "Very well, then. At the bottom of your brass cup where the metal sphere is located, is there a sub-division of the different elements composing the gas ?"
_ "There is." "Then give us the sub-divisions, and their quantities
in millimares."

R - said, " I cannot give the quantities, but they are divided, I know." My brother now stepped in with a few questions of a similar nature, and by the time he again turned him over to me, the old chap was mopping great big beads of perspiration off his face, and was looking as miser- able as a seasick steamboat passenger. But I could see that he couldn't remain in that state long, and that there would soon be a reaction of some sort.

I said, "Now look here. When the gas, in rushing through the orifice of the burner, impinges upon the atmosphere, do the polarizations of the crystals form singly, in groups, or simultaneously ; and are the results directly attributable to the chemical changes occa- sioned by the chloride of sodium coalescing with the perisulphate of bismuth, and causing the nebulee of the flame to circumambiate in an opposite ratio to the force of the current?"
He said, "Good heavens, man! Give me my burner and let me go !" and, snatching it out of my hand, he made towards the door. _

As he was going I said, " Here ! Don't you think that if the atmosphere came in contact less abruptly—" Be shouted," Oh, go to the deuce, and take the atmo- sphere with you!" We had a good laugh, and then we went to the front window to look if we could see anything of the old chap. He was leaning against a blank wall about fifty yards away wiping his face with his red haudkerchiof, arid shaking his head as if talking to himself. After he had done wiping his face he pulled his burners out of his pocket and ruefully counted them, then, looking in our direction as if bethinking himself, he shoved them suddenly back into his pocket, and, with an emphatic gesture, which plainly said, "I've had enough to-day," he hurried off. nearly got into trouble with my next burner man. I was sitting reading at home one Saturday afternoon when a knock came to the door. When the door was opened I heard a voice asking if the master was at home. Though the Missis was in the house I thought it possible that the person asking the question might not know the footing we were on. and very likely meant me, so I went to the door. It was another of 'em. He at once made his business known to me, and, it being Saturday afternoon, and business finished for the day, I cordially invited him in. Now this one was what might be termed an aristocra- tic gas-burner man. He was a man of about thirty- five, and was dressed in a respectable tweed suit and brown felt hat. He had a round face, and one of those moustaches that make a fellow look as if he could say nothing but "Haw, haw." At his left side, and sup- ported by a strap over his right shoulder, he carried a satchel. .

I took him into a sitting room on the left, on account of there being nothing but a blank wall on the right. He commenced operations by removing a gas globe. Then he lighted the gas and told me to notice what a poor light it was—it was a No. 2 burner. I noticed it. He then took the burner off and put one of his on. His burner was exactly of the same make as the one he had taken off—the ordinary two-hole burner—but with this difference, that his was a number 5, the other a No His gave a famous light, and I told him so. He seemed pleased. I asked him what advantage his burner had over mine. He said anyone might see at a glance, that it had a great advantage over mine by looking at the light. I asked him if his wasn't burning mere gas than mine, and he replied promptly that it was not, not a bit more; less, in fact, if either. _

Now this was a treat. Here was a fellow ping round with the commonest burner that is made,and depending upon cheek and audacity to enable him to persuade people that it was actually something new, and superior to their own burners of the same make, and, in all pro- bability, by the same maker. I felt a kind of exultant feeling at the thought of taking the fellow down, and, after I had gently hinted that I thought his mu,t be burning more gas than mine, and he had emphatically denied it, I said," Well, now, will you agree to haveyour burner tested ?"

"Oh, certainly," he said, "with pleasure." I don't suppose he thought I had the means of making a test, but, as our sapient Corporation had, some time before, magnanimously supplied me with a gas meter free—except for a small quarterly recognition of seven- pence, and an initial fee of ten shillings—whith had a small, insignificant looking little dial on the side which faced nor'. bi nor'-east, and which said .dial .and the . . .

pointer or hand which: circulated round it indicated every foot of gas that was burnt, with a perspicuity that was wonderful at the price, I took the gas-burner man down in the cellar, where this meter was. Near the meter was a gas-bracket, which had on it a number 3 burner. I drew his attention to the size of his burner, and casually mentioned that it was a size larger than the one in the sitting-room lie seemed to be a bit surprised that I had noticed the sizes at all.

Well, to cut the matter as short as possible,. I pulled out my watch, lit the gas, and ascertained, how long it took my burner to burn a foot of gas. I forget now the length of time it took, but when it had consumed a foot, I turned off the gas and invited "ml nabs" to put his burner on, which he did. I turned the gas on again and lit it, and, oh, dear how the pointer of that dial did rollick round. It burnt a foot of gas in a trifle over half the time it took my burner to burn it. I thought now that " mi nabs" would have given up and have got out of the job quietly, but, no, he wasn t a man of that sort, "not exactually.' Ire said, " Well, now, you cannot call that a fair test, because my burner is two sizes bigger than yours. Have you a number five burner in the house, and I will back mine against yours, both for light and quantity of gas burnt?" Now he had stated, upstairs, that his number five would beat my number two, whereas a number three had beaten him hollow. I did not taunt him with this, though I could plainly see that his intention now was to "bounce" me out of the job. Pretending to try to bethink me if we had a No. 5 burner in the house I mrt over, in my mind, that, very likely, an old burner would burn a little more gas than a new one, and probably the flame would not be either so bright or symmetrical. I reasoned that he knew this arid was intending turning the tables on me. I concluded that possibly he might fail.

I said," Have you a number 4 burner ?" He said, Yes.' " Very well," I said, "I have a number 4 in the kitchen, and I will back it against yours, if that will do." "That will do for me." he said. I picked up the number 3 burner, which was lying on the stbpstone, without his seeing me, and went upstairs into the kitchen and took the burner off the bracket, putting the number 3in its place. But while I was changing the burners I said to the Missis, who was in the kitchen, "When you hear me knock a bucket over in the cellar turn this gas on, at once, and light it, and when you hear the bucket rattle again turn it off." I went down into the cellar again and gave." mi nabs" the number 4 burner. He took his number 5 off and put my number 4 in its place, and I started the meter off again. I remember that it took something over five minutes to burn a foot, but I forget the exact time. When the foot was burnt he again changed the burners, putting his own on. I then lighted it and, stepping back, kicked a bucket over that had been standing behind me all the time. I didn't seem to notice it, but kept my eye on the meter and, Great Lands! didn't the hand of that dial just polka round! It did me good to watch the face of that aristocratic gas-burner agent. I daresay my manner irritated him somewhat, for I jerked my head from him to the gas-meter in a manner which said, quite as plain as any words could have done, " What ! Eh! See that! Look at that, old chappie ! He's sailing in, isn't he? What !" He stood it until the dial indicated a half a foot burnt, then his eyes suddenly scintillating streaks of blue and red fire, he said, "I don't know what the deuce I came down here wasting my time for !" and he turned out the light and whipped his burner off. I picked up the bucket I had knocked over and set it on its feet and followed " ini nabs"—who was "chunnering" all the way up the cellar steps. He could hear me chuckling all the way, and I think it aggravated him. When I let him out I stood holding the vestibule door, watching him. As soon as he had got out at the front door and on to the large, square top step of the four that lead up to the front door, he coolly, and aristocratically turned half way round, and, with a sneer on his face, which was intens:fied by his noble moustache, he said, "You think you're a smart bloke, don't you 2" I said, "Just about smart enough for a muff like you.,, Yes," he said, "if you were to travel with that infernal meter of yours you'd make a name, you would.' "I said, "Yes, it rather knocked spots off you, did that meter, didn't it ?" "Yes, you—! and if I had you in a quiet place I would knock spots off you, and —" That was enough for me. I made a dash for him He saw me coming and turned to flee, but he was just too late, for the toe of my boot came in contact with the softest part of his anatomy and sent him flying down the garden path at a speed that didn't allow him tin-te to find the steps at the gate. He had to jump off the garden wall to the sidewalk, which was something like rive feet down. He fell on the Sidewalk, but he was up again like an india-rubber ball, and then he proceeded to give me a specimen of anathematisation that gave me a bad taste in my mouth for a month. I made another dash for him, but he fled.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

SATURDAL—Before Alderman Burgess. A SPIXEE : SECOND DAY. Thomas Mulcrease, plas- terer, Liverpool, who was fined for drunkenness on the previous day, was brought up again for a similar offence, and was fined 5s and costs. _

MONDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Alder- men Davies, Harrison, and Holmes ; Councillors Platt and Francomb ; Major Litton and Dr. Gornall. DRUNKENNESS.—The following cases were disposed of: —James Tarpey, in the Market-prate, on Saturday night, fined 5s amd costs • Mary Ann Tarpy, at the same time and place, and also assaulting P.C. Bell, fined lOs and costs ; Patrick Egan, in Buttermarket-st., on Satur- day night, fined 5s and costs; Bridget Sankey, on Warrington Bridge, on the 28th Ahgust, fined ss, includ- ing costs; John Murphy, in Mersey-st., on the 25th August, fined ss, including costs; Edward Wilkinson, in Hay-dock-st., on the 28th August, fined ss, including costs; Martha Ellen Dickson, in Church-st., on the , 26th August, fined 5s and costs ; William Shackleton. in Golden Grove-st., on the 28th August, fined s#, in- cluding costs; William Plinston, in Buttermarket-st., on the 26th August, fined ss, including costs ; Annie Par- tington, in Winwick-road, on the 24th August, fined ss, including costs ; William Caskey, in Wash-lane, on the 25th August, fined 5s and costs. A DISORDERLY PAUPER. Catherine Dogherty was charged with having been guilty of disorderly conduct in the Warrington Workhouse oil the previous day. Mr. B. Shearer, relieving officer said that those women in the workhouse who had children at the Padgate Indus- trial Schools, were allowed to Visit them once in three months. On the last occasion, however, that prisoner, who had a son in the schools, went to see him, she did not return, but was apprehended and brought back to the workhouse, where she was guilty of disorderly con- duct. This time, therefore she was told she would not be allowed to go, but that her son would come to see her. On hearing this she became very disorderly and broke a window.—Defendant was sent to gaol for a month with hard labour.

SLEEPING OUT.—Mary Swift, St. Helens, was sent to gaol for seven days for sleeping in an outhouse in Chrime's-yard, on Saturday night. ABSENT FROM TRAINING.—James Henry Brown was fined 40s and costs, or seven days' imprisonment, for having been absent from the training of the 4th Lanca- shire Militia, in April last.

FRODSHAM HABITATION OF THE PRIMROSE LEAGUE. GARDEN PARTY AT FOX lIILL. At the invitation of Mr. James Reynolds, J.P., the ruling councillor, the members of the Frodsham, Helsby, and Alvanley Habitation of the Primrose League (No. 1662) field a garden party in the charm- ing grounds of that gentleman's residence at Fox Hill on Saturday afternoon. Fortunately an un- promising morning gave place to a bright and genial atmosphere in the afternoon, and there were about 400 persons present. With the exception of Ellison's string band no amusements were provided, and in fact were not needed, as the visitors found pleasure and delight in rambling amid their beauti- ful and picturesque surroundings. In the course of the afternoon a knife and fork tea was provided in a spacious marquee,and the following ladies presided at the tables :—Mrs Thomas, Mrs Hutchings, Mrs Barff, Mrs A Ashworth, Mrs Dimsford, Mrs Watson, Mrs Hol- land, Mrs Jolley, Mrs H Reynolds, Mrs Collinson, Mrs S Davies, Mrs Tiley, Mrs Illidge, Mrs McWaters ; Miss M E Leech, Miss Alice Green, Miss Fletcher, Miss Bate, Miss Elizabeth Forster, Miss Rigby, Miss K Rigby, Miss Layeock, Miss Davies. Afterwards, a meeting was held under the presidency of the Ruling Councillor, who was supported by Mr. H. Tollernache, M.P. for the Division; Colonel Ashton and Mrs. Ashton. (hon. sec.), Lieutenant Ashton, Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., Mr. J. W. D. Barron (Hyde), Mr. and Mrs. Collinson, Mr. and Mrs. John Weston (agent to the Weston section of the Ship Canal), Mrs. lienry Reynolds, &c. Mr. Tollemache, referring to the political aspect of affairs in Cheshire, said what mine their Ra Beal friends were going to spring upon them he did not know, but he saw in a Chester Radical paper a letter from an elector, who said the Liberals were very anxious to have an elec- tion because they had got a better candidate than Mr. Irwell. (Laughter.) He did not wish to say any more about that gentleman than this, that he ran him more closely than he cMr. Tollemache) liked, and more closely than Mr. Tomkinson did on two occasions. Therefore when he read that letter, he could not make out who the candidate was likely to be He did not know whether they had even persuaded the old gentleman to leave Hawarden and the delights of Midlothian to come down to Cheshire. He (the speaker) dared say that they might have found out that Mr. Gladstone had really been born in Cheshire—(laughter)--and that he looked upon Cheshire with an affection that he did not feel towards any other portion of her Majesty's do- minions. He was quite at a loss to think who the Liberals nad got until he saw a report of a ceremony which took place at Willington Hall, the seat of their good friend Mr. Tomkinson. He had been entertaining the Liberal Association, and there Was the inevitable speech from Mr. and Mrs Tomkinson, and there were many delights, including the presence of the popular member for the Northwtch Division, Mr. Brunner, who drove up in an open carriage (Laughter.) Mr. Brun- ner urged those who had got votes to return Mr. Tomkin- son at the head of the poll at the next election, so that this better candidate than Mr. Irwell was no one else than their good friend and opponent Mr. Tomkinson. If the Liberal electors chose Mr. Tomkin- son as their candidate, the Conservatives at any rate would have the satisfaction of knowing and respecting and liking the gentleman with whom he (Mr. Tolle- mache) had to fight. (Applause.) Referring to Ireland, the speaker contended that any- man, whether he was a pure souled patriot like Mr. Dillon, who wore broad cloth and was in prosperous circumstances, or a poor man who robbed a farmer's yard—any man who broke the laws of his country should he made to suffer for so doing. (Applause). Mr..Tollemache then left the meeting. The Chairman said the Primrose League in Frodsham was of recent origin, and one of rapid growth. The in- crease had been continuous, and the membership now numbered 470. Throughout the country there were 700,000 members of the Primrose League, which had been established but a very few years, and this was a correct sign that the thing must be right. Did the mean to toll him that 700,000 people•would beguiled am deluded. No, not if they were English men and English women He moved the following resolution—" That this Habitation of the Primrose League desires to express its entire confidence in the present Government, and ap- preciation of the means by which it has secured proce- dure in Parliament, of the course it has taken with res- pect to Ireland, and of the general legislation of the -country." As a commercial man he said that for 15 years he had not seen trade so prosperous as it was at the pre- sent time in every branch of commerce: Why was that? Because people were satisfied that the Government was one that would do right, and they invested their money because they knew there was no sudden revolution to take it away. (Applause.) Mr. J. Weston seconded the motion, which was sup- ported by Mr. Barron, and carried unanimously. On the proposition of Mr. R. Rogers, seconded by Col. Ashton, Mr. Reynolds was cordially thanked for his kindness that afternoon, and the proceedings then con- cluded.

CRUEL TREATMENT OF A HonsE.—Alfred Starkey was summoned for illtreating a horse on the 24th August. P.C. Corbett said he saw defendant strike the animal across the legs with a whip stock, bringing it to its knees. Defendant was fined 5s 6d and costs. A NEwsnoY FINED.—John Taylor, a newsboy, was fined Is, including costs, for cauzing a breach of the peace by shouting papers in the street. ANOTHER CHANCE. Two girls, named Mary Ann Smith and Maryßurke, weresummoned for having fought in Horsemarket-st, on the 25th August. Inspector Cox said that defendants did not belong to Warrington. The Chairman said that if the girls had not lost their charac- ters they would have made good domestic servants. They would be discharged to give them another chance. Funious DRlVlNG.—Charles McGuire (15) was fined 4s for having furiously driven a horse in Church-st., on the 26th August. BYE-LAW OFFENCES.—Sarah Maxwell was fined Is for obstructing the footway in Milner-st. by wheeling a coal' truck thereon.—William Savory, newsagent, Church-st., was fined 2s 6d for obstructing the footway in Church- st. with advertising boards, on the 30th August.—Eliza- beth Woods and Phcebe Marrott were summoned tor ob- structing Porter-st., by hanging clothes lines across the same. The case was adjourned for a week, in order that inquiries might be made. Sumo'. ArrEND.uscis CASEL—The following cases were brought forward under the Education Act, Mr. George Riley prosecuting on behalf of the School Attendance Committee: Mary Mercer, wife of Joseph Mercer, clerk, was summoned in respect of three children; the Bench adjourned the case for a fortnight, observing that if the defendant did not send the children to school she would either be fined or have to go to gaol. The son of Joseph Smith, joiner, Admiral-st., being proved to be beyond parental control, the Bench committed him to the train- ing ship Clio for four years —Peter Tatlock, carter, Cockhedge, fined ss; Frank Conway, labourer, Bank-st., fined ss; John Lingley, baker, Jackson's-row, fined ss; John Tickle, railway employe, Aikin-st., fined 5s ; Edward Lowe, forgeman, Foundry-st., fined Se; Ann Costelloe, Ship-yard, fined IN, two cases; William Peel, foreman, Oliver-st., fined 10s., two eases; John Sankey, miller, Blackhurst-St., fined 23 6d; and William Quinn, labourer, Bank-st., fined 2s 6d. WEDNFSDAY.—Before Messrs John Fairclough and Robert Garnett.

DRIINKENNESS.—For having been drunk and disorder- ly, on Friars' Green, on the previous afternoon, Mary Mason, who had only returned from prison on Saturday, was fined lOs and costs, or, in default. 14 days' impri- sonment.—John Culkeen, charged with having been drunk and disorderly, in Palmyra Square, on Thesday evening, was discharged on promising to sign the pledge.

THIMSDAY.—Before Major Litton. IlEGGIN6.—James Shaw, for begging in Horsernarket- st., on the evening previous, was sent to prison forseven days. DRUNICENNESS.—DanieI Crosby was sent to prison for seven days for this offence. It was his 60th appear- ance.

FRIDAY.—Bef ore Aldermen Harrison and Holmes, and Dr Gornall. DRIINKENNESS.—For being drunk and disorderly in Arpley-road, on the previous day, John McKenzie, labourer, was fined 5s and costs. A WIFE BEATER.—Feter Farrel was charged with hav- ing assaulted his wife Bridget Farrel, on the sth inst. Prisoner denied the offence, and the prosecutrix admit- ted having "called him for all the scamps she could," bnause he would not give her money for iimu TI • Chairman said that he was not surprised that she should use strong language to him. As there were other con- victions against the prisoner he was fined lOs and costs, or in default a month's imprisonment.

LODOINGS.—WaIter Whitley, a youth, for hav- ing been staying in the Market-place under suspicious circumstances, on Thursday evening, was committed toprpoisoinsofliouamsa pontßhosc ,wiitunN hhoarsd.Lasboalur. Lo ei Havert, Mor- ris's-yard, Silver-st., was fined 103 and costs for having kept lodgers without a license. Mr. Norman, nuisance inspector, said that the house, which was adapted for six lodgers, contained nine, and he asked the Bench to assist in putting down the practice, which was on the in. Thomason, for a similar offence on the sth September, was fined a similar amount.—lames Scully, for having on the same date kept five lodgers in an unregistered house, was also fined 10s and costs.— William Wright, for the same offence on the 4th Septem- ber, in her house, which was only adapted for four, was fined 2s ed and costs.—John Smiler admitted a similani offence, on the 4th September, there being in the house an excess of three persons. RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. YON TYRANT AT HOOAM. Hey, aw'm weary as weary con be, An' eawt o' consate wi' misel' ; Wod a quare do this is—Dear o' me! Mi troubles ther's nobry con tell. Aw'm tyrannised o'er wi' you lad, An' aykin' i' every limb, Thro' tryin' to suit, an' t' wife too, hoes as bad, It's useless—ther's nowt as suits him! ' He's a tyrant, an' wastrel beside, He's melted mi payshunce like wax, When he skrikes aw con herdly abide, It pricks i' mi earhoyles like tacks. He'll hew wod he wants—his own way— An' do as he likes wi' us ; At midneets he's woos than a cat-fret tened jay, An' wakkens ot' nebburs th' row. Tawkin's useless; he ne'er teks no heed, So whether yo' praise him or blame; An' his ways welly tnek mi heart bleed. It's nowt but a scandalous shame To watch heaw he mauls wi' thad cat, An' chucks id abeawt wi' id tail, Or empties th' ink bottle o'er t' wife's Sunda' brat, Or mops among t' suds wi' her vayl. He's o sooarts o' auare monkeyfted tricks; He squeezes between t' spQoakes o' t' cheers, An' roaks t' drawers wi hard mortar an' bricks; His cloorts, too, i' tatters be tears. He trill chew at cinders an' coy', An' ged under t' boyler 'mong t' soot, An' iv tiler's a hit o' nast getten th' hoyl, He'll spreyd id o'l o'er wi' his foot. He's a habit o' cmwlin' to th' suff, An' tillin' id up wi' eawr knives, Spoons, and forks; an' cause thad worn'd enuff T'other day he took t' locket o' t'wife's, An' dropt Mad t' suff, too, wi' id cheon ; Then skreet because t' playthings wur done. Aw raylee believe as thad rascal's so moon He'll be killin' us soon, just for fun. He will be i' some mischief, that's true, If ther's onny at o to ged in. Heaw he likes to mix traycle wi' blue, An' poke up his nooase wi' a pin! He's fost class at dissectin' a book, Or rivin' a papper 41,1. bits, An' iv he's disturbed we a smack, or rebuke, Then—he'll skrike 'Asset welly i' fits! Aw kornd tell yo' one-hawf ow his ways. l'th' midden he puts mi best shoon ; Aw'm expectin' o' some o' these days Findin' t' windo' planrs rammed into th' oon. Heat the cobst scamp qv onny aw've known, Considerin' his wonderful age, For when next Sprin g's bonny primrooases are shown He'll ha' bin just two year o' life's stage. Neaw, aw've moythered miser a good bit, An' thowt wur aw ever as bad; Because aw've bin peyled.poo'd an' hit, An' trampled on, too, wi' you lad. But hell awter for t' better, aw know, When Time's led him eawt among men, An' no deawt we'st hew quateness an' comfort i't' row— For it's wanted—a while afooar then. • JACK 0' ANN'S.

div.head: CHAPTER IX. VALENTINE DURAND.
div.p: CHAPTER IX. VALENTINE DURAND.

About five o'clock that afternoon the shadows were lengthening in one of the narrower streets, picturesque with its stalls of street-sellers, and resounding with the clatter of tongues, and the stir of life from a con- tinual stream of hard-working men and women. Some of them were passing through to the larger thoroughfares, and others returning already from their places of business, and marketing for rolls and bread, garlic, cabbages, and other provisions of the cheap and simple sort, for their frugal evening and morning meals. The vehicles in this street were comparatively few, the shops small and dirty, the handles of the doors rust eaten, the shutters gaping from their hinges, the windows difficult to open and cobwebby. Still there was about it an aroma of departed magnifi- cence, not to say an old-world air of antique and scholarly civilisation which enabled it to hold its own, thanks to its archaeological interest, with the more pretentious and Babylonian splendour of the newer streets which had risen in Paris during the days of the second Empire. The staircases were dilapidated, but had once been handsomely carved—the carvings ' in most places having been carted away for money ; the masonry was still solid, and a few of the window were still ornamented with rickety-looking balconies which no one dared approach, leaving them to be rusted and dirt-begrimed. Some of the houses had to be propped, their cor- rugated roofs leaning suspiciously forward and darkening the-windows beneath like bushy eye-brows over eyes which years had dimmed; and their doors closing with a sulky click and opening with difficulty. These last were under Government surveillance, having to be rebuilt by degrees. The few inhabitants who remained in them were every now and then sub- ject to the same inspection from a " paternal " Government as if they were thrown into the lot and taken as a part of the bargain. Meanwhile the rooms were let at an exceptionally low rent. In one of these apartments on a mattress on the floor, propped up on a square piece of deal which had once done duty as a kitchen table, and from which the legs had been sawn away, to protect the mattress from the possible depredations of rats, an old man was lying, writhinv alternately with the pains of rheumatism and the pangsof hunger, cursing as he writhed.

Beside the bed stood a smaller table, littered with pieces of lace, fragments of coloured muslin, a pair of scissors, a few needles and reels of cotton, and a couple of broken chairs. The fireplace had once been handsome, but the fire was nearly out, and the invalid had made futile attempts to get to it to make it up, or to use the cooking utensils to warm some water for himself. There was nothing else for him to warm. The milk ,had been exhausted hours before. A little bread was in the cupboard at the other side of the room, but to walk across the room even with the aid of crutches and the assistance of another person was a feat difficult to accomplish, so numerous were the holes in the flooring, and so likely was it for a cripple to stumble into one of these man-traps, from which it would he difficult for him to extricate himself. He swore, partly because there was nothing else for him to do, and the time had been hanging , heavily all that day, partly because he was agonised with bodily pain, and partly because his heart was being consumed as with inward fire. There was nothing to ease this inward fire—none of the pleasant memories of earlier years, with which so many of the old ones comfort themselves; and none of those hopes for the future with which sonic of his Catholic neighbours could soothe themselves. There had been a crucifix occr the mattress which was dignified by the name of a bed as long as his wife had lived. But the idol, as he called it, had been taken down when the old woman, who had helped him for so many a day with a vendor's stall, which stood for years in front of the Church of St. Medard, had died in the hospital, whence even her body had not been restored to him for interment, because he had not sufficient money to bury it. It did not much matter. Long before the faithful creature's death Pierre Laroche's last vague hope of a good time coming to him had been taken away leaving hini blind and desperate, and subject to sudden fits of fury, like a beast of prey. His wife's fate had been but the natural fate of the poor, who, when they have worked and starved and suffered to the utmost to satisfy the tyranny of their rich oppressors during their little spice of "life's fever," returned again to their dust. Their bodies were mere machines of carbon and hydrogen, their sick and suffering souls were delusions and not realities. Long ago Pierre Laroche had been de- luded by this talk. No one welcomed the idea of the expulsion of the Jesuits with greater enthusiasm than he did. Time was when he had known better quarters, when he had read his newspapers, taken part in politics, and talked grandly of the advent of the Re- publie. Only lately had he accused himself of being seduced by high-sounding words and great expecta- tion respecting the reign of "the people." He had talked grandly of the "theories of tyrants," and the delusions of priestcraft. But "the people" did not seem to do so much for him as he had I expected. He grumbled at the small amount of help given to him by the organisation called "the Public Assistance," and shore at the inter- ference of livened officials who came every now and then to make entries in a book with regard to the state of the house, but did not mend the holes in the floor. Liberty and fraternity had been high-sounding watchwords, but in his jaundiced moments Laroche felt as keenly as ever how cruel it was for the un- seen forces of the world to be stronger than the "people." The old difficulty remained of grappling with the tyranny of property, and the grinding poverty by which thousands as miserable as himself were reduced to a condition to which death would be preferable. It was a jaundiced moment, now—the old man's head was hot, his tongue was parched, his veins were burning; when he did not curse he relieved his feelings by knocking on the floor with a rough-knobbed stick, convenient for annoying his neighbours. For hours he had knocked like this, and no one had answered the summons till at last there was the patter of light footsteps on the stairs, and a girl, neatly dressed in the white cap and coloured petticoat suitable to her class, pushed open the creaking door with the deftness of one long used to its infirmities. "Grandfather," she said, going straight to the dying embers of the fire, and busying herself with re- storing the flame, as she rapidly 'gave her explana- tion, " I could not help being late. We had to work for extra hours." "And you expect me to believe that. It is for you, all the fetes of life, the Dimanches, the things that are amusing. And while you are holiday keeping you leave me to starve." The girl looked up from her kneeling position, by the fire. Here was a striking face. But the brilliant eye with the sallow complexion, the small mouth, and the narrow chin, told the story of a hard life, with too much work and too little sleep, and not much time left for dissipation. There was no sign of degradation in the young face as yet. "I could not refuse the four sous for extra work —it is little enough I get—even at artificial flower- making," she answered, simply enough. An expression of greed distorted the old man's features. He held out his skinny fingers, crippled into the semblance of claws by rheumatic disease. " An-i you have spent it on ribbons—on frills for your new cap." "No, I have not, but we want it for bread. I could not give it to you; it would go for the opium smoking." This was an old bone of contention between them, and Pierre Laroche burst into a torrent of abusive
and ,

lang,uage. • • And you leave me here to die while you are bent on your pleasures. I am chained like a dog to my kennel, and you—you care nothing for my sufferings. One day you. will come home and find me burnt to death in trying to cook my own food, or I shall be dead of starvation, and you will care nothing for it." She took no notice of his accusations, but busied herself in clearing the needlework from the table, setting out the roll of bread and the pint of milk which she had brought home with her, and after- wards in tidying the little bedroom, scarcely larger than a closet, in which she slept herself. She knew how useless it would be to urge him even to take food while the present fit of " rabid " Is as on him. Suffer- ing people, as she said to herself, must indulge them- selves with tempers. She had a calm indifferent way of meeting Laroche's reproaches; but, as lie indulged in stronger superlatives, adding, "It would be easy enough for y3u to snake away with me—none would be any the wiser," she Slashed with sudden pain, and clasped her arms round his neck. "Grandfather—oh, grandfather," drawing the grog

hairs and the wrinkled face to her tender bosorni "you know that I am not ungrateful." The chill barrier was broken down. Victor Hugo, in his " Legende des Siecles," tells the fable of selfish and dissolute soul summoned before the judg- ment seat to hear the sentence passed on an ill-spent life. Before the verdict is irrevocably given, he is challenged to relate one act of kindness performe4 in his period of probation on earth. A deed of mercY is accorded to a suffering pig, and for this one act of f. human kindness his sentence is remitted. Pierre Laroche had also one tender spot in his heart, one softening recollection of a deserted child whom he had suffered his childless wife to take to her heart. Valentine Durand was the one living thing for whom lie cherished a spark of affection, and as she kissed him with quivering lips, her tears falling on his distorted hands, the hard lines round his toothless mouth relaxed, his glassy eyes became more clear. He watched the little one, whom he yet loved, with admiring glances, as she drew the table nearer to his bed; warmed the milk, and broke the bread in RI feeding him as if he had been a child. Then the greed which which 1164 distorted his features suddenly frightened

her again. "Monsieur St. Beven has been here again," he sad; denly blurted out, "talking of your pretty face. The girl shivered and averted her eyes. "Oh, grandfather," she said; yet at that moment she was glad he was not really her grandfather. "Work, work I " he continued, vaguely, ,412 or ;) 16 hours out of the 24 that the ladies might have flower gardens on their heads—your's is a good deal prettier—and how do they pay you? Little enough, I isn't it —a few miserable sous a day, when 4. ; you are only short of funds, you have but to up your little finge,r. And why shouldn't some of the pretty things fall to your share in life? WI 3 shouldn't we be fed on dainties ?" asked the o , man, smackirrg his lips. " Why should You be frightened by the bogies which the priests dress' . up for you? Who can tell what is good or what is evil? They invent all that about purgatory to 1 terrify cowardly women—they want to keep down, and to deprive us of the present life—and the present is all we've got. Dressed like a lady yon ' ought to be—proper shoos and neat gloves, like the ladies wear. And you who can get anything you want forthe asking. What's the good of the doctors ordering me medicines when we have to live on prison diet?, for a paltry prejudice which Louise Michel----- She sternly waved him into silence. The tirade against the marriage laws which he had once take° her to hear had made no impression on her. wasted time with his words. His mouth grew a trill dry again,and he shifted his position, overcome by all inclination to sleep, which was the reaction from the violent passions with which he had exhausted his feeble flame. He dreamt of cheques which Valentiq brought hint and which he was allowed hiineell to fin up; of champagne and turtle soup, eiderdol quilts, cigars, and, best of all, an unlimited supplY °l* opium. Valentine waited till his breathirr, became regular' and then drawing a deep breath', she threw on a cloak with a little hood, which she drew careful over her head. e "I did not tell him I meant to marry a gentleman, 'i. littli imile which dimpled tbe

she said, with a little corners of her pretty mouth as she glanoed aII note which she drew out of her pocket. f.he "Meet me to-night at eight o'clock near church of St. Medard's. I have something urgent "'" tell you." She crept down the stairs with a stealthy steP' walking quickly as soon as she left the house. ao On a piece of neglected open ground such the members of the Kyrle Society are UP': to ornament with flowers in London,iltlf mond met her at the appointed traie. the abodes of the dead as well as the livingtheysiv° b as they had sworn before eternal fidelity to e!'cr, other: "You will see other fine ladies, you will get me," she sobbed. FM answer he took a ring off his little finger—it belonged to his mother—and fitted it on hers. Ansoi theu as if to clench the engagement with se° tional incident°, the lad took a penknife from pocket, deliberately cuttino one of his fingers till • =7, blood flowed, and signing with pen on paper— "l swear .by all this loly as soon as I am 011 to make Valentine Durand my wife. May I (lie early death, and may ill pursue me to my grave fail to fulfil my oath.

TIIE UNITED STATES AND CANADA: THE , PRELUDES TO WAR. It will be well for the President and Government of the United States to remember, remarks the Staniard, that Canada is a dependency of the British Govern- tent, and that if the necessity should unfortunately arise she has behind her the gnus of the English iron- clad& If our American cousins fail to understand this allusion, if—in deference to the tone of coarse bru- tality which seems to be the distinguishing feature of their domestic politics—they invite us to rc.ply to their insults and to their invectives in a strai, they will comprehend, perhaps we may be allow “ recall to their recollection the affair of the Trent, in which the "British lion" by no means came off second best. The indignation that has been aroused in Canada by the extraordinary proposals of President Cleveland to the United States Legislature ought surely to induce that body, before it is too late, to save the American People from one of the severest reproaches that can be addressed to a nation. If we have to deal with a nation of filibusters let us at least know it. But it is as manifest as the sun at noonday that President Cleveland, in the tone he has adopted towards Canada, II animated simply by the desire to outmanceuvre his Political opponents, and to secure for himself and the Party of which be is at present the head a renewal of the presidential term of power. /ism YORE, MONDAY NIGHT.—The New York Evening Post makes the following remarks upon the leading article in the Standard of this morning:—"The word 'filibuster' has a definite meaning, as the Standard knows; it signifies one who seeks to possess himself of his neighbour's territory by violence. It is amazing that the chief Tory organ can ascribe such a character to a country that has repeatedly refused foreign terri- tory offered to it in the way of peaceful negotiation. So far as Canada is concerned, we venture to say nobody ever thinks of annexing by force the smallest scrap of her 'territory. But if the Standard is a bad interpreter Of our intentions•it ought not to be se of our intelligence. If there was any lurking purpose of filibustering among us it would be first discovered in the adaptation of toeans to ends. We should make preparation commen- surate with our means and with the end we had in view." Several journals discuss the readiness of the united States for war, not with a view to attack, but 'defence and their unanimous conclusion is that the 'united states are at the mercy of any naval Power. WASHINGTON, Mc:IN-am—ln the Senate to-day Mr. 'lliddleberger, of Virginia, called attention to an article 'in a London morning paper respecting the Reprisals Bill, in which it was said that behind Canada were the guns of the English ironclads. Commenting on this the Senator said," We have men behind our guns, and not liasvpsL"
O'rTAWA, TUESDAY.

In connection with the fisheries dispute Her Majesty's •ship Caroline has been ordered to San Juan to make a survey of the defences of the Straits of Fuca% which form part of the British and United States boundary line.

OTTAWA, WEDNESDAY. On surveying the Lake St. Clair Canal yesterday it Was proved that the canal is in British territory. The stars and stripes were hauled down, and the union-jack sent up by the British settlers on the completion of the canal. THE ITALIAN DEFEAT NEAR MASSOWAH. The official report on the disaster to Italian arms at Sagauerte has been issued. The force charged with the duty of driving out Debfib consisted of 600 Bashi- Razouks; under the command of Captain Coruacchia, who had the assistance of four other Italian officers. A carefully pi-roared plan had been laid down for the con- duct of this difficult operation, and it is believed that success would have crowned the movement but for the treachery of some of the pretended allies of the Italians.' As all the Italian officers were slain, the accounts of the fight are very confusing. it seems, however, that Debeb's' Fort was gallaixtiv attacked, hut that an over- whelming force of Abyssinians cut off the retreat of the Italian levies, a great part of whom were slain or taken Prisoners. It is urged that if the expedition had been carried out according to orders it tnust either have been entirely succeSsful,•orif unsuccessful, bloodless, so far as the attacking force was concerned. DREADFUL TRAGEDY BY A SOLDIER. ST.•PITERSIRTRG, SuNDAY IVIonT.—A dreadful tragedy lately occurred at Ardahan. One of the soldiers of the Pialognrsk- reeiment stationed there, a Pole by origin, was sentenced by his commander to be beaten with rods for an offence against the military regulations. As his comrades werg, preparing to carry out this punishment, which is now contrary to the Russian law, the in- furiated soldier snatched a knife out of his pocket and stabbed the soldiers severely rigtkt, and left. Three Of them were wounded, and the remainder being Without weapons took to flight. The Polish ! soldier then rushed to a tent, and seized two Government rifles and fired with one on his commanding officer. 'Fortunately the rifle was loaded with blank cartridge, and thus no harm was done. The soldier, quite infuriated, commenced to' break the rifle. Whilst busy doing this, another officer approached him and tried to bring the man to reason. The soldier, instead of listening to this officer, instantly levelled the other rifle and firedi mortally wounding, the officer. On hearing the report another officer came running up to the place. Seeing his comrade weltering in his blood, and the sol- dier preparing to fire at him, he gave orders to some of the soldiers who had assembled- on the spot to fire at the soldier. This they did, and a bullet soon terminated the unfortunate man's existence. EXCITING SCENE IN 'A MENAGERIE. PARIS, MONDAY.--An, exciting scene took place last nightin the Pezon Menagerie, now exhibiting at the fair in the Avenue des Gobelins. During the performance Edmond Pezon, a nephew of the celebrated tamer, was Putting a black lion thr.ugh sundry performances, when the animal—a new acquisition brought from London, and which had proved untractable from the beginning —pounced upon him and struck him with its paw. Edmond Rezon, who is 25 years of age, and of wonder- ful agility, was quick enough to start back. Never- theless he got scratched on the cheek, and his right wrist was rather badly lacerated. Seizing a pitchfork, he thrust the prong in the lion's mouth and nose, and drove it back until he reached the door, when he made his escape, REPORTED REVOLT IN AFGHANISTAN. ST. PETEIsSI3IOIO3, THIIRSDAY.—The " Novoe Vremya " to-day publishes a report that the whole of Northern Afghanistan has revolted froin the authority of Abdur- rahman and has ackowledged Ishak 'Khan as Ameer. It is added that a conflict has occurred between the in- surgent troops and Abdurrahman's forces, but the result of the engagement is- not known.

THE WHITECHAPEL TRAGEDY. -- ANOTRER. DESPERATE OUTRAGE.—SUPPOSED CLUE. On Saturday afternoon. Wm. Nicholls, husband of the woman who was found lying dead and fearfully muti- lated in Buck's-row, Baker's-row, Whitechapel, early on Friday morning, was conducted from his residence at 37, Coburg-road, Old Kent-road, to the mortuary, where he recognised the body of the murdered woman as being that of his wife. The son, who resides with his grand- father at 15, Maidwell-street, Albany-street, Camber- well, also identified the remains el his mother. This removed all further doubt as to the deceased be- ing Mary Ann Nicholls. It has been ascertained that the unfortunate woman was one of th^.e who last year were in the habit of sleeping in Tn otar-square, and when a clearance of the nightly visitors was made, it being found that she was destitute and had no means of subsistence, she was admitted as an inmate to the Lambeth Workhouse. After her discharge from the workhouse and subsequent disappearance from service at Wandsworth, little was known of her whereabouts by her relations. Lately it seems that she had been lodging in a common lodging-house in Thrawle-street, Spital- fields, leading an immoral life, and known by her female acquaintances as "Folly." It was first sup- posed that the crime had been committed by a maniac: but this opinion has been abandoned, likewise the belief that the woman was lured into a house in the vicinity and murdered, the body being afterwards re- moved. The conclusion now arrived at is that the woman met with her dreadful fate where her body was found. What were at first supposed to have been pools of blood for some distance upon the pavement cannot be relied upon as such, owing to the darkness of the stains. That the lower portions of her clothes were not stained with blood is due to the fact that the three dreadful wounds in the abdomen, believed to have been the first inflicted, had bled inwardly. Their nature, too, was such as to have prevented a removal of the body in the state in which it was found. Although a small pool of blood was found near the head, still the ' greater part from the throat had trickled down the neck and saturated her under garments. Another theory is that from the moment the woman was last seen till the discovery of her body by the police constable sufficient time would not have elapsed to have admitted of the murder taking place in a house and the dragging of the body to a distance. The police have obtained no definite clue to the author of the ghastly crime, but are using every available means in their power to obtain a trace of the murderer, and bring the criminal to justice. In- spector Helson, as well as Inspector Aberline, Sergeant Godley, and Sergeant Enright. experts from the Criminal Investigation Department, have the case in hand, and are of opinion that there is some connection between this and the other two murders which have taken placein the , same locality. A house-to-house inyestigation and Inquiry has been made in all the streets adjoining Buck's-row,'but with no tangible result. The assumption is that the brutal crime was committed by one of a High Rip" gang, who are known in the neighbourhood to be in the habit of blackmailing unfortunate women, and treating them in a brutal manner. The names of some of this hand of roughs are known to the detective officers, who, it is,stated, are empowered by the Chief Commissioner to give money payments for confidential information which may lead to the discovery of the actual perpetra- tor of the murder. Considerable consternation and horror prevail in the neighbourhood of the three succes- sive murders, and there is a general demand, for further police protection and supervision. The Central News says: Another desperate assault, which stopped only just short of murder, was committed on a woman in Whitechapel on Saturday night. The , victim was leaving the Foresters' Music Hall, Cambridge Heath-road, where she had been spending the evening, when she was accosted by a well-dressed man, Who I asked her to accompany him. She invited him to go to her apartments, and he acquiesced. requesting her in the meantime to walk a short distance with him as 'he wanted to meet a friend. They had reached a point , near the scene of the murder of the woman Nicholls, when the man violently seized his companion by the throat and dragged her down a court. He was imme- diately joined by a gang of women a.nd bulliesowho stripped the unfortunate woman of her 'necklace, ear- rings, and brooch. Her purse was also taken, and she as brutally assaulted. Upon attempting to shout for aid, one of the gang laid a large knife,across her throat, remarking, "We will serve von as we did the others." The was eventually released. The police have been in- formed, and are prosecuting inquiries into the matter, it being regarded as a probable •clue to the previous tragedies. THE INtaTiEgT. The inquest was opened on Monday on the bedy of Mary Ann Nichols, who was found murdered on Friday morning, in Buck's-row. Inspector Spratling, of the J division. said that at 4 30 a.m. on Friday, when in Haekneyetoad, he 'received in- formation of the finding of the body. He went to the mortuary, in company with a constable. Witness de- scribed the nature of the injuries. The Inspector was unable to describe the precise condition of the clothes at the time the body was found. It was stated to the coroner that another officer, inspector Helson, would give evidence on this point. Witness, proceeding. said that between eleven o'clock and noon he examined Bucks-row, but found no blood stains. Afterwards he examined the 'London District Railway and the embankments of the Great Eastern Railway without discovering any traces of -blood or any weapon. Witness was of opinion that thewoman was murdered in her clothes, and at the .place where the body was found. insi)ector Flelson, J Division, described the condition of the deceased's clothing, and said there were no cuts on any part of the apparel. There was nocut under the stays. • Henry Tomkin, horse slaughterer, who was working in Winthrop-street, adjoining Buck's-row, with two eompanions, said they heard no suspicious noises during the night, though the gate of the slaughter-house was open. They left at about 12 20. On hearing of the murder he and the other ti,o men went to the spot. Charles Cross, carman,,Sin the employ of Messrs. Pick- ford, stated when he discovered the body on his way to work the clothes were above the knees. From the position of the body he formed the impression that the woman had been. outraged. William Nichols said the deceased was his wife. She left him about seven years ago, and was given to drink. He believed she had been living with various men. Ellen Holland stated that she knew the deceased for about six weeks. She last saw her about half-past two on Friday morning last, when the deceased was the worse for drink. She was alone. Witness did not know any of deceased's acquaintances. The inquest was adjourned for a fortnight. It was stated on Tuesday night that the roliee eee. ducting the inquiries into the Whitechapel murder be- lieve they have a clue to the perpetrators of the crime, and thatsertain persons are kept under surveillance.
HOCKING TRAGEDY IN WALES.-- ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE BY A

MAGISTRATE A terrible tragedy' was enacted on Sunday morning in a fashionable suburb of Wrexham, when Mr. A. Wilson Edwards, a Justice of the Peace, attempted to murder one of his servants and afterwards shot himself. The first intimation of the grim occurrence wag given at shout seven o'clock by a female servant, who, scrainh- ling, over the spiked entrance gate to High Grove, a genteel residence overlooking the park in which the Eisteddfod pavilion has been erected, rushed along the Grove and Grosvenor roads to the residence of Dr. Davies, shouting out that her master had shot, the cook. After briefly obtaining such particulars as the horrified girl could give, Dr. Davies sent her to the County Buildings for a policeman. and Mr. Wilde, Deputy Chief-Constable, and Police-constable Roberts accompanied him to Mr. Edwards's house. Arriving there they found the front entrance gate locked. Climbing over, Mr. Wilde and Dr. Davies made their way into the house and to Mr. Edwards's bedroom, where they found that gentleman lying insensible on the floor. with a bullet wound in his right temple. Near him Mr. Wilde found a six-chambered revolver, on examining which he ascertained that, three chambers had recently been emptied, and that the other three remained loaded. Dr. Davies did what was possible for the unconscious gentleman; and Mr. Wilde, proceeding to the seavant's bedroom, discovered a woman named Mary Stevens, aged about 40, lying apparently lifeless on the floor. She was placed in bed, and efforts made to restore consciousness , with a certain amount of success: but her pain and f rigl it combined rendered her delirious, and her restlessness made it impossible for the doctor to ascertain the precise nature of the injuries. From the statement of the housemaid, ' Annie Smith, who gave the alarm, it appears that about half-past six o'clock, Mr. Edwards went into the bedroom, where she and Stevens were sleeping, carrying a revolver in his hand. Stevens sat up in bed and asked, "What's the matter, master ? " He then fired two shots at her, both of which struck her in the body. He then went• out of the room, and Smith, who had pulled the bedclothes over her head when she saw the revolver, jumped out of bed when she heard him leave. Hastily dressing herself she escaped from the house and ran for the doctor and the police. Mrb. Edwards, an elderly lady of 70, who has been ailing for some time, states that she noticed her husband enter her bedroom early in the morning with a revolver, and on her speaking to him, to her sorrow, he placed the revolver against his temple and fired, the bullet piercing the skull. No adequate cause for the tragedy seems to have existed. It is said, however, that Mr. Edwards had been much depressed lately, and had complained of money difficul- ties, which, however, were more imaginary than real. Dr. Davies states that when he saw Mr. Edwards on Saturday he seemed to have recovered from his recent depression. Mr. Edwards occupied a prominent position in the town and was highly respected by all sections of society; and the attempted murder and suicide created the utmost constereation. Be was a magistrate for the borough, a vice-chairman of the Wrexham Board of Guardians, director of the Wrexham Waterworks Com- pany and the Wrexham Gas Light Company, a member of the Free Library Committee, the Wrexham School Board,. and other Public bodies.

At the inquest on Wednesday in connection with the Wrexham tragedy a verdict was returned to the effect that Mr. Wilson Edwards shot himself and endeavoured to murder his servants while suffering from temporary
