div.head: IRELAND
div.p: IRELAND

An explosion occurred at Guinness's brewery, Dublin, on Saturday. A number of men were insured, and seven had to be conveyed to the hospital. It is expected that all will eventually recover. LORD HARTINGTON'S VISIT TO Itexterm.— The Ulster Liberal Unionists' Committee yesterday completed the preliminary arrangements in connection with the forth- coming visit of Lord flartington. The banquet to his lordship is definitely fixed for October Bth, and the meet- ing for the following night.

Miss Keegan, a young lady living at Kilkelly, counts. Galway, went out for a walk on Sunday evening, with her brother and a gentleman named Leech. Mr. Keegan was carrying a loaded gun, and Leech went behind him, and, is fun, pulled the trigger, with the'result that the entire charge lodged in the body of Miss Keegan, who if. in a dying condition. Both gentlemen are in custody. _ _ - - • -

. - The Freeman's Journar , referring to the Woodford evic- tions, says the people have practised patience to the bounds of human endurance, but we fear to contemplate the results .of so much evicting as is now taking place. The winter prospect is appalling, and, unless something be done during the autumn session to stay rackrenting and eviction it is not the Irish people who will be responsible for the consequences.

div.head: VANDELEUR EVICTIONS.
div.p: THE VANDELEUR EVICTIONS.

Several evicted tenants on the Vandeleur estate, co. Clare, have brought actions to test the validity of their eviction. One of them, Matthew Magmth, has prose- cuted criminally the sub-sheriff, Mr. Croker. and also Colonel Turner, the district magistrate, and Mr. HAI, the district inspector of constabulary, who were pro- tecting the Sheriff with a party of constabulary, charg- ing them with taking forcible possession of his holding: but the Xilkee magistrates having made no rule on the charge, counsel on his behalf applied yesterday to Mr. Justice Gibson, as vacation judge, for an order directine the magistrates to hear evidence, which, it was alleged, they had refused to do, while convicting Magrath's sou far obstructing the Sheriff. Judge Gibson directed the application to stand till Tuesday week, meantime notice to be served.

div.head: DECREASE OF CRIME,
div.p: DECREASE OF CRIME,

The report of the Irish Prisons Board, just issued, con- tains some interesting information. There has been a further reduction in expenditure of £2,790 during the past year. and of £34.000 in the past 10 years. Nine prisons and nine bridewells have been dispensed with during the year, but the disturbed condition of county Clare, in October, rendered it necessary to open a part of Ennis prison as a temporary lock-up, but the Board do not anticipate, from the condition of the country, the neces- sity for this arrangement will be of long continuance. There has been the substantial decrease of prisoners punished during the past year as compared with 1880-81 of 60 per cent., and out of a total number of 28,385 pri- soners in custody during the year. the proportion a 24,592, or 6-7ths, received no punishment. The number of prisoners punished under the Gladstonian regime in 1880-1 was 8,604, under the present Government only 3.793. The report speaks of the improved sanitary arrangements, and points out that, while the average death-rate in Ireland is 183 per 1,000, the prison average was only 5.1.
MR. BALFOUR AND THE EX-CONSTABULART MAN.

Mr. Balfour's secretary, writing to a correspondent, on Monday, comments upon a letter written by the Rev. Father O'Neill. in which the rev, gentleman charac- terises Mr. Balfour's references to Patrick Murray, the ex-constable, who travelled the country with the Home Rule Union van, as a dastardly imputation noon Murray's character. Mr. Balfour now gives some further particulars in reference to Murray. On the 20th June, last year, he was returned by the Medical Officer at Athboy as unfit for further service in the con- stabulary, on the ground that he was suffering from diseases of the brain. Murray had at that time been upon sick leave for over three months. Dr. Gordon, surgeon to the forces, subsequently certified his unfitness, and the man was accordingly dischaxgecl in August, 1887, with a gratuity of £39 17s. 4d. Mur- ray's statement that he left the force rather than takn part in evictions is, therefore, declared to be absurd. After his discharge, Murray applied for a pension, on the plea that he had acquired brain fever while on duty, and because he would have to look to an adverse public for employment This, however, under the rules of the service could not be granted. Mr. Balfour's Secretary adds: "Patrick Murray has succeeded in'obtaining em- ployment frcm an adverse public but only under false pretences." AN APPEAL TO REASON._

Mr. Michael Davitt, speaking at a proclaimed meeting, on Sunday, at Ballygarrett, in county Wexford, said he did not know that it would be any use for him to appeal to the common sense of the landlords or of the• Gover- nment with reference to the recent evictions. But he might tell the landlords that idle land grew no rent„ and he would say to Mr. Balfour that men driven out of their homes by the battering-ram of his subordinates were not turned into law-abiding citizens by seeing the law which they were called on to respect driving their parents or their children from beneath their sheltering roof. Did the landlords hope to improve their fortunes by exterminating those who made them? If they did, they were like the individual who cut off his nose to spite his face. Did they lessen the number of their enemies in Ireland or increase their admirers outside of it by carrying on this policy of extermination? He thought not, and he questioned if even amongst the ranks of Edglish Tories and Liberal Unionists an Irish landlord evictor was, politically speaking, popular. He was cer- tainly not loved more in Ireland, unless it were by ex- gaol birds and those salaried ruffians known as emer- gency men. Why, then, did they persist in carrying on this pOlicy of eviction? Possibly for vengeance. If so, it was a dangerous game to play at by a class who had been taught nothing better for the people of Ireland than a policy of extermination. In his judgment it would be far better to try and discover some rational way to a final settlement of this agrarian war, rather than to count on being rescued from ruin by the cupidity •of some of their dunes.—Resolutions were carried ex- pressing confidence in Mr. Parnell's leadership, and con- demning the evictions that had taken place in the dis- trict.—At Courtown, later in the day, an effort was made by the authorities to prevent Mr. Davitt from ad- dressing a meeting, but there was no conflict with the police.
SHOCKING MURDER NEAR BARNSLEY.
A SERVANT GIRL SHOT WY AN INNKEEPER.

On Monday, Millhouse, a hamlet about eight Miles from I,arnsley, was the scene of a deliberate murder on the. ,)art of Henry Hey, an innkeeper, who shot his domestic servant, a young woman named Maggie Hill, daughter of a working man residing at Bullhouse. Fley is a slater lw trade' and two years ago he entered upon the tenancy of the Blacksmiths' Arms, Millhouse. He of late has taken to drinking, and has led au unhappy life with his wife, who has repeatedly left him. Deceased went to Or master's bedro nn with a letter about nine .o'clock. the prisoner not having come downstairs. A IsA, years of age, son of the prisoner, soon afterwards heard the report of firearms, as did other people outside. Jos. Flardsey, schoolmaster at the Thuristone Board School, and another man, rushed upstairs. The prisoner was secured by the neighbours, who flocked into the house, end attention paid to the dying woman. Information was given to the police, and Pollee-constable Catherall 'alai two other officers arrived, and took the prisoner into custody, and conveyed him to Penistone. He was then taken to Barnsley, in custody of Inspector Caleraft and' Police-constable Catherall.

Joseph Dolor, schoolmaster at the Millhouse Board Fichool, describing what took place after he entered the bedroom, says: When we got inside a horrible spectacle met our eyes. The gun was lying on the bed, and it was picked up to prevent Her from doing any further harm. Hey VAS sitting in a chair, and the girl Hill was sitting on tile floor. Her head was resting on one ot Hey's hands, and with the other the landlOrd was holding one of her hands. Hey was trembling violently. We could st onee see the girl was very badly hurt. She was call- ing out,." Oh, dear; oh, dear," and "Lord, isave mercy." She was conscious at this time, but I believe she after- wards became unconscious. I could see that Hill had been shot in the arm, but that wound did not appear to be a very bad one. She also had a wound en the side of her abdomen. This was a very bad one. I think I could have got both my fists in the bole. Mira bowels were protruding from this. There was a large pool of blood on the floor, in which Hill was sitting. The girl was fully dressed. She said she did not want mov- ing but we thought she would be easier on the bed, and she was afterwards lifted on the bed. Hill was iii so much main that she once or twice called out. "Will no one give me something to finish me?" Just before Hill was lifted on the bed Hey kissed the girl, and said, "Oh, do forgive me," and Hill replied, "Yes, I will." To me prisoner appeared to be suffering from delirium tremens. He said, "They put a platform on the stairs, and got on it and tried to shoot me, but I wouldn't let them." When he was a little calmer he said, "I know I shall be hung. Such a thing has never happened in Millhouse before, and I know I shall be hung." Apparently getting wilder, he said, "My wife is doomed, and if you go to the window you will see they are punching my children about the streets." We told him that this was not so, and tried to calm him. I never saw the wife at all; she was never in the bed- room. Hill moaned piteously all the time I was in the room, but-she never said anything against Hey. I think it is generally believed that Hay intended to shoot his wife, and that was why she kept out of his way. Hey was brought up before the magistrates at Barnsley a few months ago for assaulting his wife, but I believe the case fell through because the wife would not prose- cute him. When his wife went away the last time she said she would come back and live with her husband if tie would send the girl Hill away. He would not do so, and I think she was away from him some few weeks. I am told her parents did not want her to come back, but she came back last Tuesday. It is well known in the village that the wife was jealous of Hill, and she has said that she had good reasons for being so. INQUEST. • • •

_ At Millhouses, Thurlstone, on Tuesday, the inquest re- lative to the death of Margaret Hill, was held; and a verdict of wilful murder returned by the coroner's jury against Henry Hey, the innkeeper, who shot the girl. The son of the accused gave evidence, and said that when his flatlet had fired at the servant he threw him-

div.head: • CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: • CURRENT POLITICS.

The Parnell defence fund in the Freeman's Journal now amounts to £1,412. The coition! of Aberdare. assembled in mass meeting on Monday, passed a resolution unanimously in Savour of Proceeding to the selection oi a labour candidate for Merthyr. The agents of The Mimi have, it is stated, secured some valuable information for their case, in the West and South-west of Ireland. What is likely to be still more sensational is the statement of a man who, it is rumoured, is on his way from New York, prepared to swear that he torged some of the documents on which The Timms relies. In a letter to a Welsh paper, Mr. Shaw-Lefevre says he has the strongest conviction that whenever the Liberal party is again in power it will treat the Welsh questions from the point of view of Welsh people. Chief among these questions would be disestablishment, the tithe question, and intermediate education. Mr. Gladstone, having been asked by a resident of Shepherd's Bush, whether there was any foundation for a statement published in a pamphlet under the title of " Echoes from the Vatican," giving details of an alleged interview between the Pope and himself. the ex-Premier has written that the pamphlet forwarded to him is a pure forgery and fiction, and one of a large family pub- lished from time to time by the followers of the Govern- ment, and apparently without its disapproval.

The Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, Mr. W. S. Caine, Mr. Jesse Collings, Sir Benry M. Havelock-Allan, Bart., Mr. W. Morrison, Mr. W. Kendrick, Mr. T. Richardson, Mr. Powell Williams, and other Liberal Unionist mem- bers of Parliament will attend the demonstration of Radical Unionists at Bradford, on the nth inst. The local association will entertain the delegates, and Mr. Chamberlain will also be the guest at a breakfast on the 20th. Already the names of over 200 delegates have been received at the Radical Unionists' headquarters at Birmingham, and this number will be largely increased.

COLONEL KING-HARMAN'S WILL. Probate of the will of the late Right Hon. CoL Edward Robert King - Harman, Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Ireland, who died on the 10th June last at his resi- dence, Rockingham Bolc le, county Roscommon, has been granted from the Principal Registry of the Probate and Matrimonial Division of the High Court of Justice. Ireland, to the two executors appointed therein, namely, Sir George Allanson Cayley, of Brompton Hall, Brompton, county of York, Baronet, and Illejor Douglas King-Harman, of Rockingham, brother of the testator. The personalty is sworn over £44,000. By his will, Col. King-Harman has left his only daughter, Miss King- Harman, the Rockingham estates for life, with a proviso that anyone she marries should take the name of King- Berman. Ample provision is made for his widow, whom he has appointed residuary legatee, after bequeathing several small legacies, including £lOO to the Masonic Orphan Schools.

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETIES AND INCOME TAX.
div.p: CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETIES AND IN- COME TAX.

_ Replying to a correspondent, Mr. Goschen, through his secretary, states: '• It would, of course, be possible to collect income tax on the aggregate profits of Co. operative stores. When, however, the shareholders in any such stores are notoriously all or almost all persons of an income of less than £l5O, it would not only not be a gain, but it would be a positive loss to the revenue to levy income tax upon the total profits of the stores, only in order to return it again after much trouble and correspondence in small sums to the individual shareholders. It is quite a mistake to suppose that co-operative stores as such are free from income tax. Their profits are subject to it like those of any other industrial undertaking, but where any such under- taking, whether it be a co-operative store or anything else, belongs to an aggregate of persona whose indps- trial incomes are under £l5O per annum, it is mere waste of time and money to collect income tax on the aggregate profits of such ft business when net sum so collected has by law to be returned to the Individual shareholders."
PROPOSED BIRMINGHAM AND LIVER- POOL SHIP _CANAL.

The provisional coMmittee appointed to consider the scheme for a ship canal from Birmingham to Liverpool, utilising existing canals and the Weaver Navigation, have reported that; in the opinion of the slcilled experts the scheme is not only practicable, but promises to be highly profitable, and they recommend that a guarantee fund be at once raised, with a view to obtaining parlia- mentary powers, and that public meetings to urge the adoption of the scheme be held in all manufacturing centres which the canal would cover. The recommen- dations will probably be carried out at once.

The MURDER or A SERVANT.—At Thurlstone. yester- day. a coroner's jurY returned a verdict of wilful mur- der azainst Henry Hey, innkeeper, who shot and killed his servant, Margaret Hill. on Monday morning. The evidence showed that. Hey was under the influence of drink when he committed the crime.

'RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT KIRKBY STEPHEN.—d. serious block occurred at Kirkby Stephen early on Tuesday morning. An axle of a goods train broke near the goods shed, and threw several trucks off the line, blocking the road. A breakdown gang from Carlisle was quickly on the spot, but it was .five hours before the line was cleared; several passenger and other trains having to shunt till the debris was removed. No one was injured. A TEAR'S INQUESTS IN LANCASHIRE.—During the year ended May 31st 'last 2,205 inquests were held by the Lancashire coroners, and Mr. Molesworth, of the Roch- dale district., visited 151 cases in which he deemed in- quests'unnecessary. The total cost, including salaries. was T 4,759 13s. 7d. In Blackburn district there were 264 inquests. in Salford 610, Rochdale 230. Bolton 237, West Derby 562, Preston 209, Lancaster 39, Furness 45, Walton-le-Dale 2, and Prescot 7. In the Manor of Hale there was not a single inquest. ' SUFFERINGS OF IL SHIP'S CREW FROM TIELT.—On Mor- day a communication was received in South Shields from one of the crew of the screw-steamer Inchlonga. of Liverpool, which arrived at Aden from Cardiff, stating that during the voyage the whole of the crew suffered severely from intense heat while passing through the Bed Sea. One of the firemen was suddenly missed from his place, and although diligent search was made for him he could not be found; and there was no doubt he had been attacked with delirium through intense heat and-jumped overboard. In Birken- head it was 193, Birmingham 17-1, Blackburn 14.9, Bolton 21-S, Bradford 'l5-2, Brightdn 17-0, Bristol 11-5, Cardiff 154, Derby 152, Halifax 18.2, Huddersfield 17-1, Hull 16.5, Leeds 25'3, Leicester 21-0, Liverpool 197, Lon- don 16.4, Minehester 24'1. Neweastle-on-Tyne 22-3, Nor- wich 211, Nottinetain 12-0, Oldham 16-2; Plymouth 10-1, Portsmouth 20-S, Presten 221, Salford 166, Shef- field 18-3, Sunderland-20-6, Wolverhampton 141. A SINGULAR Witt,—Probate has been granted of the will, dated the 18th of 'lone, 1887, of a testator who died recently and left all. his residuary estate to two grand- daughters, having appOinted RS sole executrix a daughter, to whom he bequeathed 25, and to his wife one farthing, which he directed the executrix to forward to her by post unnaid, as an indication of his disgust at the treat- ment which he had received at her hands, and especially in respect of the 'abusive epithets, such as "old pig" and others, which she used in circumstances which he ex- plained, but did not think justified such opprobrious language. The will has evidently been carefully drawn, although not, apparently by a solicitor, and is engrossed in a clerk-like manner, and *duly executed by the testator.

A SinuormanS' 'cAVE AT MARCIATE.--A, discovery of human remains has been Made at Margate in a rather remarkable manner. A man was engaged in digging a hole in a field adjoining Trinity Church. His pickaxe suddenly penetrated a cavity; the earth gave way, and subterraneous chamber, about 12ft. in height, was discovered. Upon examination it was found to contain a number of human and other remains. There is also a long underground passage; probably connecting the chamber with the seashore. Within one hundred yards of the spot are some very remarkable smugglers' caves, and there is little doubt that what has just been dis- covered is an obscure portion of this retreat. How -the skulls and bones came there is a mystery. THE -I.4ATIONAL, DRINK Ittr,r..—The Commissioners .of Inland Revenue issued their report en Monday. The tota: drink income for the year ending March of this year wis £55,916,974, which was a decrea.e of £206,786 on the preceding year. • There were 26,117,246 gallons of spirits consumed as a beverage during the year, an increase of 36.116 gallons on 1887. Of this quantity 15,139,099 gallons were c,onsumed in England, 6,02.1,718 gallons in Scotland, and 4,954,428 gallons in Ireland. The gross receipt from boer.cluty for the past year was £8,875,510, and the repayments on beer exported £162,977, making a net receipt of £8,711,533. It is stated that this is the greatest amount to which the beer duty has ever reached. The report also shows an increased consump- tion of tobacco, the number of samples analysed this year being 39.224, an increase of 11,580 on the previous year.

The value of the minerals raised in the United King- dom in the year 1887, according to an official return, was £55,326,164, and in 1886 the total value was £55,010,231. Of metals obtainable from ores in the year 1887, the average market value was £12,997,847; and in 1886 £12,848,739. /isw MAGISTRATES.— The names of the following gentlemen have been inserted in the Commission of "the Peace for the County Palatine of Lancaster :—James Booth, Turton, Bolton; Charles Timothy Bradbury, Ashton-under-Lyne; James Beardoe Grundy, Ashton- under-Lyne; William Hugh Hughes, Ashton-under- Lyne; William Richardson, Rainford, St. Helens; and John Kenworthy Stoney, Ashton-under-Lyne.

A Snocanen SITICILM—A man named Murphy drowned himself on the Marsh, at Flint, in only one foot of water, under dreadful circumstances. on Saturday. On Thurs- day the poor fellow's wife died from the typhoid fever epidemic prevailing, and on Friday he attempted to cut his throat, but failed. Next day he went upon the Marsh, and thrust his head under water till dead. He leaves three little children unprovided for. EXPLOSION OF A LOCOMOTIVE.—A Great Northern bogie engine exploded while standing in Sleaford Station on Sunday. The engine had just arrived withna passenger train from Grantham for Boston, which was well filled with passengers, who, terrified by the report of the explosion, made their escape by means of the windows. Luckily there was no loss of life. It is sup- posed the explosion was caused through a flaw in the boiler.

THE LAST SHOT AT WIMBLEDON.—The Queen, who it will be remembered fired the first shot at Wimbledon in 1860 at a target which has ever since been a conspicuous feature of the exhibition tent on the Common, has accepted the cartridge case of the last shot fired there by the Princess of Wales with the Maxim gun prior to the distribution of prizes on the 21st July. The cartridge ease has been prepared by Mr. Gregory, optician. to the National Rifle Association, and bears the following in- scription :—" This cartridge was fired from the Maxim gun by H.R.H. the Princess of Wales at the termination of the Wimbledon meeting, 1888." SIR C. WARREN.—RDMOURED INTENDED RESIGNAT/ON. —lt is stated that Sir Charles Warren has decided to resign the position of Chief Commissioner of the Metro- politan Police, which he accepted on the retirement of Sir Edward Henderson after the West End Socialist riots. The salary attaching to the office is £1,500 a year. It is exceedingly probable that the appointment will be offered to Mr. Malcolm Wood, the Chief Constable of Manchester. Mr. Wood was an applicant when Sir Charles Warren was selected, and his admirable qualifi- cations were recognised in very influential quarters, but it was thought desirable that the Chief Commissioner should be a military man. A NEW MODE OF DISPOSING OF THE DEAD.—A Pittsburg physician is said to have discovered an entirely new and original manner of disposing of our departed relatives. It is to supersede the cremating and embalming process. It is cheaper than either, and more satisfactory. The doctor proposes to deal with the deceased by means'of hydraulic pressure, and in a very short time to reduce him to a cube of 12 inches—a solid block of handsome material resembling veined marble, tasteless, odourless, and apparently imperishable. The doctor has on exhibition the body of a late infant which has been converted into a capital cross suitable for a lady's deessing-room. If the doctor's invention is widely accepted it will open up infinite possibilities in domestic art. •

AN AMERICAN DOCTOR AND HIS MATRIMONIAL SCHEMES —An extraordinary fact has come to light in connection with the career of Dr. M'Lean, the American doctor, who is awaiting his trial on a charge of indecently assaulting a little girl, who was brought to him at Birmingham as a patient. Among his papers were found a receipt for £2 10s., which he paid to somebody connected with an English matrimonial paper for introducing him to a number of "well-selected ladies." The address of a number of ladies said to possess large incomes were for- warded to him, and he seems to have corresponded with some of them. Several letters from London ladies are found among his correspondence, and one lady in a fashionable suburb makes an appointment to meet him at the Marble Arch. M'Lean passed in America as a Baptist minister, but was dismissed for immorality. THE GREAT INCREASE IN FREIGHT RATES.— The activity in shipping circles continues, and the present tendency leads to the belief that freights will even be higher within the next few days. This is a hope which is now inducing shipowners to feel disinclined to fix their vessels at the present rates. The great "jump" which rates took within the past couple of weeks is most unusual—indeed it is said that it would be necessary to go back for many years to find a parallel. The increase in the rates seems to be greater than perhaps it really is when compared with years back, on account of the com- parative depression which has existed in shipping circles during the past three years. The freights which have gone up further within the last day or so are cotton and grain. In the latter case shipowners in some instances ask something like 10s. a ton over the present high rates. , The prevalence of unfavourable weather—particularly rain—causes the market to have a firmer tendency. So many vessels are now going that at Liverpool there , appears to be a scarcity of seamen, a most unusual cir- cumstance.

ANOTHER PERILOUS BALLOON TRIP. —OR Satin, day evening, three aeronauts, Mdlle. Leonadaire, Signor Spelterini, and an assistant, made a perilous ascent from the Clarenclonia Grounds, at Leicester. A strong wind prevailed, rocking the balloon very violently. Spelterini awl his assistant were in the car, but the lady hung on by her teeth to a trapeze under the car. The balloon shot away rapidly, swaying the lady most violently backwards and forwards as she was carried over the town. She, however, stuck to her performance on the trapeze until she disappeared from sight. The balloon travelled eastwards, and owing to the late ascent darkness was coming on before the aeronauts could descend. An effort was made to alight near Great Dalby, hut the gra.pplint iron failed to hold, and the strong wind carried the balloon drifting along over fields and through hedges for two miles. To avoid contact with buildings the balloon had to be lightened to enable it to re-ascend. The next descent the grappling iron held fast, and the party safely alighted. All three were very much shaken and bruised, but otherwise they were uninjured. BOILER PATCHING EXTRAORDIISARY : FATAL RESULT.— A boiler explosion which recently occurred on board the Yarmouth trawler Proceed, causing the death of two men and severe injury to several others, is an example of the outrageous conditions under which steam is sometimes employed by uneducated people. The Proceed, in common with most modern Yarmouth smacks, is fitted with a steam capstan for getting in the net. On the particular voyage during which the explosion occurred instructions were given by tie owner that the capstals should be worked by hand, as the boiler was known to be unsafe, the uptake being badly burnt, prolably from neglect in blowing off the lowness of water, the engine being worked non-condensing. The firm who were to supply a new boiler had purposely knocked a hole in the uptake to prevent it use, and the owner of the boat had sent extra hands to sea to work the capstan. It would therefore seem that every precaution had been adopted to prevent the use of the boiler. With an ingenuity worthy of a better cause, however, the crew proceeded to patch the holt in the uptake with an old paint tin, canvas, and red lead, the whole being well lashed with rigging chain. With this original and unique style of boiler repairs, four hauls were made, steam being adjusted by men at the capstan bars. At the fifth haul, with steam at about 301 b. pressure (bythe gauge), the patch flew off, with the result stated, the only wonder being that the patch held on so long. The coroner's jury exonerated the oWner, and found that deceased's death was due to the negligent use of the boiler, adding to their verdict a recommendation that the local dubs in which smacks are insured should ap- point competent inspectors to periodically examine the boilers at short intervals. Tax ROLL OF CoIINTY MAGISTRATES—The newly-pub- lished list of justices of the peace for the county Palatine of Lancaster contains the names of 718 noblemen and gentlemen. By far the largest proportion, viz., 265, are located in the Salford Hundred. The others are thus distributed :—ln the West Derby Hundred, which com- prises the district around Liverpool. 168; Lonsdale Hundred, the extreme northerly portion of the county, 101; Blackburn, including the extensive East Lancashire district, 113; Arnounderness, the neighbourhood of Pres- ton, 41: and in the Leyland Hundred, 30. During 1887 and 1888 there have been 53 new justices appointed, of whom 22 were for Salford, 10 each for Blackburn and West Derby, six for Lonsdale, and foie for Amounderness Hundred. The total number of magistrates in the county a year ago was 724, so that the pre- sent Toll, allowing tor 59 deaths which have taken place during the 12 months. shows a decrease of six. Sir Matthew Wilson, Bart., of Esht,on Hall, Skipton, is the senior justice of the county, his qualification dating from July 16th. 1827. He is attached to the Salford Hundred. The Duke of Devonshire, and Mr. W. Bolden Bolden, of Hyning, Carnforth, both belonging to the Lonsdale Hundred, come next in order of seniority, the commission of the former being dated January 4th, 1836, and that of the latter April 4th in the same year. In the Amounderness Hundred the oldest magistrates are Mr. Chas. Roger Janson' of Barton Hall, Preston, who qualified Chitober 17th, 1849, and Mr. Edmund Birley, of Clifton Hall, Preston, July 3rd, 1850. In the Blackburn Hundred there are seven justices whose commissions were granted more than 30 years ago. They are Mr. John F. Hodges, of Bolney Court, Henley-on-Thames, and Major M. J. Feilden, both April sth, 1838; Mr. T. H. Whitaker, The Holme, Burnley, January 10th, 1842; his Honour Judge Ingham, Marton House, Skipton. and Mr. Jas. Pilking,ton, Blackburn, February 26th, 1847; Mr. Joe. Birkbeck, Giggleswick, Oct. 20th, 1847; and Lieut.-Colonel Hy. Holden, Reedley House, Burnley, Nov. 30th, 1848. The senior magistrates in the West Derby Hundred are :—Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., of Walton Hall, Warrington; and Mr. Henry Stan- ton, Warrington, both of whom were placed on the Com- mission on Jan. 12th, 1643. Mr. Thomas Townley Townley-Parker, of Cuerden Hall, Preston and Lytham. ranks as senior in the Leyland Hundred, his commission dating from Nov. 3rd, 1847. Next to him is Mr. N. Eckerstey, of Standish Hall, Wigan, Jan. 2nd, 1850; and then coraes the Rev. T. R. Baldwin, of Leyiend, July 4th, 1855.

THE PLEASURES OF A TRICYCLING TOUR. (No. 2.) rSV-731,1 BY "TOWNSMAN." Though we had a large share of trouble, it must not be inferred that our excursion was devoid of pleasure. Indeed, when we got fairly on our way, our troubles were forgotten amid the pleasurable excitement of tricycling. and eventually our dis- comforts were completely outweighed by the varied enjoyments of the journey. The pleasures were made up of a variety,of circumstances, and so keenly were they appreciated, and so vivid is the impression they have left, that the ladies of our party are quite annoyed that I should have given only the black side of the picture. " People will think," say they, " that we had nothing but disas- ter. whereas we had abundance of delight." So we had. We were delighted in the first instance at what was to us a novel mode of journeying. Our friends were so unanimous, and so astonishingly frank in their condemnation of our expedition, that what they regarded as the perils of the enterprise gave to it an additional charm. Then there was the sense of absolute freedom. For a week at least we should be free from the restraints of society, free to dress as we pleased, to live as we pleased, and to go as we pleased, and well we availed ourselves of our liberty. In the matterof dress the ladies looked charming in their neat costumes, which, as regards style, were simplicity itself. Attired in light pink bodices, and light grey skirts, with canvas shoes, and woollen caps, they all, on the secand day, looked pictures of health. We men wore dark suits, with knickerbockers, canvas shoes, and caps to match those of the ladies. Our mode of living I babe already related. As to our progress, it was of the "go-as-you- please" order; and herein lay one of the pleasures. In sauntering along we had an eye for the pictur- esque, and whenever an unusually interesting land- scape presented itself a halt was called that we might thoroughly take-it in. We had flat, undula- ting, and hilly roads, and with villages, towns', and cities on our route,there was variety enough to satisfy the most fastidious. It would be bard to say which pleased us most—the peaceful village, the bustling town, or the serene city. Then there was the open country, with its ever-changing scenes. Here it was given over to pasturage, and the numerous well kept cattle moving on its emerald velvety surface, gave life to the panorama. There, the fields smiled with heavy crops of corn, which the gentle breeze kept in constant motion, and which were rapidly ac- quiring a golden hue under the influence of a burn- ing sun. In the distance arose the metallic whirr of the labour-saving mowing-machine, and looking over the well-trimmed hedge-rows, in which the dog-rose, the honey-suckle, and the briar asserted them- selves, we could see the ripened hay-grass quickly falling at its remorseless touch. Beyond, the haymakers were busy scattering the drying grass across the fields, filling the air with a fragrant perfume, very gratifying to our sense of smell. Often the roads were fringed with neatly whitewashed cottages, covered with time-worn thatch, and set in the midst of a well-cultivated patch of ground. The side walks were bordered with the warm- looking Sweet William, or still warmer Nasturtium and around the doors clambered rich, colour-giving Scarlet Runners, set off by the less assertive hue of the tender Clematis, or it might be the More modest and delicate Convolvulus. The ever-open doors were invariably filled with the toiling housewives, who stood with arms akimbo as we went by,and the young urchins at home clambered on the garden gate to greet us with waving hats or piercing hurrahs. Here and there, fre- quently embowered with trees, nestled substantial homesteads, and right away on some commanding emin- ence stood the many-windowed hall of the local squire. Attractive villas,ablaze with the fiery geranium ,the gentle fuschia and the tender tea-rose, were dotted at intervals along our route, and on some of them the proprietors had expressed their minds respecting the erection of their houses by quotations over the porta,ts. None of them pleased us better, or gave us more satisfaction than the one—

"East or west, Home is best," a sentiment we heartily re-echoed. Had we possessed a camera we should have lost many hours in obtaining negatives of lovely scenery. As it was after toiling up to some noble prospect we sat down and gazed upon the scene until we were satiated. How often did our oldest and liveliest lady break out into loud exclamations of admiration, when on gaining the summit of a hill she surveyed the surrrounding landscape! Particularly loud in praise was she at the sight which met her gaze after a long and tedious hill ascent under a broiling sun. On the right rose a range of well wooded hills, the highest we had yet seen, below us wound in and out among the rich verdure, the light brown road whichwe had travelled; and on our left, in an amphitheatre of hills glittered the silvery waters of an extensive lake, overlooked by a large and noble hall. As we got further south amongst the red bricked, red tiled dwellings that formed such an agreeable contrast to the surrounding greenery, we came , across many picturesque nooks and corners which made charming pictures. On we travelled, and as the days came and went our admiration for the natural loveliness of our native country correspondingly increased. Now we were speeding along a rough and lonesome road miles from any dwelling, again along the banks of a meander- ing stream, and on through a charming shady avenue, or across an extensive common. The constantly varying route possessed in itself a special charm. Whenever we approached a village or passed anyone on the road the first question asked was "How far is it to the next town?" The answers given were as various as were the passers-by themselves. It was very .rarely we got a correct reply. Some people seemed just as fond of minimizing the distance as others did of exag- gerating it. Our first inquiry would elicit the fact that we were four miles from a town, and after travelling half I that distance we should be told the town was still six miles away, and probably the very next man would I vow it was ten miles off. The secret of these replies leaked out later on, when a woman, after giving a ridiculous reply, exclaimed "They know, perhaps, better than we do !" The sight of ladies on wheels was quite a treat to many country people ; and to numerous townsfolk, especially women, our progress was as diver- ting as that of a circus procession. Girls giggled, young women laughed, and matrons were amused; but their amusement gave place to astonishment as our youngest member, a bit of a wag, gravely inquired " Is this the way to London ?" Passing drivers were all curious as to our destination, and must have been greatly puzzled as one answered "Lichfield," a second Coventry," and a third "Warwick." One gentleman in a dog cart, with whom I kept up for some time, imparted some good information as to the roads and the district through which we were then passing. In the heart of Newcastle we got mixed up with a club procession and I fully expected a spill; but, saving that one Of the ladies ran into a stupid and astonished young man, we came safely through. In Stone also we were in for a little excitement as the same lady had a narrow escape of being run down. We were all gently turning a corner leading to the main thoroughfare, when a carter, who was coming towards us, suddenly stopped, and drew his lurry straight across the street, thus barring all progress. The young lady, who was in front, was taken aback by this conduct, and only just managed to avoid a colli- sion.

It was difficult at first to induce some of the riders to follow the example of other cyclists, and take to the foot- paths where the roads were bad. But having once tasted the delights of the smooth country side walks, there was no keeping them off. They fairly revelled in the luxury, and mile after mile wag done upon'this level track. Of policemen they had no fear. Indeed, we only saw one in the whole course of our pilgrimage, and as we had stopped on the footpath to oil our machines, he, to show his authority to the crowd which had collected, summarily ordered us off into a road at least three inches deep in mud., Such a hold had the footpath taken upon our youngest member that he seemed to prefer it even where the road was as good, although to ride upon the path meant the exercise of greater care and nicety in steering. He would even come crashing down hill upon a three feet track when the slightest error in tittering

would have sent him flying across a gutter, and landed him and his lady goodness knows where. Our bicyclist, in trying to get upon the footpath in a park-like road, miscalculated the height of the sodded border, and went over the handle of his machine, in which he seemed inex- tricably mixed up. A few wriggles, however, set him free, and when a passing tramp came to his assistance and asked if he were hurt, he received the gratifying as- surance that "it's nothing when you're used to it!" Of tramps we passed lots on the road in the neighbourhood of large towns, and most of them had a word for us. One young man acknowledged that cycling at the slowest speed "beat Ivalking any day," and a weather-beaten elderly female was vigorous in her de- nunciation of us for riding on wheels. The ruling passion was strong upon some of them, as in the case of another female of uncertain age who wanted to sell me a pin- cushion as she "was on the road." "Sure, I'm there myself," I replied; and as there was no other likely cus- tomer about she leisurely resumed her walk. The unusual exercise had created an unusual thirst amongst the party, and early and often were the calls for water. Every few miles there was a stoppage for drinks, and so numerous and different were the qualities of the sparkling beverage we tasted, that by the end of our journey we had become connoisseurs in this matter. At least, so anyone would have thought who had heard the discussion which ensued as to the merits of the water placed before us at our stopping place. But some of the company were rather partial to milk, and one of the ladies obtained a quart at the farm where I offered to dig the potatoes, but to save herself the toilsome journey back to the house she left the jug and glass in the avenue and came away. Many pleasant rests had we on the wide grassy bor- ders of the roads, beneath overhanging trees, or the un- usually high hedge-rows, from which the bramble threw its octopus-like branches, and beneath which England's champion weed—the nettle—grew in great profusion. Whenever a good opportunity presented itself we dis- mounted and lay upon our backs on the grass, gazing at the cloudless, deep blue sky above, whence the sun look- ing like a disc of gold, cast its genial rays. Daily the sun became more powerful, and daily our loiterings in- creased, until our outing partook of the nature of a pic- nic. As we neared our destination the towns and vil- lages had a bright, cleanly appearance that northern towns cannot assume, even on festive occasions; and the quiet loveliness of Dr. Johnson's town of Lichfield, especially in the vicinity of the cathedral, quite capti- vated our party. The triple spires of the edifice, rising high out of a wealth of refreshing foliage, had arrested our attention in the distance, and a closer acquaintance with the dignified pile increased our admiration. Though the smallest cathedral in the country, it is as prettily situated as any I have seen' being separated from the town itself by a large pool. The surrounding close is charmingly laid out, and the cathedral, built in the decorated Gothic style, is imposing in its quiet grandeur. On the west front the kings and 'queens of England have equal honour with the Apostles, and the lovely stained glass windows and beautifully inlaid floors of the interior extorted the admiration of the ladies.

At Kenilworth we visited a reminiscence ef the feudal times, leaving our machines amongst others under the walls of the old castle. Of the massive masonry com- paratively little now remains to mark the site of a once magnificent stronghold, and what little there is, is almost completely hidden with the tenacious ivy. Situated in the midst of a great plateau, the ruins command exten- sive and lovely views of the surrounding country, which were much appreciated by the numerous visitors. It is but a step from Kenilworth to Warwick Castle, and on the way we pass Guy's Cliffe, one of the beauty spots of England, and of legendary fame. The house overlooks old-fashioned gardens that border the gentle Avon, and from the adjacent highway a stately avenue of noble woodland trees leads up to the front of the mansion. Warwick Castle is one of the few feudal strongholds still the dwelling-place of a noble family. The massive towers that look down on the peaceful reaches of the Avon, and the castellated walls, about which the town of Warwick has gathered, have stood in storm and sunshine for many a century. Through the lines of Beauchamp, Nevill, Plantagenet, and Dudley, the castle has descended to the Grevilles, its present possessors. Its outer walls are massive in structure and commanding in their bold out. ; while its inner court is venerable and picturesque. In the interior of the castle are innumerable antiquarian treasures, some of almost priceless value. Amongst art treasures are pictures by Raphael, Rembrandt, and Vandyk, the like of which are not to be seen elsewhere. From Csesar's Tower, a magnificent specimen of Norman architecture, rising to a height of 147 feet, can be- seen the populous and growing town of Leamington. In a hundred years it has grown from a church, a couple' of inns, and a few old cottages, to a well-arranged, compact town, with many natural beauties. Here vale- tudinarians flock to drink the far-famed waters, and they can be seen' between drinks 'basking in the sun in the pub- lic gardens and along the Spa. Of course we had to follow the practice of all visitors, and taste its liquid treasures.. For once Mr. Faintheart was courageous, and handling the cup as if it contained the sweetest of lemonade, he- placed it te his lips and proceeded to drink most man- fully. He seemed, however, so to tilt the cup that as much of the water ran on the floor as passed his lips, but he must have had a decent drink, for the grimaces he made soon afterwards would, if sketched on paper, have earned a fortune for a comic artist. We subsequently visited Stratford, but of our experiences in Shakespeare's. town, I may write on some other occasion.

div.head: TRADES Ui.sTION CONGRESS.
div.p: TRADES Ui.sTION CONGRESS.

The Trades Union Congress commenced its sittings at Bradford on Monday, Mr. O. Shipton presiding, in the absence, through illness, of Mr. Crawford, M.P., Chairman of the Parliamentary Committee. The Congress proceeded to the election of officers for the week, Mr. Shaftoe, of Bradford, being chosen president, and Mr. Connellan, secretary. Mr. Henry Slatter, Man- chester, was appointed treasurer ; Mr. Holmes, Burnley, vice-chairman ; Mr. B. Pickard, M.P., and Mr. John Fielding, Bolton, auditors. The Standing Orders Com- mittee was appointed as follows :—Mr. Wilson, Durham; Mr. Drummond, London; Mr. Threlfall, Southport; Mr. Judge, Leeds; Mr. Walker, Newcastle. The Trade Unions Congress resumed its deliberations at Bradford, on Tuesday. The Chairman (Mr. Shaftoe) in his inaugural address dwelt upon the urgency of a reduction in hours of labour, and submitted that steps should be at once taken to secure an eight hours day, but whether this reduction was obtained or not they must not cease from insisting on immediate land reform, which was the only permanent remedy for the existing state of things. It was also essential that the number of labour representatives in the House of Commons should be trebled. The actual business of the week commenced with a resolution on the subject of increase in the num- ber of factoryinspectors. This was carried. The Con- gress further condemned by resolution the Employers' Liability Bill in its present shape. The sittings of the Congress were resumed on Wednes- day. The discussion on Mr. Threlfall's resolution on the subject of labour representation was continued, and Mr. Fenwick, M.P., complained of the treatment which the labour members had received from the Labour Electoral Association and the Executive of the Trade Unions Con- gress. It was futile to talk about the desirability of hav- ing working-men in Parliament when no opportunity was lost of stabbing them in the back and endeavouring to weaken their influence. The only reform which would lead to a solution of the question of labour representa- tion was the payment of members. Alor. Keir Hardie accused the labour representatives of neglecting the in- terests of working-men, and Messrs. Broadhurst, Fen- wick, and Pickard, whom he mentioned by name, denied the imputation. An amendment widening the scope of the resolution was negatived; and Mr. Threlfall having controverted Mr. Fenwick's allegation respecting the ,Executive, the resolution was adopted, with the addition: of words dealing with the payment of members. Reso- lutions were also adopted expressing sympathy with co- operation', and calling on the Government to deal at once in a comprehensive manner with the question of , land law reform.

At the sitting of the Congress. on Thursday, numerous resolutions were disposed of, the first adopted being One condemning the infusion of steam into weaving sheds in North-east Lancashire for facilitating the adulteration øf cotton yarns. Mr. Broadhurst was re-elected secretary to the Parliamentary Cemmittee without opposition. Resolutions were afterwards adopted with reference to the attendance of the relatives of deceased miners at coroners' inquests; the granting of certificates of compe- tency to engine and boiler attendants; the desirability of mending the law of limited liability so as to prevent the floating of bogus companies; the question of deductions from workmen's wages for fines, &c.; and the Merchandise Marks Act. In regard to the last- named resolution, it was agreed to recommend certain. amendment& with a view of preventing fraud.

Groceries, Peas, Cheese, 'Salt butter; Cod Liver and Paraffin Oil; Quinine; good Beef, to consist of vein and brisket pieces, the price to include about 40Ib. per week of the best butcher's meat for the officers, and Sides of Mutton; Best Brand (ists) Ameri- can or English Bacon; Potatoes; Wheat Straw; Drapery and Clothing; Men's, Women's, Boys'. and Girls' Shoes, of various sizes, as per samples to be seen at the Workhouse, Dutton; House Coal (colliery to be named); Coke; good Deal Coffins specifying size and including plate with name, age, and date of death, to be delivered in the Union when and where required; Carting at per mile, and Funerals at per funeral. Parties tendering for the supply of the above-mentioned goods will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free a cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be ac- companied with samples (except drapery goods), as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter to my office, in Frodsham, for a printed form of tender (and none other can be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles required and further particulars QUI be , obtained. Sealed tenders addressed to the Guardians to be forwarded to the clerk's office, Frodsham, on or before Mon- day, the 24th day of September, 1888, endorsed "Tender for ." The tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board-room, Dut- ton, on the 25th September, 1888, at two p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if required by the Guardians.—Bv order of the Board. H. LINAKER, Clerk to the Guardians. Frodsharn, 6th September, 1888.

CUTTING A Rim's Fgor OFF.—In Birmingham, on Tuesday, the inquest was opened respecting the myste- rious death of the infant Minnie Ferriday, who was seriously cut on the legs with a knife during its mother's absence a few days ago, one of its feet being nearly severed from the ankle. Evidence was given to the effect that when the mother came home a girl named Forrester said, "Oh, Ada ; look at the blood !" The mother em- phatically asked her what she had been doing, but the girl quitted the house hurriedly without reply. The in- quiry will be continued on Monday. THE MANCHESTER AND LIVERPOOL AGRICULTURAL SO- CIRTY.—The annual show of the Manchester and Liver- pool Agricultural Society, which extends over three days, was opened on Wednesday at Lancaster. A drizzling rain fell till late in the afternoon, which soon reduced the Marsh eatate to a condition which gave abundant justi- fication for its name In 'respect of numbers the show is rather under the average. The total of the entries was 2,852, including 157 in the cattle classes, horses 242, sheep and pigs 205, chee.selos, butter 70, dogs 223, and ,poultry 436, the balance being made in implements and miscellaneous articles. At Manchester last year the total of the entries was 3,468, and at Chester the year before 3,778. When the show was at Lancaster ten years ago the entries numbered 2,475. In prizes £2,250 was offered on,this occasion, of which the local society has c4ntribu- ted £450. The arrangements of the show are much the same as in previous years, and under the aus- pices of Mr. Rigby everything woi!ked with perfect smoothness.

A MERSEY BRIGADE.—It has been notified at the War-Ace that the Commander-in-Chief has ap- proved the formation of a new brigade of infantry volunteers composed of Lancashire and Cheshire corps, under the scheme of mobilisation for home defence, to be called the "Mersey Brigade." The brigade will consist of sixteen battalions, and will number close upon thirteen thousand men. Though the headquarters have not yet been selected, there is every probability that Liverpool will be chosen ! as the centre, that city contributing the greater part of the force. The corps which are to form the brigade are the lst (Liverpool), 2nd (Liverpool), 3rd (Southport), Ath (Liverpool), sth (Liverpool Irish), and 6th (Liverpool Press Guards) volunteer batta- lions of the King's Liverpool Regiment; the Ist (bury), 2nd (Rochdale), and 3rd (Salford) volunteer battalions of the Lancashire Fusiliers ; the Ist (Bir- kenhead) and 2nd (Chester) volunteer battalions of the Cheshire Regiment ; the Ist (Warrington) and 2nd (St, Helens) volunteer battalions of the South Lancashire Regiment; the Ist (Preston) and 2nd (Bolton) volunteer battations of the North Lanca- shire Regiment; and the 22nd (Oldham) Lanca- shire Rifle Volunteers. The brigade will, be com- manded by a brigadier-aeneral, who has not yet been nominated. , One of these objections, and one which may ' assume serious dimensions in densely popu- • lated districts—where you have large towns every few miles—is that for every increase of population it is necessary to enlarge the dimensions of the sewage farm. It is laid down by Dr. A. CAR- PENTER, that for the proper working of this plan, there must be not less than an acre of ground for every 250 of population, and it is easy to see that in the industrial centres of the country where many times 250 are added every week to the al- ready swarming hives of human beings there would be a continual process of adding acre to acre. Where this would end it would be hard to say, but it would undoubtedly have the effect of giving up immense tracts of country to the mere utilisa- tion of sewage. This would be a consummation certainly not to be devoutly wished for. A sarcas- tially inclined Yankee has defined an English sum- mer to consist of "three fine days and a thunder storm," and, were this system of sewitge disposal —which acts so well In many cases—carried out universally, the same gibing wit might very well be excused for describing some of the most important parts of England as being a mere alternation of "big towns and sewage farms." • Taking everything into account, it would be difficult to altogether dissent from the statement of one of the speakers at Glasgow, "that it was a lamentable fact that in the broad daylight of the nineteenth century, we were still in the dark as to the best means of meeting the difficulty of sewage disposal." It is an art which is yet in its embryo or experimental stage, and those who have the carrying out of the sanitary arrangements of our towns and eities have great and serious obstacles and impediments to overcome on every hand.

THE Warrington magistrates appointed to act as a Licensing Committee held a sessions at the Borough Police Court on Monday, and, contrary to the policy which has been pursued for a considerable number of years, they decided to recommend the granting of two new applica- cations for full licenses. A course so extraor- dinary, and, as is generally believed, so unwar- ranted, has naturally excited a great deal of adverse comment. It is due to some of the justices who were on the Bench, on Monday, to say that, inasmuch as they were not members of the Licensing Committee, they were in no way responsible for the new departure. _ The licensing justices Who were present and took such a serious responsibility upon themselves were the MAYOR (Alderman StJTTON), Alderman HARRISON, Major LITTON, and Councillor FRAN- OOMB—four only out of the seven magistrates who constitute the committee. The whole of these four, with the exception, we believe of Major LIT- TON, are comparatively recent creations as justices of the peace. They are new brooms, but it can scarcely be said that they sweep clean. If their recommendations are confirmed by the full bench of magistrates—which is much to be doubted— they will be remembered in the annals of the town as the J P.'s who thought fit, while drunkenness was on the increase, to increase drinking facilities in the borough. For there is no escaping the fact that the proposal is one to increase the facilities for drinking. It is all moonshine to argue that it means anything else. Granted that Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. are willing to give Up the licenses for the FOx and the White Bear in or- der to be permitted to set up a large and brand new drinking shop in Battersby-lane, does any- one imagine that this is because Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. have suddenly become so virtuous that they wish to sell less Wilderspool ale? Not so ; when their consciences prick them to that extent, they will go out of the business altogether. They desire to obtain something like a monopoly of this Battersby-lane district. It is a very good thing for them to give up. two licenses where he competition is killing, and set up business in another part of the town where they may have it all their own way. We do not blame them for wishing to extend their operations; it is, we sup- pose, their business to extend their business. But we do blame the Licensing Committee for setting up a new monopoly in a now district, when there is no evidence that the inhabitants either need, or desire it. Councillo; Bovrox, who has an off-license in Battersby - lane, is entitled to urge, as he does urge, that his license should be extended, if further facilities for obtain- ing liquor are to be provided. BO he is Email fry as a brewer compared with Messrs. GREENABL, ' WHITLEY, and Co.; and it would seem that he may go to the wall in order that his great competitors may flourish. We do not argue, let it be under- stood, that Councillor BOLTON'S application should have been granted, and the other, refused; it would have been better if both had been refused as heretofore, but as the matter stands Councillor BOLTON has a just ground of complaint. Then as to the proposed six days' license for the Grove, we would, ask—ls it seemly that magistrates who have been party to fining the applicant for a recent breech of his license should (practically) reward him for his misconduct by granting a full license? If this is to be the way in which fay°. urs are to be distributed, may we not expect that other beersellers will qualify for "honours" at the hands of Warring- ton magistrates? It would be very wrong of us, of course, to seek to bring the Licensing Commit- tee into contempt; but they are public men, acting on behalf of the public, and are therefore subject to public criticism. They have acted unwisely, to say the least of it, and it will be for the magistrates sitting in due course as a full Com- mittee to see that their folly is not foolishly con- firmed.

"TOUCH AND GO." "Works like madness in the brain." There have been two inquests during the past week—one at Derby and one in Kent—on the bodies of young women who have committee suicide through being crossed in love. In both cases the girls had recourse to drowning. "'T is true; 't is pity, and pity 't is 't is true."

Mr. Bradlaugh will not have to retire-from Par- liamentary life through inability to, maintain his position; he is altogether too good a member for that. Lord Hobhouse in contributing £25 to the subscription fund which has been opened, says:— "I am glad to hear that others have been moved as I have been. It is a fitting ackrowledgment of gallant service done for mankind." This is plain speaking, and it has the further merit of being true.

The through train to Constantinople is quite horrifying to the "Old Turks;" they have not read of such things in the Koran' and it must not therefore 'be encouraged. But the Turks of the new school welcome the new train as a sign of progress. The Sultan is being pulled at from both sides; but, it is thought that, as Turkish coffers are always empty, and, as railway conces- sions will help to fill them Abdul Harald will in the end be found on the side of the locomotive.

Mr. H. J. Tollemache, M.P., wont the whole hog, at Frodsham, on Saturday, in defence of ,Mr. Bal- four and coercion. "Great complaints," he said, "were made by the Gladstonians about the treat- ment of political offenders in Irelarrl, but his con- tention was that it was absolute twaddle, and that he who broke the laws of his country, whether a pure-souled patriot or a poor peasant,' ought to be made to suffer for it, and that men like Mr. O'Brien, if they offended, should be the first to be imprisoned."

• "Absolute twaddle" is a strong phrase; but perhaps Mr. Tollemache thinks he is entitled to speak as a master twaddler. But is there, or is there not, such a thing as a political prisoner? And, admitting that there is, has it, or has it not, been the custom to make a distinction in their treatment ? Ernest Jones, Thomas Cooper, and scores of other Chartists "broke the law," (but it was recognised that they were "political prison- ers"—not felons—and they were treated accord- ingly. It has been left for a Balfour to introduce a new and villainous bad system, and for a Tolle- macho to defend it.

It is satisfactory to see that racing by locomo- tives and steamships is not encouraged by the i public. The rush from London to Edinburgh sat an end—to tha relief alike of travellers who care for their lives and of shareholders who care for their money. As to the so-called race at sea between the Umbria and "the City of New York, the Cunard Company wrote to say "that there was no race at all. The engines, as the log proves, were not driven one fraction over their usual speed during the voyage." And quite right too; speed should always play second fiddle to safety.

The substantial present that was given to the Rev. John Yonge on Thursday evening must have afforded great gratification to the reverend gentleman, not because of its commercial value alone, but because the spirit in which it was offered made it evident that his par- ishioners thought it a labour of love to do him honour. The , meeting that was held in Wycliffe Hall was a most successful one, and the compliments that were made did not • all go in favour of the pastor; his wife came in fora very well-deserved share. It is the ardent wish of the congregation of Wycliffe, and of many others who are not identified with that place of worship, that Mr. and Mrs. Yonge may long be spared to carry on a work of usefulness in Warring-ton.

Jt is evident from what Alderman Burgess said at the Town Council meeting on Tuesday night that the Warrington Sanitary Committee intend to be equal to the emergency caused by the break- ing out of fever and smallpox cases. The healOiy state of the borough is what they intend to secnre, if possible, and in furth,wance of this object they set aside all pettifogging consideration 'as to whether a patient who needs their hospital happens to live a few yards within, or a few yards without, the borough boundary. Hence the cordial ap- proval, expressed by the Chairman of the Com- mittee, of the prompt action of the Medical Officer in taking charge of a smallpox patient who lived just outside the borough, but who, if unisolated, might have been a wide-spreading gouree of in- fection.

This is alike the most generous and the safest policy, but at the same time the Corporation are abundantly justified in asking the Rural Sanitary Authority to make proper accommodation for the isolation of infected persons in their own district. The request is not an unreasonable one. The rural authority is asked to do nothing that is not easily within its power to do, and certainly within its duty. It is. as Alderman Burgess pointed out, merely a matter of money, and so long as the money is not spent, the rural district—including a pretty large urban population—is left to some ex- tent unprotected, and the borough authorities are seriously handicapped in their struggle against disease.

LACEY-ST. BAND OF HOPE, WIDNES.—A picnic organised by this society took place out Saturday, when 36 mem- bers journeyed by train to Froclsh-am, and spent a pleasant afternoon on Overton Hills, under the guid- ance of Mr. W. Davies. Tea was provided ,at Mersey View.

RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS.—The Sun- day school teachers had their annual treat on Thurs- day and were conveyed by Messrs. Yarwood to Eddisbury Lodge, Delamere Forest. The start was made at one o'clock, and after a most enjoyable day they arrived at Runcorn shortly after nine in the evening. WIDNES PARISH CHURCII.—The annual sermons on be- half of the Parish Church Sunday Schools were preached on Sunday in both St. Mary's and St. Paul's Churches. The preachers were the Rev. G. H. Garratt, 11. D., vicar, and the Rev. John Connell, B.A. There were good con- gregations at each service, and collections were made in aid of the schools. SHOCKING ACCIDENT TO A CHILD AT WIDNES.—About noon on Saturday, , ThOmas Henry Green, 4 years of age, son of Joseph Green, of 10, Flutehinson-st., was crossing Victoria-road, near the Drill Hall, when he was knocked down by the cart ot the Co-operative Society. One of the wheels passed over the child's body, which was terribly crtished, causing paralysis of the legs and serious internal injuries. The child is under the care of Dr. Hutchinson,

. REVISION IN NOUTHWICR DIVISION.—We are enabled, through the kindness of Mr. W. Handley, to give full particulars of the claims and objections made in the Northwich Division :—Ownership claims, 49 Liberals, 17 Conservatives ; occupiers' claims, 332 Liberals, 108 Con- servatives ; old lodger claims, 62 Liberals, 76 Conserva- tives ; new lodger claims, 47 Liberals, 26 Conservatives; owners' claims objection, 8 Librrals, 3 Conservatives ; owners' register objection, 18 Liberals, 1 Conservative ; occupation list objection, 98 Liberals, 105 Conservatives: old lodger objections, 12 Liberals, 1 Conservative. The total , figures are—Liberal claims and objections, 626 ; Conservatives, 337 ; with a difference of 289 in favour of the Liberals. LIBERALS AT WINNINGTON PARK.—At the invitation of Mr. J. T. Brunner' M.P., the members of the Executive of the Liberal Association of the Northwich Division,and their wives, spent Saturday afternoon at Win- nington Park. The party numbered about 120 persons, and they spent a most enjoyable and profitable time. The picturesque old Hall was thrown completely open to the visitors, who had an opportunity of viewing the many curious articles that "our member" had collected in:his Indian travels, and when not thus engaged saun- tered through the spacious park. In the course of the afternoon a meeting of the Executive was held under the presidency of Mr. Milner, each division of the constit- uency being represented. Arrangements were made for lectures and public meetings to be held during the com- ing winter, and it was announced that during the present month Mr. Brunner will address his constituents at Runcorn, Northwich, Middlewich, and Winsford, his first appearance being made at Runcorn, where the Public Hail will if possible be engaged. The physical require- ment of the party were not neglected, and at a conve- nient hour, a capital repast was spread in w marquee erected on the lawn in front of the Hall, and was much appreciated. The Crescent band was in attendance and played a selection of music for the delectation of Mr Brunner's guests. The Ruhcorn contingent arrived home ih good time. A BRAVE RITIsICORN YOUTB.—The Liverpool Shipwreck and Humane Society have awarded a silver medal and a sovereign to a Mr. Fred Mack, a youth employed in the telegraph department of the Runcorn Post -Office., for gallantly saving a boy named Frank Bailey from drown- ing. The brave deed was recorded in this journal at the time, and Mr. William Shaw, missionary to the Mersey Missions, forwarded a copy of the newspaper with a let- ter to the Humane Society with the result stated. It appears that Bailey, who is eleven years of age and lives in Fryer-st., was playing near the wooden bridge at No Man's Land, on August 10th, when he fell into the "Gut." A strong ebb tide was running and the boy was being rapidly carried away, when Mr. Mack, who happened to be in the vicinity, throwing off his coat, plunged into the water. Ile quickly reached and seized the boy, but he was obliged to swim a considerable distance before he could get to a landing place, as the sides of the " Gut " are perpendi- cular. Happily the rescued and rescuer were little the worse for their immersion, but a silver watch Mr. Mack: was wearing was completely ruined. This is the Second time that Mr. Mack has risked his life in the endeavour to save that of another person, and it is suggested that a public presentation of the medal should take place. _ MEMORIALS AT nA.LTQN.—A memnrial cross about Bft. high has just lven erected in the centre of thq Brooke burial around in this Cemetery, standimr ui a space about 26ft. square and enclosed by a stone kerb. It is in fine Runcorn stone, and enriched on each face with con

ventional floral ornament, having the sacred monogram I.H.S. for the centre. Immediately above the base are the arms of the Brooke family on either face. A small headstone has been placed at the head of the late Sir Richard's grave, bearing initials and date. An enriched Cross with handsome border has also been built in the wall of the Brooke Chantry of Halton Church. The ap- plied effect, so often seen in mural tablets, has been ob- viated by this treatment. Depending from A sculptured architectural tree are the arms, properly emblazoned, and the label with family name. Below the latter is the Brooke motto and inscriptions, which have been gilded. The foot of the cross has an ornamental band charged with the scripture words "Kyrie eleison." The work has been carefully carried out by Messrs. William; and Clay, of Warrington, from the designs of Messrs. Douglas and Fordham, of Chester. RuNconi; Scimot BOARD. The ordinary monthly !meeting of the Board was held on Tuesday, 4th Septem- ber. Present—Mr. John Pritchard, chairman. Dr. Gas- taldi, Messrs. F. A. Lake, E. Imison, and S. C. Beckett. —Visitors' Returns : The returns for the fortnight ending August 24th, show a total number on the rolls of 3,1901, an average attendance of 2,385, and a per centage of 75. There is an increase on the rolls of 76, and an increase in the average attendance of 237, as compared with the corresponding period of last year. During the past fort- night the visitors have served 285 warning notices, and found 42 children whose names were not on the rolls. School fees of 36 children attending the various public elementary schools, were remitted by the Guardians.— Resignation of Member A letter was read from Mr. J. R. Frith resigning his seat at the Board.—Precept A precept on the overseers for £5OO was signed, to provide for the expenses of the Board during the ensuing six months—Cessna of Children : It was resolved to have a census taken in order to ascertain the number of chil- dren in Runcorn under 13 years of age, the two visitors to act as enumerators. This work is to be commenced on Monday next.—The Chairman explained that eight years had elapsed since the last census was taken, and as the children who were then five would now be 13 years of age, it was improballe that the whole of the children of school age were in attendance at school. It was also desirable that the census should be taken while the population was in a normal condition, and if it was , not taken now the population would be in an abnormal condition through the advent of the Ship Canal. , RUNCORN STARR-BOWILETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—The 1 annual meeting of the members of the Runcorn (406th) Starr Bowkett Building Society was held in Bethesda Schoolroom, on Tuesday evening. There was a good at. tendance, and Mr. T. Handley presided. The secretary , (Mr. W. Handley) read the seventh annual report of the directors, who stated that during the year the sum of £1,072 15; has been received as subscriptions, and the repayments on mortgages have been £505 4s. There has also been received £6 as commission on transfer of ap- propriations. Fines, transfer fees, interest on advances to members and bank interest, have yielded £8 13s 7id, making a total income of £1,590 12s 70. The expendi- ture on account of working expenses for the year °Moun- ted to £6B, being a reduction of £9 4; 10d as compared with last year. A nett sum of £553 18; 10d has been paid to withdrawingmembers, and the sum of £l5 2s 61 has been paid to the representatives of a deceased mem- ber, the balance in favour of the society after writing off the usual amount for depreciation being £75 2s 60. Seven Appropriations have been made during the year, only one of which has been as yet taken up, the advance on which, £2OO, has been made immediately subsequent to the closing of the financial year. 54 members have during the year, under notice of withdrawal, received back their subscriptions less fines and working expenses the membership at the close of the year being 391. The report was adopted on the motion of the Chairman, se- conded by Mr. W. Betney. The retiring directors, Messrs. W. Armstrong, J. Povah, and A. Riley were re- elected, and Mr. D. Bisbrown was appointed in the place of Mr. W. Booth, who declined to serve again. Messrs. W. Riley and F. Scott were appointed auditors.—After this business an appropriation meetiny, was held, Messrs. T. S. Carr and P. Riley being the scrutineers. The first num- ber drawn was 433, and Alice Coates. of Runcorn, was entitled to £lOO for 121 years, free of interest. A second ballot was taken and number 460 resulted, the lucky hol- der being Mr. Alexander Thorpe. of Widnes and Penketh, who is entitled to £2OO free of interest.
