A SHIPOWNER'S GRIEVANCE AT RIINCORN.—OR Monday ,t Runcorn Police Court, Charles Edward Millar, a youth, ' sued John Ellis, senior (Liscard), John Ellis, junior , (Bridgewater-st., Runcorn), and Thomas C. Cooper (Runcorn), for the sum of £3 6s Bd, wages due.—Mr Burton appeared for the complainant, and stated that I the case was brought under the Merchant Shipping Act. IMr. Ellis', senior, represented the defendants.—The corn-: plainant said the defendants were the owners of the schooner Thomas.. and he had been employed on the ves- sel 15 months. His wages were £2 a month. On the 23rd 'August he had £2 due, and the defendant, said he could go to " Old Harry" for the money. There was now also due 10 days' pay at 2s 4d a day.—By Defendant: He was engaged by Captain Dunbavand his grandfather.—Mr. Ellis conten- ded that this was a made-up job between the grandfather , and the boy. To give a boy like that £2 a month and find himself, was an "unjust bill." The grandfather was under contract to him to sail the vessel by thirds. Cap- tain was to have two-thirds, and find the victuals, pay wages and the port charges, and a clear thiad was to be handed over to the owners. He had done nothing of the ' kind, and now he owed the owners £3O. He (the de- fendant) had recently to pay the mates' wages.—ln an- ewer to Mr. Burton he denied that he had discharged the captain at a moment's notice, but admitted that he had drawn the freight. If the captain had drawn the freight he could have paid the mate's wages.—He had no objection to paying this boy if anybody would swear that he had £2 a month.—The Bench (Mr. Henry Rey- nolds and Mr. A. Thomas) considered the defendants liable, and made an order for the payment of the claim with costs, £1 3s; total £4 9s Bd. SHOCKING FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—A shocking accident occurred on Monday at the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., Widnes. About noon, Mr Robert Young; an assistant manager at the works, was standing in the yard, when a locomotive with several waggons attached came along. Wishing to get to the office for lunch, Mr Young attempted to jump on the step of the engine, but he missed his footing and fell. The wheels of the engine and several waggons passed over his legs, and he sustaineel injuries of a terrible description. The , right foot was smashed and almost severed at the ankle, and there was a large wound on the thigh. The left leg up to the thigh was crushed into a shapeless mass. The unfortunate gentleman was immediately conveyed to the Accident Hospital, and four doctors were quickly in attendance. The doctors pronounced his case hope- less from the first, and his father was telegraphed for. He arrived just before his son succumbed, and was pre- sent at his death. Dr McLennan and Dr Hutchinson, and others, were also gathered round the dying man's bedside. The immediate cause of death was Shock to the system. Mr Young, who was only 29 years of age, was the son of Mr James Young, merchant, of Radstock- road, Liverpool.—Mr W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body on Tuesday morn- ing, and evidence bearing out the above facts was given by Mr William Brown, an assistant chemist, and Miss Downie, matron at the hospital. A verdict of accidental death was returned.—Mr. Lewis (foreman) said the jury wished to express their deep sympathy with the relatives of the deceased at the sad loss they had sustained. It must be a great blow to them that the life of one so young should be se suddenly terminated.—The body was interred at the Necropolis, Liverpool, on Thursday. At half-past nine in the morning it was conveyed front) the Accident Hospital to the London and North-Western station. It was carried by the foremen from the works, and among those present were Mr Pride, one of the part- ners in the firm, the manager Mr Smith, and Mr J. T. Allen, clerk to the Local Board. There were about fifty ; foremen, clerks, chemists,• and others in the procession. The party proceeded to Liverpool by the 10-33 train, where a hearse and coaches were waiting at Lime-st. station. The cortege went first to the residence of Mr Young, at Fairfield, and then wended its way to the Necropolis, where numerous friends, including Mr and Mrs Thomas Snape, Mr Richard Lewis, and Mr T. W. Reed (Liverpool) were awaiting its arrival. The funeral service was read in an impressive manner by the Rev. George Lord, pastor of Green-lane Independent Chapel, Stanley, at which deceased worshipped. Numerous beau- tiful wreathe were placed on the coffin, including one from Mr Pride, one from the clerks, one from the fore- men, and one from the Pairfield uricket Club, Acc.

Ruscom POLICE COURT.—Yesterday, before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. James Handley, John Albeson, pow- der packer, of Granville-st., was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on the previous night.—P.C. Harrop proved the case, and stated that the prisoner at- tempted to kick his young child. The prisoner's house did not contain an article of furniture, and his children were filthy- and nearly naked.—ln default of paying a fine of 10s, and costs 78 4d, the prisoner went to gaol for 14 days.—The prisoner's sister asked what should be done with the children, and she was referred to the re- lieving officer.--Michael Williams, a young man, was charged with begging, but on promising to leave the town he was set at liberty.--Enoch fiawlinson was fined 5s and costs for being drunk.—Maria Bryant, a well-known character, just released from serving five years' penal servitude, was fined 5s and costs for being- drunk and disorderly, or, in default, seven days' impri- sonment.

ALLEGED INDECENT ASSAULT ON A GIRL AT WIDNES.— Yesterday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. Deacon, Win. Williams (aged 47), of 8, Ellison-t., Widnes, was charged on warrant with having unlawfully and inde- cently assaulted a girl (aged 12) named Catherine Jane Jones, daughter of Edward Jones, 35, Warrington-road. Mr. Knowles defended. The girl said that about eight o'clock on Wednesday night, while she and a younger sister and brother were in the house alone, the prisoner, who was her mother's cousin, came in, took her into the parlour, exposed himself and her, and said he should like to make her pregnant. A girl named Mary Anne Smith came in, and told the prisoner to go away. She did not give prisoner any permission to do what he did. P.C. Moores said he apprehended the prisoner on Thurs- day, and in reply to the charge he said, "I will make them believe different to that."—Prisoner, who reserved his defence, was committed to Quarter Sessions for trial. He was admitted to bail.

THE NEW Vicen OF lIALTON.—The Rev. George Daniel Wray, M.A., of Jesus College, Cambridge, in- cumbent of St. Peter's, Warrington, has been ap- pointed Vicar of Halton, Cheshire, by the patron, Sir Richard M. Brooke, Bart. Mr. Wray will enter upon his new sphere of work about the middle of November. The presentation of St.. Peter's is in the gift of the Rector of Warrington for this turn.

SUCCESSFUL Local, ATTILETES.-At a meeting, held on Saturday. promoted by the Manchester Central A.C., G. Hartland. of Widnes, won the second heat in the 125 yards handicap, and R. Briggs, also of Widn-s, secured a /Ace in the eighth heat. Hartland took third place in the final. At the same meeting Briggs obtained a place in the 220 yards maiden handicap, but he did not succeed in the final. R. E. Garnett, of Warrington, ran at the Glasgow Exbibition sports, but he was over-handicapped, and returned home empty- handed.

WEST LANCASHIRE RUGBY UNION.—The first meeting of the season was held at the Goat Hotel, Liverpool, on Thursday evening, when Mr. Mills, of Wigan, occupied the chair there being also present delegates from Tyldesley, Leigh, St. Helens Recrea- tion, Aspull, Southport Olympic, Liverpool Hornets, Ince Conservatives, Blundeilsands, St. Helens, Litherland, together with Mr. Wilcock, treasurer, and Mr. F. T. Parry, hon. secretary of the union. The minutes of the previous meeting having been approved, on the proposition of Mr. Parry, the Frodsham, Thatto Heath, Latchford True Blues, and Haldwick Clubs were admitted members of the Union.

DARESIIIIRY Pnridnosn tEAGETE.—On Tuesday the members of the Daresbury Divisonal Habitation (No. 2,058) of the Primrose League, by the kind per- mission of Mrs. W. C. Jones, held a fete at The Elms, Daresbury. The committee who undertook the arrangements for the day was composed of the ! following :—Walton, Miss Greenall and Miss B. Greenall; Walton Inferior, Mr. John Weir; Dares- -1 I bury. Mr. John Ellison, Mr. Henry Hayes, Mr. C. W. Phillips (secretary), Mr. Jones (treasurer) ; Halton, Mr. R. Hewitt; Preston Brook, Mr. John Whitlow, Mr. A. Broome, and Miss Jessie NI e Whannoll ; Moore Mr. W. C. Jones, Mr. Walter J. H. Jones (The Elms). Mr. C. Duprez ; Acton Grange, Mr. Thomas Hewitt; Newton-by-Daresbury, Mrs. W. C. Jones (The Oak- lands), Mr. Henry Percival, and Mr. Walter Darby- shire; Keckwick, Mr. Thomas VI eir. The Sports Committee comprised : Mr. Gilbert Greenall, Mr. W. Jones, Rev. T 11. Clarke, Messrs. T. Weir, J. Whit- low, Henry Percival, IV. Darbyshire, and C. W. Phillips. Mr. J. 0. Speakman, of Wilderspool, catered in an admirable Style, and gave the utmost , satisfaction. The ladies who presided at the urns were—Miss McW hannell, Miss Weir, Miss Darby- shire, Miss Brereton, Miss Whitlow, Mrs. Tickle, Mrs Duprez, Miss Ifayes,MrsiWeir, Mrs Broome, Mrs ' Hamblett, who were ably assisted by the Misses Greenall. After tea an informal meeting was held in an adjoining tent, the chair being taken by Mr. W. C. Jones, who was supported on the platform by Lady Greenall, Mrs. W. C. Jones, Messrs. Robert Davies (Warrington), D. Logan Wright, N. C. Schou, Hewitt, Percival, J. Weir. W. Whitlow, C. W. Phil- lips (secretary), Walter Darbyshire, J. Whitlow, and T. Weir.—The Chairman said he was of opinion that they might justly congratulate them6elves on that their first meeting,on having so good and creditable an assembly. They had not done yet with their work. There were a few Radicals in the division, and they must clear them oat. (Laughter.)—Mr. D. Logan Wright proposed a resolution of confidence in the policy of her Majesty's Government, and said he was sure they would receive the resolution as it deserved to be received.—The resolution was secon- ded by Mr. R. Davies, supported by Mr. Shaw, and carried. Afterwards sports, &c., were indulged int by the company.

ELECTION OF RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS. The annual election of gentlemen to serve upon the Runcorn Board of Improvement Commissioners took place on Thursday. There were six vacancies to be filled up, the retiring members beinz Messrs. James Pritchard, J. W. Lightburn, W. Mellor, E. Imison, and James Dobson. The sixth vacancy was caused by the resignation of Mr. W. Farrell. The interest in the election was of a very lukewarm nature, no doubt owing to a great extent that seven gentlemen came forward as candidates for the suffrages of the ratepayers. The five retiring gen- tlemen offered themselves for re-election, and in an address pointed to their past serviceB as the best qualification for the office they desired. Mr. Samuel larwood claimed the votes of the townspeople on account of his acquaintance with the wants of the town acquired during a residence of 40 years. In his address, Mr. Wass stated that he would not make any rash promises either with regard to public baths or other matters not previously discussed and fully explained, but it would be his endeavour and his study to promote the interests of all. The polling station was the Inspectors' Office, at the Market Hall, and the several adjoining shops were converted into a com- mittee-room by the candidates. Mr. W. Fisher, the chairman of the Board, was the returning officer, and he was assisted by Mr. W. H. Linaker (law clerk), Mr. E. Marshall (secretary), and Mr. W. Sutton (assistant over- seer), and Mr. J. D. Jones. The result of the poll was declared shortly after four o'clock as follows : James Pritchard 421, J. W. Lightburn 410, W. Mellor 401, E. Imison 396, James Dobson 393, W. R. Wass 344, and S. Yarwood 305. The first six gentlemen are elected. In response to repeated calls, Mr Was, the new member, returned thanks for the honour conferred upon him.—Mr Imison was then called upon, and thanked them sincerely for the honour they had done him. He should try to do his best to serve the town as he had done during the pa.st three years. (Applause.) The old members did not admit that any new member, or anybody else, had a monopoly of efficiency and economy. He proposed a vote of thanks to Mr Fisher for the able manner in which he had discharged the du- ties of presiding officer.—Mr Wass seconded the motion, which was carried by acclamation—ln replying, 'Mr Fisher said since he had been a member of the Board his object had been to do the best he could for the town, and as long as he remained a member that would be his aim. (Applause.) The proceedings then concluded.

div.head: WARRINGTON LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON LICENSING SESSIONS.

The Licensing Committee sat at the Borough Police Court, at Warrington, on Monday morning, for the purpose of hearing applications for new licenses. The following members of the Licensing Committee were present :—The Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Major Litton, Councillor Prancomb, and Alderman Holmes. Dr Gornall, Mr. R. Garnett, and Mr. E. J. Guest also occupied seats on the bench. There was a large attendance of the public in court, amongst those present being several clergymen and ministers, and other local advocates of the temper- ance cause.
MESSRS. GREENALL, WHITLEY, AND COMPANY'S APPLICATIONS.

Mr. T. Swift, barrister, Liverpool, instructed by Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., appeared in support of the application of John Sampson, spirit merchant, for a full license for a new hotel proposed to be built by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Company, in Battersby- lane. If the license was granted, Mr. Swift said, it was proposed to give up the license of the Green Dragon, a fully-licensed house in Bridge-st., and also to give up the beerhouse license in connection with the White Bear Inn, Buttermarket-st. The fitness of Mr. Sampson to hold the license would not, he thought. be disputed, and with regard to the proposed new house it would be seen from plans submitted that everything , necessary for the convenience and comfort of the residents of the neighbourhood, and of guests and customers who would use the hotel, was to be provided. He might mention that in Warring- ton there was a population of about 48,500 people, and for the supply of the population, together with commer- cial men., travellers, and other visitors to the town, there were at the present time 87 fully licensed houses, 48 beer- houses, and 70 grocers' licenses for the retail of intoxica- ting liquors. This was equal to one licensed house to 236 of the population. In some districts that would not be reckoned a large average, but he must say that the distribution of accommodation in Warrington was any- thing but equal, because while in some parts of the borough the licensed houses were very thickly • planted, in other parts the accommodation was exceedingly sparse, or, perhaps, absent altogether. It was in view of the existing state of things with regard to accommo- dation that he came before the Bench that day. He could not for a moment suppose, knowing what had taken place at other times, that he was going to be al- lowed to have matters all his own way with their wor- ships. He was not afraid of his opponents if they would fight him with lawful weapons and fairly. It was pro- posed, if this license was granted, to give up a fully licensed house, the Green Dragon, Bridge-st. and a beer license attached to the house called the White Bear in

Buttermarket-st., so that it would be seen the company were not by any means proposing to increase the num- ber of licensed houses or the drinking facilities within the district. On the contrary, taking the present appli- cation along with the next, in which he wouid represent the applicant, it was proposed to reduce the nureber of existing licenses by three, namely, to give up five exist- ing licenses in place of the two for which they were ask- ing their worships that day. The others were the Fox in Buttermarket-st. and two off-licenses for the sale of beer. The number of fully licensed houses would re- main the same, and he ventured to think that if licenses were to exist at all for consumption upon the pre- mises, it was infinitely better that there should be one class of good all-round hotels or public-houses. With regard to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., he might say that they had no interest whatever in the manufacture or sale of spirits and wine. , They were brewers, and nothing but brewers and dealers in the beer which they brewed, so that while they asked the Bench to give them two respectable fully licensed houses, they did not do so to put a single farthing into their pockets out of the sale of either spirits or wine ; their only drink was the beer and its associates, ale and porter. It was their wish that every house which bore their name, and for which they were responsible to the Bench and public, should be a credit to them, and one to whiph no one could cavil or object. There was not a fully licensed house nearer than 430 yards from the present site, and that was the GUssmakers' Arms. The next nearest fully licensed house was the Manx, 560 yards away. There were, however, some off-beer licenses which were nearer. In conclusion Mr. Swift admitted the right of rate- payers to put in objections but he asked the bench not to be dictated to by what he would call a bastard kind of local option before it had been sanctioned by the legisla- ture. The magistrates must consider the facts, and apply their own judgment, and they must not surrender their judgment upon bald objections made on general grounds. Evidence in support of the application was then given by Councillor John Pierpoint, J.P.. architect, who sub- mitted plans of the house proposed to be built. He had not, he said, any interest whatever in regard to houses for which licenses were to be asked that day. The cost of the house to be built in Battersby-lane would be about £2,500.—Mr. W. J. Stewart, barrister, Liverpool, ap- peared to oppose the application on behalf of some rate- payers resident in the neighbourhood of Battersby-lane,l and put several questions to the witness.—Mr. Thomas John Down, managing director of Greenall, Whitley, and Company, said that that firm was prepared to give up the two licenses mentioned if the application was granted. In reply to Mr. Stew- art, ,witness said that the application had been, made and refused several times. The Green Dragon was not now so popular a house as it used to be. There was IL9W a tenant who could pay his own way and make a respectable livelihood, but he believed that there had been a tenant for whom the rates and taxes were paid. The White Bear, for a beerhouse, was 'a prosperous house, and did a good respectable trade.—Mr. Stewart Said that the question before the Bench was not one so —much pf law as of common sense. If the Bench found that the WifTleesl ./.16 001:114 call—respeetable men and property einere in the neighbourhood—made wU- founded objections to the establishment of such a house in their immediate neighbourhood, he should ask them to take such witnesses as a sample of the bulk. The house proposed to be built would be a public-house, and not lan hotel in the ordinary acceptance of the term. There was a cottage population in the neighbourhood, and there was a fully-licensed house only 560 yards away. There was ne need for the proposed public- house, and its erection was not desired by the people living in the neighbourhood. A number of clergymen and ministers of all denominations were present, and through him they joined most earnestly in asking the Bench to fully and carefully consider the general require- ments, not only of the small district under discussion, but of the whole town. The returns of the Chief Con- stable for the borough showed that there had been an increase in the number of cases of drunkenness, and it was:reasonably urged that the requirements of Warring- ton were amply supplied by the licenses existing at present. It was proposed to build the house near to the barracks; but the soldiers had their canteen, and it was not:an advisable thing to establish a large drinking place in the neighbourhood of a barracks. Mr. Stewart then called Mr. Joseph Titchett. a property, owner in Sharp- st., off Battersby-lane, who said that he believed the in- terests of property owners in that neighbourhood would be prejudicially affected by the establishment of a pub- lic-house there. He did not think that there was any need for the house.—Mr. George Urraston, of 56, Sharp- at., said he thought there was sufficient public-house ac- commodation in the neighbourhood. Mr. Swift then applied for a license to a house pro- posed to be built by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. in Catherine-st., off Bewsey-road. This application, he said, was in many respects similar to the previous one. It also would have every accommodation, and would be made a respectable commercial hotel. The nearest fully- licensed house, the Three Pigeons, was situated nearly half a mile away.—Mr. John Pierpoint said that the cost of the proposed house would be £2,600, and it was pro- posed to expend £2OO on a bowling green. The district was a populous one, and public-house accommodation was so limited that he had often seen people drinking in the fields at Bewsey. A greater want of accommodation he never experienced anywhere. There was a public- house in Pitt-st. known as the Bewsey Inn. In answer to Mr. Stewart, witness said that five or six applications lead been made for the license.—Mr. Down said that the company were, in consideration of the license being granted, prepared to give up the Fox Inn, Buttermarket- st., and two out-door beer-houses situated in the imme- diate neighbourhood of the proposed house. Replying to Mr. Stewart, witness said that the Fox was a paying concern, and the out-door licensed houses were remunera- tive to the company. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. did not expect to be much the gainers, but they thought that there was now a favourable opportunity for taking away houses where they were too thick, and putting them where they were required. They had not been moved by the possibility that the houses might be per- emptorily shut up, because they commenced making the application before there was any reason to think that.— Mr. Stewart said that he opposed the application on be- half of the property owners in the neighbourhood. He had nothing to say against the company. They were a business concern, and they would not act in this way unless they had a very good reason to believe that the investment they were anxious should be sanctioned would be a profitable one. No evidence had been called to prove that the house was re- quired in this neighbourhood, and he submitted that it was not required. If the Bench had from time to time refused to grant this application there must be some better reason assigned than was the case for it to be now acceded to. Mr. Westgarth, a property-owner in Bewsey-road, said that he owned property close to the site of the proposed house. There were in the vicinity a number of outdoor licenses, and in Pitt-st. there was a beerhouse known as the Bewsey Inn. He thought that the neighbourhood was amply supplied. He had heard no desire for a new house expressed. He was not a teetotaller himself, and he had no objection to the fair and legatimate wants of the neighbourhood being sup- plied'—Mr. T. H. Pilkington, also an owner of property in Bewsey-road, said that he found the existing licenses o. source of annoyance, caused by people loitering, wait- ' ing about, and sitting on the parapet. The night men at the works in the neighbourhood loitered about before the publichouses were opened in the morning. He did not think that the nuisance would be lessened by the erection of a large publichouse, because the men, who had been sweltering all night, would rather drink in the open-air than go into a room. They also took the beer

out because it was cheaper—they got more measure— three gills for a pint. (Laughter.) They got nearly a quart for a pint. Asked if it was not the forge that in- jured his property, witness replied in the negative, and remarked, amidst laughter, that at the back of "our house" he "could grow cucumbers 244 inches long." His family was as healthy a one as there was in War- rington. He enjoyed the smoke because he could go in a casual way and wash it down with a glass of beer. (Laughter.)—Mr. Henry Roberts was then called by Mr. Stewart. In answer to questions, he said that he was the son of Mr. Richard Roberts, who was an owner of property in Bewsey - road. His father had opposed the granting of the license on previous occasions, but he was not able to attend that day because he was suffering from paralysis. Witness was an employer of labour in the neighbourhood in ques- tion for the Warrington Slate Company. As an em- ployer of labour he thought that the house would be a disadvantage. There were too many houses in the neighbourhood. He had no objection to a man taking , drink at all. It was a matter for the man himself, and not for witness. In answer to Mr. Swift witness said that so far as his own example went he discountenanced , the use of drink by others. Personally he had no need , whatever for a public-house. He had been ventilating his ideas in the newspapers, and he was the gentleman who signed himself " Vigilans."—Mr. Swift: Perhaps you can tell us now we have got you here what magis- trate sitting on the Borough Bench of Warrington is owner of the site of some place which is the subject of an application to-day P—Witness : When I wrote that letter—Mr. Swift (sharply) : Tell us which it is.—Wit- ness (emphatically) : I shall explain in my own way.— Mr. Stewart interposed.—Mr. Swift: You have nothing to do with the witness.—Mt. Stewart: If my friend will allow the witness to explain—Witness : I was about to tell him that when I'wrote that letter--Mr. Swift: Answer my question. First, to what magistrate ,is the allusion ?—Witness: I will explain it.—Mr. Swift: An- swer first, and explain afterwards.—Witness: I shall not; I will answer as I desire to answer. If the Bench will permit me to make my own explanation I will make it; if not I will not answer at all.—Mr. Swift: I say this witness ought by the onler of the Bench to answer this question first, and explain afterwards if he likes. This witness has no right to set himself above the Court.— Witness: I am doing nothing of the sort.—The Mayor: I can only repeat what I said before, that we don't wish to interfere with the witnesses. We would rather leave the matter to yourselves to decide.—Mr. Swift: Very well then. I will not trouble this witness any further.— Witness: I thank you for nothing.—Mr. Swift: You are very polite.—Witness : I am as polite as you.—Mr. Stew- art said that the Revs. J. J. Langham, Father Sumner, G. L. Young, Edward Moore, W. Graham, J. W. Varley, and John Yonge were present, but they could only say they thought Warrington was amply, supplied already with public-houses, and they did not speak to any speci- fic facts. They could be called if the magistrates wished to hear them.
"THE GROVE," BEWSEI ROAD.

Mr. Segar, on behalf of Elijah Lawton, applied for a full alehouse license for the Grove Inn, Bewsey-road, in respect of which an off-license is already held. Mr. Law- ton, the barrister said, had been licensed nine years in respect to this house, and eleven applications had been made for a full license. The nearest fully-licensed house was the Three Pigeons-660 yards away. He conten- ded that the people of the neighbourhood required the house, and referred to the nuisance caused in this vicin- ity by people drinking in the highway. It was impossible to prevent people getting drunk in the highway under existing circumstances. These people ought to be ac- commodated in the public-house, and they would not then be a nuisance to people passing along the highway. Then, in reply to the argument of the "long pull. The proper way would be to let people go into the public- house, where they would only get their short pull— (laughter)—and they would spend their money quicker and get less drink for their money. (Laughter.) There were about 3,000 people employed in the immediate neighbourhood. There were Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' works, the Bewsey Wire Company's works, and the London and North-Western Railway Company had a shed there. Many of these people were engaged in " hot " trades, which created a considerable amount of thirst, which the men would satisfy either in the gut- ter or, if the Bench would allow them—by granting the application—out of the way of the public, where they could not be seen drinking. If a license in that neigh- bourhood was desirable, it was obvious that The Grove, having been in existence for a number of years, ought to have the preference and ought to have a license gran- ted to it. It was perfectly suitable for the purposes of a fully-licensed house. It had 12 rooms, a bowling green at the back of the premises,l and three stables, and was ready to supply all the immediate wants of the neigh- bourhood. Mr. Lawton proposed to spend £1,500 in improving the premises. He asked only for a six-days' license. If a public-house was required in the district at all, his client came first, and his house was now ready. The applicant, Elijah Lawton, said that people occasion- ally purchased drink at his house and got drunk either on the fields or in the roadway. He saw about a hun- dred persons on the fields the other day. He had fre- quent applications for spirits, but was not allowed to sell more than a bottle at a time. Several persons who had been injured at the works had been brought to his house, and one poor man died very suddenly before any- thing could be got for him. He had been fined for al- lowing drinking on the premises, but he had not been disgraced. The fine was only a shilling.—Councillor Wright gave evidence in regard to the plans, and, in re- ply to Mr. Segar. said that he did not know whether the road near the house was called " Boosey-road," because people were often found " boozing " there. (Laughter.) In opposing the application Mr. Stewart said he could not see because people went and drank beer in the road it was any reason for building a place and giving them the opportunity of drinking not only beer, but spirits on the premises. Another point urged was that there were larg fe works near; but he certainly did not think that "-- the aei Ides fv, rncrl j,piig Off odd tinm on the pre- tence of going for a tool or something or other, and get- ting a nip across the road, was a good reason. It was true that the population was increasing year by year, but the Bench had had that plea before them on many previous cccasions, and had thought the present accom- modation sufficient. He submitted that the wants of the neighbourhood were already amply supplied, and that therefore there Was no need to grant the application.

div.head: tROIN LICENSED VICTUALER TO GIZ' 0C- Ell.
div.p: tROIN LICENSED VICTUALER TO GIZ' 0C- Ell.

On behalf of John Clark, of the Old Coffee House Inn, Horsemarket-st., Mr. Segar applied for an off-license for premises now being built at 148, Orford-lane. The ap- plicant had, Mr. Segar said, for nine years carried on business as a licensed victualler. He now proposed to give up the business of a licensed victualler, and to open a grocery and provision shop. Mr. Clark, who had the highest possible character, was the owner of beer-house premises at 87, Dallam-lane, which he would give up if the present application was granted. He wanted to be- come less a licensed victualler and more a grocer, and Mr. Segar did not see how any one could object to the change.—Applicant having given evidence, Mr. A. Browne opposed the application on behalf of .Joseph B. Caldwell, a resident of the neighbourhood.—Mr. Segar said that he understood Mr. Caldwell was an interested party, who was going to mike an application of a similar character on the 24th inst. If Mr. Browne was appear- ing for a would-be license-holder, he had no locus standi. --The Magistrates' Clerk observed that Mr. Caldwell had not applied; he simply owned premises adjoining Mr. Clark's. The tenant was to make the application.—Mr. Browne said that the only section under which the pre- sent application could be made was section 22, which read as follows :—" Any person interested in any pre- mises about to be constructed, or in course of construc- tion, for the purpose of being used as a house for the sale of intoxicating liquors to be consumed on the premises, may apply to the licensing justices, and to the confirm- ing authority, for a provisional grant of a license in res- pect of such premises?" He submitted that the case in question did not come within that section.—Mr. Stewart opposed on the same ground. Their worships had no power to grant an off-license for premises which were not yet built; they had only power to give permission to sell beer to be drunk on the premises.—The Mayor said that in such case it would be necessary to make a fresh appli- cation on another occasion.—The Magistrates' Clerk: Next year.—Mr. Segar asked that the sessions be ad- journed until such time as would enable Mr. Clark to serve notice, so that the application might come before the court again.—After some discussion, the Mayor said No far as they could they would undertake that on the adjourned day they would further adjourn until the 28th inst.
APPLICATION' FOR WINE LICENSE.

Mr. Wallhead, solicitor, on behalf of Henry Moate, provision dealer, 112 and 114, Battersby-lane, applied for a wine license to sell at off-licensed premises. The ap- plicant already held a license for the sale of beer to be drunk off the premises, and his application now was for an excise license to sell beer and wine either on or off the premises. It had been a beerhouse since 1874, and therefore he thought if anyone was entitled to an addi- tional license it was the applicant. If a license were granted to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Company, to build their hotel opposite his client's house, he scarcely thought it would be right, seeing that the house had been licensed for so many years.—Councillor J. E. Wright produced j)lads of proposed alterations in the premises, the value of which, when completed, would be £9oo.—Councillor William Bolton said he had owned the property in question since November, 1882, and it was licensed then for the sale of beer off the premises. He had the right to prevent any license being granted for the adjoining land, to the extent of 7i acres. If Messrs. Greenall and Company got their license it would depre- ciate his property to the extent of £3oo.—Mr. Swift , characterised the application as one of the most impu- dent that had been put forward before any licensing jus- tices—it was asking for that anomaly,7a new beerhouse.— Mr. Stewart opposed on the ground that the neighbour- hood was sufficiently supplied already, and that the pre- sent off-license was all that was necessary.

THE WOOLPACK INN. Mr. W. Fl. J. Jenkins, solicitor, said that Messrs. Walker and Son had desired him to say to the Bench in reply to a lettex in "The Examiner, calling attention to their house, the Woolpack. in Sankey-st., that they would be most happy to give the information asked for in that letter to any gentleman who chose to ask them the question. Any inquiries would be answered.—The Mayor said he had not read the letter, and knew nothing

THE DECISION. These were all the applications, and the Bench retired at 1-30 p.m. for consultation.—On their return, after an absence of 35 minutes, the Mayor said they had fully considered the various applications, with this result: They had decided to grant the application for a new license in Battersby-lane on completion of the premises according to the plans, and on condition that the licenses of the Fox and White Bear be given up. They had de- cided to refuse the application for a license to be granted to the house proposed to be built in Catherine-st., and the object of granting the other license to the one in Bat- tersby-lane was that two other licenses might be given up. The public-houses were very crowded in the borough, and the Bench had a great desire to reduce their number. They had decided to grant Elijah Law- ton a six days' license on completion of the premises according to the plans. All the other applications were refused.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening, t‘he Mayor (Alderman Sutton) presiding. Thera were also present Alder- men Burgess, Harrison, Holmes, Davies, Pickmere ; Councillors Platt, J. Pierpoint, Jolley, Tinsley, J. Shaw Green, J. Taylor, J. V. Taylor, Dixon, F. A. Roberts, Blackhurst, Marsh, Percival, Wright, W. Pierpoint, Francomb, Bolton Monks, Fleming, Hutchinson; Messrs W. H. Brook (town clerk); C. Chorley (borough treasurer) ; Dr. Gornall, (medical officer).
TUB WATCH ,COMMITTEB AND PUBLIC ROUSH SINGING ROOMS.

The MAYOR proposed and Alderman HARRISON secon- ded the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Committee, which contained nothing of importance. Councillor DucoN said as there had been some reference to the singing rooms in connection with various public houses, might he ask if it was the intention of the Watch Committee to take any notice of these rooms. The MAYOR : What rooms do you refer to ? _ . . . .

Councillor DIXON: Those rooms which were referred to as singing rooms at the police court lately. The MAYOR said he thought there was a reply given to that at the time, to the effect that there was nothing came before them in the police reports, and that they had no information, except outside information, as to the misconduct of those houses. He had no other reply to give on that occasion. He had no doubt whatever that if the matter came properly before the Watch Com- mittee, and there was any reasons for taking any action in the matter, they would do it. The minutes were then confirmed.

STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that the plans of the following buildings be approved :-17 houses in Orford Avenue and Orford Lane for Mr. John Appleton; 54 cottages in Longford-st. for Mr. James Livesey ; Iron shed in Haydock-st. for Messrs Hutchings; Alteration and re-erection of slaughter-ho Use off Percival's Fold for Mr. William Fairhurst; Two shops in Bridge-st. for Mr. J. B Isaac and Mr. J. E. Wright; also, "that the Town Clerk be instructed to approach the London and North- Western Railway Company and make all the necessary arrangements respecting the making of the new street from Bridge-st. to Bold-st." ; and " that the offer of Mr. Hutton Wright to set back his proposed new shop in Sankey-st. three feet for the sum of £4O be accepted." Councillor PLATT, in moving the adoption of the min- utes. said that until they Shad taken the step with regard to the proposed new street from Bridge-st. to Bold-st., they did not intend to go any further in that matter. Alderman .HARRISON seconded the adoption of the minutes. _

Councillor DixoN was sorry that scheme with regard to the new street had come up again. It had been be- fore them several times before, and now that Bridge-st. was widened there was less need for the street than ever. _ _

The MAYOR: Are you bound to make the street if we pass this ? Councillor J. PIERPOINT I think you are. The Tows CLERK : I may say you are not com- mitted to the making of the street at present. Councillor PLATT said that before they went any fur- ther they intended to get a renewal of the offer made by the London and North-Western Railway some years ago, that they would give the Corporation the land if it made the street. If that offer was accepted he thought they would have to make the street. Alderman BURGESS recollected the time when the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company made the offer of the land for that street, but a good many things had happened since, amongst others there had been Mr. Hughes' works established on part of the land. He also believed that there was a lease of 14 or 15 years in these premises. It did appear to him to be legislating for 15 years hence, when none of them would be there to see the thing carried -out. (" Oh, oh.") Oh, well, there was a great many things that could happen in 15 years ; there was an association outside that dispose] of the members of that Council at their own sweet will'. (Laughter.) He thought they had better let the future do something in that matter. As long as Arpley Station was open there would be a street round by there that would not be disturbed. (Hear, hear.) He hoped and trusted that no money would be spent in that matter until the time wheg the street came to be made— he trusted they would protect themselves in that res- pect. 4 Councillor PERCIVAL supported Alderman Burgess's re- marks. •

Councillor PLAIT, in replying, said the unexpired term of Mr. Hughes' lease was now only 11 years. Besides, it must not be forgotten that if the vacant land in Bridge- st.' over which the street was to be taken, were sold, the cost of the street might be trebled. After they had the offer of the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany the whole matter would be gone into: (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then confirmed. THE SANITARY COMMITTEE AND ITS POLICY.—LIVELY DISCUSSION.

The minutes of the Sanitary Committee contained the following items :—" That a license be granted to William Cook to slaughter cattle at the slaughter-house in Ashton's-yard, Wilderspool-causeway, Mr. Cook agree- ing, in the event of the Corporation establishing public slaughter-honsPs, to relinquish the license, and not to claim compensation in respect thereof ; " and that the tender of Mr. W. Smith Pierpoint to supply 25 gross of bolts and nuts at 2s 8d per gross be accepted. At a meet- ing held on the 15th August it was further resolved that the annual report of the Medical Officer of Health for 1887 be approved and printed and submitted to the Council. [A summary of this report was given in our columns last week.] It was also resolved "That the Town Clerk be instructed to call the attention of the Rural Sanitary Authority to the prevalence of fever in their district, and to the necessity of their providing proper hospital accommodation for the treatment and isolation of the persons suffering from infectious di- eases." At a meeting held on the 27th August, the com- mittee having fully considered the question of • the management of the Longford works, it was resolved "That Mr. Dinwiddie be requested to send in his resig- nation as manager of the works." It was also resolved that the Medical Officer of Health be authorised to pur- chase, if he thinks necessary, a second Ducker's NO. 10 Portable House, with the necessary arrangements for connecting the two together. Alderman BURGESS, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said he might preface his remarks by saying that pone of the subjects he had to speak about com- mended themselves to his special regard; in fact, he would rather be excused talking about them. The first matter to which he would refer was the minute on page 4 :—" That the Town Clerk be instructed to call the at- tention of the Rural Sanitary Authority to the preva- lence of fever in their district, and to the necessity of their providing proper hospital accommodation for the treatment and isolation of the persons suffering from in- fectious diseases." He felt it right to say that the Rural Sanitary Authority had within its district a very large amount of scarlet fever, and there was no provi- sion made for its treatment, except in the houses in which it happened to be found. That was a calamity, and he had no hesitation in saying that they were suf- fering to a serious extent from the condition of things that existed. He hoped the time was not far distant when the Rural Sanitary Authority would make provi- sion for diseases of this character, so that the borough would not be placed at such a disadvantage. It was simply a question of money; and he did not think that such a body as the Rural Sanitary Authority should allow a reasonable and proper expenditure of money to prevent them making the provision they ought to have made some time ago for infectious disease. (Hear, hear.) There was another minute of the committee—" That the Medical Officer of Health be authorised to purchase if he thinks it necessary, a second Ducker's No. 10 portable house, with the necessary arrangement fer connecting the two together." On the 27th August he received a communication from Dr. Gornall, medical officer of health, with reference to the condition in which he found himself as far as hospital accommodation was concerned —" To-day we have 105 patients in hospital. During the week ending yesterday we have admitted 31 and dis- charged 20, so that our admissions are much in excess of the dismissals, and I look forfkard to a repetition of this for many weeks yet. I thought it as well to let you know that the epidemic is increasing, and the time must come when I am afraid I shall have to refuse cases of

fever. At the present moment I can only admit with my present accommodation one kind of fever." The Sanitary Committee had determined that neither scarlet fever nor any other infection should overpower them. (Hear, hear.) Immediately on the receipt of the letter he had read, and feeling the responsibility that was placed upon them by it, a resolution was passed with reference to the portable house, although the Medical Officer had not up to the present monaent availed himself of the power granted to him, and he thought his judg- ment was very much to be commended. Dr. Gornall had very much at heart the best interests of the town. and its financial position also—(hear, hear)—and he (Alderman Burgess) would have to read another com- munication to show that the Medical Officer had acted wisely in the mktter. His letter was as follows : " Late last night (31st August) a case of small-pox was reported

from 5, Percy-st, one of the streets on the t borough boundary. As it was dark I could not detect any line of division and even if I had, in a crowded district like this, I had no alternative but to take the case for our own protection • in fact, I am act. lug in the case as if it was in my district. The house is just outside. To have small-pox outside is bad enough, but to jeopardize the health by allowing it to remain un- isolated would be worse." It was very creditable to Dr. Gomall that, without consulting anyone, and acting upon his own judgment and responsibility, for the pur- pose of protecting the public in the borough, as well as those outside, he had acted in the manner described. Re- ferring to the likelihood of a spread of smallpox, he said he could tell the Council that the Committee woad, without the least delay, make preparations tor the re- ception of patients suffering from smallpox. (Hear, hear.) He entirely agreed with Dr. Gornall that it was not desirable to have smallpox cases treated in the hos- pital so near to 100 children who were suffering from scarlet fever. It was not desirable to have the two diseases in such close proximity. If necessity arose they would have a house wherein the poor people could be taken. Although the state of things he had described. was very much to be deplored, the health of the town generally was in a very satisfactory condition. There had been 42 deaths from scarlet fever, 57 from whooping cough, 6 from fevers, 9 frdin diarrhcea, 3 from diptheria, andl from smallpox.; yet, in spite of all, he was glad to say that the death-rate for the eight months of the year now just finished (the end of August) was only 201 per thousand. Dr. Gornall, in another letter wrote :—" If may venture to prophesy, I believe we are on the turn , towards fewer cases of scarlet fever. Week ending Aug. 25 41 cases notified, 34 admitted to hospital. Week ending September Ist-12 cases notified, 11 admitted to hospital; and during the present week I hope to dis- charge-about 30 cases from hospital, so that with our present accommodation, if we have only scarlet fever to , deal with, I think we may manage, but if we have small- pox as well, it will be imperative to have increased room, as smallpox ought not to be treated near such a congregation of children as we have atpresent at the hospital.'—Referring to the minute of the Committee in which Mr. Dinwiddie was requested to send in his resig- nation as manager of the Longford Works, Alderman BURGESS did not wish to make any observations upon it.

—Councillor WILLIAM PIERPOINT :—I think it would be better if you did. Alderman BURGESS said he was considering the best interests of his town, and the best interests of Mr. Din- widdie as to the future, and he was determined that he would not do anything to hinder his chance in any way as far as making statements publicly which might be prejudicial to him. (Hear, hear.) ' Councillor Faawconts seconded the adoption of the minutes._ ' _ .

Councillor PLATT said he heartily supported all that Alderman Burgess had sketched forth as to what he had done 'arid what he was going to do with regard to the health of the town. With respect to streets such as Percy-st., which were part in the borough and part out- side, he thought it was high time that the borough had control of those streets by extending its boundary. He wished to call the chairman's attention to the depot in Lythgoe,s-lane, which, he said, was prejudicial to the health of the residents in that district, and he would like to ask whether the Sanitary Committee were satisfied with the state of that place as it was at present. Or if not, when were they going to amend it, and what steps were they going to take to bring about an improve- ment? Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT said he was exceedingly sorry to have to support these complaints, but he heard from some of his tenants that the depot was very dis- agreeable. One person who had been a tenant in the same house for over 28 years was obliged to go, not be- ing able to stand the stench any longer. Councillor Dixoti said the question had been put to him within the last three or four days whether the fact of asking Mr. Dinwiddie to send in his resignation was not the making of a sort of scapegoat for the Sanitary , Committee? (Hear, hear.) He considered that the I plant at Longford was so defective that whatever mana- ger they obtained they could not get either the quantity or the quality out of the stuff that they ought. Councillor PERCIVAL said with regard to the intercept- ing depot, that complaints had hem made in the South- East Ward, and he asked if any remedy could not be got to prevent those "atmospheric "smells. _

Councillor WILLIAM PIERPOINT said he rose for the ' purpose of proposing an amendment to the minutes of ; the Sanitary Committee. It was "That the minutes of the Committee be passed with the exception of the por- tion relating to the proposal that M. Dinwiddie be re- quested to send in his resignation as manager of the works." They had had a very long and important , speech by Alderman Burgsss on the health and sanitary condition of the town, and he would like to say that, individually, he was very much obliged to the Sanitary Committee for the active care they seemed to be taking of the health of the people of Warrington. At the same ' time, he felt that something shotild have been said by the chairman of the Sanitary Committee with reference to the particular matter spoken of in his amendment— that Mr. Dinwiddie should send in his resignation. It was well within the knowledge of every member of that Council—they had had it dinned into their ears whenever they had raised a question as to the capabilities of the management of the machinery at Longford, they had been told that it was the most perfect system of machinery that was ever devised, and was doing all the work that they had claimed it would do. Mr. Dinwiddie was appointed in the beginning of January, 1883, at a salary of £l5O a year. It was said that the management of Longford prior to his appoint- ment was something deplorable; and if they would refer to the yearly accounts furnished by the Borough Trea- surer, they would find that the annual output at the time of Mr. Dinwiddie's appointment was in round figures £6OO. in February, 1885, a resolution was pro- posed in that Council Chamber—to which an amendment was brought, and for which amendment only three voted—that Mr. Dinwiddie's salary should be raised to £2OO a year. And if they would again refer to the Cor- poration accounts they would find that at the time they were asked to raise his salary the yearly output from Longford was still £6OO. From that time until six or eight weeks ago he had never heard a word said against Mr. Dinwiddle, either by the Chairman or by any mem- ber of the Sanitary Committee. Speaking in that Chamber on June 30th, Alderman Burgess said: " Agreat deal had been said inthat Chamber about the extrava- gant and excessive expenditure on sanitary matters, but he could assure all present that they were in possession of the best machinery for the work they had to do at Longford that had yet been devised. He contended that there was no failure about it, and that there was no ofence." If there was no failure in that particular machinery why had a change come about, or the neces- sity for a change? Either Alderman Burgess Or the Sanitary Committee—he said the committee, although ,he believed that the Sanitary Committee consisted of Alderman Burgess—(laughter)—either Alderman Burgess knew that the machinery was a failure, or he did not. He told them there was no failure and no offence, and that) the machinery was doing all that it possibly could. in Other words, that however good their management might be, the machinery could not possibly do more than it,was doing. One or two of the members of the Council had, however, managed to get the committee to give them a few details' from which they found that the output had not been what the com- mittee estimated it would be. Their income had also been less than their expenditure, and then it was found that the manager • at Longford was not quite the 'man to go on with those works. He might point out to them that their yearly , output when Mr. Dinwiddie was appointed was £6OO a ; jittit;and the same at the time they raised his salary, but , now that they proposed to discharge him the output had risen within 31 years to £2,137. Was it quite fair that , when a man had given them good work for their ma- chinery he should be asked to go? (Hear. hear.) No member of the Sanitary Committee had ever shown that , Mr. Dinwiddie had done anything wrong. He would , like to have a little bit of fair play. They talked about : the management of Longford. He contended that Mr. Dinwiddie had only been playing second or third fiddle there. (Hear, hear.) He would tell them who had managed Longford—Alderman Burgess and the Borough ' Surveyor; and it would be better for the business of the other committees if they had more of the time of Mr. • LOriedin at their disposal. (Hear, hear.) He hoped the ; Chairman would give some reason for Mr. Dinwiddie's dismissal. He did not care if it was a reason prejudicial to Mr. Dinwiddie ; that had nothing to do with him, it was Mr. Dinwiddie's fault for placing himself in such a position. He was there as a public representative in the act of doing a public work, and he said that he had no , right to vote blindly on a resolution of that kind. (Hear, ' hear.) Councillor DIXON seconded the amendment.
-Councillor MONKS -supported it because he believed that the results at Longford, whatever they might be, were not attributable to Mr. Dinwiddie's management.

(Hear. hear.) If Mr. Dinwiddie were dismissed he thought the only thing he deserved it for was in sub- mitting to a system of treatment which no man receiv- ing £2OO a year ought to allow himself to endure. He did not believe in a dual or a treble management. He believed that Mr. Dinwiddie would court an inquiry, be- fore an independent committee, as to his conduct in re- ference to his duty and his management at Longford; but he defied any man if he was in such a position that he could not dismiss, what he would call an inefficient engineer or any other man, and if he had not the power to order a cartload of slack without the permission of Alderman Burgess and the borough surveyor—he said that such a system of management, he did not care who they had, would lead to just such deplorable results as they had had at Longford. Councillor RENRY ROBERTS: It does not exist at all. Councillor MONIES said he would not be interrupted by Councillor Roberts' or anybody else. Ile should support the amendment in the hope that there would be a com- mittee appointed to do, what he conceived to be, an act of justice to Mr. Dinwiddie. He thought the time had come when the question of the Longford depot should be sifted to the bottom. (Hear; hear.) . .
Councillor TINSLEY remarked that inasmuch as the question would come to a vote he should like to have an explanation on the subject frem the Chairman of the
Committee, in order that he might vote as he thought best.

Councillor HENRY ROBERTS said that the system of management to which Councillor Monks had referred ex- isted only in his imagination and in the imaginatien of those who thought with him. Such a state of things as he spoke of was an absolute—he would not say fabrica- tion, he did not want to use strong language, he would say it was a purely imaginary state of things. That Mr. ' Dinwiddie had to ask permission of Mr. Longdin and the Chairman for every pettifogging thing was untrue. The question of his resignation had been under the con- sideration of the Committee for over 12 months, and the decision they had arrived at was one which had been forced upon them. The Chairman would bear him ont when he said that he personally had been the means of putting the matter off for the last six months, in the hope that Mr. Dinwiddie would meet the wishes of the Committee. It was not kind or wise in Mr. Dinwiddie's future interests that the matter should be ventilated. If the Council had not sufficient confidence in the Sanitary Committee to believe that they had come to the decision in what they considered to be the best interests of Long- ford and of the town, by all means let them dispose of the Committee, and let another Committee take their place. {Hear, hear.) .

Councillor F. A. ROBERTS said that he, like Councillor Tinsley, was in some difficulty in regard to this question, but perhaps his difficulty arose from another cause. He did not wish to ignore the opinion he expressed openly at different times that the manager at Longford, according i to his idea, should be a man brought up n some know- ledge of machines. He was very sorry himself that Mr. Dinwjddie had been unfortunate enough to get into that position, for he had from the first not considered him a right man in the right place. He suggested that in some way the Sanitary Committee might lessen the difficulty as regarded Mr. Dinwiddie personally. Could not some method be found by which there could be a dignified withdrawal of Mr. Dinwiddie without his future pros- pects being injured. If they would say that the change was being effected because a more practical man, who would be of more value to the town, was required, Mr. Dinwiddie might then make a dignified withdrawal. As the minutes stood, it was practically making his future as dark as dark could be.
- Councilor Bovrox thought that the question should be discussed in Committee.

Alderman DAVIES said that every member of the Council had the fullest confidence in the Sanitary Corn mittee, and in the general way in which they carried out their duties. He might say, in addition, that as re- garded the disposition of excreta at Warrington, he thought they might rest satisfied that there was no turn- ing back upon the plan they had adopted. If anyone proposed that they should change to the old, or any other system, they could not do so. As regarded the management of Longford works there seemed to be a great diversity of opinion in the council, and he thought that it was rather a misfortune that the broad question as to the management at Longford should have, as it were, dwindled down to the disposal of Mr. Dinwiddie. It was a much wider question in the minds of the Coun- cil, and if they took the matter in a broader sense than individualising Mr,t Dinwiddie it would be better for all of them. As regal•ded the management of the works he thought it would not be unwise of the Sanitary Commit- tee to call in the assistance of some members of the Council who were not on the committee who had some mechanical knowledge that was not, he believed, at pre- sent available to the committee. He was not speaking of anyone in particular in the Council, but he thought, if possible, that by resolution of the Council, they might have a committee that would examine as to the condi- tion of Longford. He was really prepared with an open vote on the question'before the meeting, and he should wait to hear the reply of the chairman of the commit- tee.

Alderman HOLMES observed that every member who had spoken had done so with a desire to help Mr. Dinwiddie if they possibly could, and he should be very glad if the course suggested by Mr. F. A . Roberts could be adopted by Alderman Burgess and his coadjutors. He was always willing to trust a committee in the management of its own affairs, and he had no doubt the committee had looked at the subject very carefully, to see if there was any other course that they could adopt. He hop:A, how- ever that they could adopt the course suggested by Councillor F.A. Roberts.

Councillor PLAIT said he was afraid it was too late to adopt any such course. He understood that Mr. Din- widdie did not refuse to send in his resignation, and therefore he d d not see why it should have been put on the minutes. Alderman PICKIVIERE : Mr. Dinwiddie was appointed by the Council. The MAYOR: Having been so appointed, he can only be discharged by the Connell ' • therefore, it is neces- sary that a minute should be put upon the agenda paper. Alderman PICHMERE : That is where the dual control comes in. (Laughter.) Councillor PLATT: Perhaps I may be allowed to pro- ceed now. The MAYOR: That is Nthy I interrupted you, with that explanation. Councillor PLATT said it seemed to him that if they had asked Mr. Dinwiddie privately to send in his resigna- tion, it would have had the effect of avoiding all this un- pleasantness with regard to it. (Hear, hear.) Undoub- tedly he would have taken that course if the matter had been represented to him in a proper way by the coat. mitte,e. He quite agreed that the Borough Surveyor was not competent to manage those works, and, moreover, was not supposed to be competent. It was no part of Ms duties to understand the machinery which had been put up at Longford, and the attention which he gave that depot took him away from his other and more legitimate dutiesin the town. He certainly thought that considering that Mr. Dinwiddie had been manager of the Longford works for five years, he had been treated rather seurvily by the Sanitary Committee. It was the duty of the Council to sgrutinize the proceedings of every committee, and if they were not satisfied to get an ex- planation which would satisfy the,m.

Alderman BURGESS. replying to the discussion, said that the 14alth of the town was the chief concern of the Sanitary Committee. There was such a thing as revenge inmany things, and revenge came into that room. (" Oh, oh.") Councillor PLATT: I rise to a point of order. Alderman BURGESS (interrupting) : Never mind. Councillor PLAIT: I appeal to the Mayor, and not to you, Alderman Burgess. Alderman BURGESS: I mean to have my say. The, Mayor is the gentleman who will call me up if I say any- thing that I should not say. The MAYOR : I will call him to order if I hear him say anything he should not say. Alderman BURGESS: I am too much in the habit of be- ing stopped by Mr. Platt. The MAYOR: I don't think Alderman Burgess will do any of you any harm. Councillor PLATT: I don't think he will do us any harm. I think he will do himself harm by insisting on this language. Alderman BURGESS Leave me to it. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS : I also rise to a point of order. I raised this question amongst others, and I ob- ject to being told in this chamber by Alderman Burgess that there is a spirit of revenge here. Councillor PLATT: I tell Alderman Burgess flatly, as far as I am concerned, that the assertion he has made is not true.

Alderman 131CRGESS : Nothing that is said will alter facts. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS : I rise to a point of order on behalf of Councillor Platt. We cannot allow anything of this sort to exist in the Town Council. I ask Alderman Burgess to withdraw the remark as applied to me. 'Alderman BURGESS : I never intended it to apply to

you. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS : You said it was a spirit of revenge. Alderman BURGESS: I repeat it. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS: I think Mr. Burgess should at once withdraw that remark. Alderman BURGESS: I won't. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS: Then I shall take a division upon it. I beg leave to move the adjournment of the Council. Councillor MARSH : I think Alderman Burgess ought to be heard. He has not interrupted any gentleman who has spoken, and I do think the Council should listen to him. I don't think there is anything to call him to order about.

Councillor TINSLEY : I second Mr. Roberts's motion. The MAYOR: I must ask the Town Clerk if there is power given to make such a motion. The TowN CLERK : If you move that Alderman Burgess is not out of order he is entitled to be heard. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS: Then I understand you (the Mayor) to move that he is not out or order? Do I under- stand youlo rule that Mr. Burgess is not out of order in saying there is a spirit pf revenge? The MAYOR: I do. At this stage of the meeting . Councillors Blackhurst, 'Platt, Dixon, Monks, F. A. Roberts, Jolley, John Pier- point, and William Tinsley left the room, and did not return. The MAYOR: In my opinion it is a very foolish thing to retire for so simple a thing. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS: Take a note of those who have retired. 'I am glad to see there are some sensible men in the Council. It is a difficult matter to me to reply to gentlemen who have left the room. Alderman HARRISON: You can have it all your own 'way now. (Laughter.) Alderman BURGESS: It is not so pleasant after all. The MAYOR: I am sorry certain members have re- tired, because I think the cause has been so very trifling. I have often heard the same gentlemen make remarks quite as bad as those to which objection has been taken. Alderman BURGESS, in the course of a lengthy reply, said that Mr. Dinwiddie was appointed at a salary of £l5O a year, with the understanding that at no distant I date it would be raised to £2OO if he gave reasonable satisfaction, The advance was subsequently agreed to by the Council. At that time the committee had no reason to doubt Mr. Dinwiddie's attention to their affairs, and his capacity too. They had, however, had I great reason to doubt both since then; not only to I doubt, but to be satisfied in their own minds, that there I was a want of attention to their interests and a want of

div.p: that intelligent capacity to do what was required in the manager at Longford. They found that they could not in justice to the inhabitants of Warrington and to the Corporation allow that state of things to go on after they found what they did. Mr. Dinwiddie was not restricted . to the time he was to be at Longford. It was found after', he had been at the works nearly three ' years, and by an accident, that Mr. Dinwiddie was enly at the works five hours and seven minutes a day. Mr. Dinwiddie had been trying, not to manaffethe works at Longford, but the Committee. greater injustice was ever done to a man than had been done to Mr. Longdin with reference to the discussion on this ques- Hog.* The members of the Council could pitch into the Committee as much as they pleased—but they must not destroy a man, who depended upon his employment, by insinuations and innuendoes with reference to what he had done and what he was doing now. That was not manly. The manager, having machinery that in 24 hours was calculated to treat the material that was col- lected in 24 hours—without a word having been said to his Committee, stopped the machinery for an hour at mid-day and an hour at mid-night. Mr. Dinwiddie was never there at mid-night, and he did not, therefore, know how long the machinery stopped. He was not often there at midday, and they did not know how long it was stopped at that time ;but having two hours taken out of the working of the plant, in 22 hours the machinery could not do what it was calcuated to do in 24 hours. Mr. Dinwiddie stopping the plant for an hour meant at least an hour and a half at each stoppage before he could get steam up. Something had been said to the effect that the manager could not have a load of coals without obtaining the sanction of the Chairman of the Committee and the Borough Surveyor. Speaking from memory, the account for coals, instead of being a matter of trifling importance, became a ,constant drain. ' With reference to every other matter connected with the works they had to keep perpetually reminding Mr. Din- widdie of the unsatisfactory condition that things as- sumed under his management Gas was consumed to a , fearful extent., as Mr. Dinwiddie was not there to check it, and the expenditure on coals last year amounted to £172, when they did not suppose they were giving him authority which meant anything beyond £lO. Notwithstanding what Mr. Monks had said as to the deplorable results of the working at Longford, they be- lieved as a committee they were working the place in as satisfactory a manner as any other part of the town was worked; and if it had not been that Mr. Monks had been foiled and baffled in the Council Chamber, they would not have had him as fierce as he was now. The committee believed that they were acting in the best in- terests of the town.

This committee recommended that the tender of Messrs Walton Bros. to supply 500 yards of flags at 3s lid per square yard be accepted. The attention of the commit- tee having been called to the depositing of bark and other rubbish on the River-road, Wilderspool Causeway, it had been resolved that notice be given to the persons offending requiring them to remove the same. The minus were adopted on the motion of Alderman DAVIES, seconded by Councillor WRIGHT.
SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

From the Inspector's report, it appeared that 81 cases had beea inquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in all cases for 175 children. 10 cases had been taken before the magistrates, and fines inflic- ted in eight cases, and two sent to the ship "Clio." 18 cases were, brought before the committee and dealt with. The average attendance at the public elementary schools during the month of June was 7,394 ; correspon- ding period last year 6,996 ; increase 398. Thi minutes were confirmed on the proposition of Councillor FLEMING, seconded by Councillor J. SHAW GIIEEN.

The minutes of this committee, which were confirmed, on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman HARRISON, stated that in July the visitors to the Museum had been 2,940, the books issued from lending library 1,873, and the books issued from reading-room 1,228.

CEMETERY COMMITTEE. The report of this committee, which was adopted, on the motion of Alderman HARRISON, seconded by Coun- cillor FRANCOME, stated that the interments for the past five weeks were :—Adults 39, minors 55, stillborn and premature 10; and for the corresponding period last year—adults 37, minors 61, stillborn and premature 11. The receipts for the past five weeks were £74 lOs 6d, and for the corresponding period last year £72 17s.

TIM BRITISH ASSOCIATION.—Previous to the inaugural meeting of the British Association at Bath, on Wednes- day evening, the General Committee assembled at the Guildhall, under the presidency of Sir H. Roscoe. and re- ceived the report of the Council for the year 1887-8, which was at once approved. The Treasurer's report was also presented, its most interesting feature being the figures which pointed out the extraordinary success of last year's meeting, when the number of tickets issued was 3,833 and the receipts £4,294. At a brilliant gathering held in the Drill Hall in the evening, the President's address was delivered by Sir Frederick Bram- well, who was introduced by Sir Henry Rescoe, the retking,preSident.

div.head: OAS COMMITTEE:
div.p: OAS COMMITTEE:

This committee recommended that the tender of Mr. William Williams for excavating trenches for pipes in Scotland-road and Stockton Heath according to the schedule of prices be accepted.—Confirmed on the mo- tion of Alderman HOLMES, seconded by Alderman Bun- GESS.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. This committee had resolved that Mrs. J. Warrington Wood having offered the whole of the casts of the works executed by her late husband, a sum not exceeding £75 be expended in cases, packing, freight, and carriage from Rome of the casts offered by Mrs. Warrington Wood, and that the selection be left to the Museum Com- mittee. It was also resolved that the best thanks of the Council be given to Mrs. J. Warrington Wood for her kind and generous offer to her late husband's native town. The committee submitted the following resolu- tion :—" That the Parliamentary Sub-Committee. with Messrs. Platt, Francomb, and Wright, be requested to consider the desirability of applying for an extension of the borough boundary, and, if so desirable, to report what the nature of such extension should be; and also to report as to the best mode of dividing the borough for the election of County Councillors." This was all the business.

THE BOUNDARIES QUESTION. ffir,—lt is just to say, on the authority of a member of the late Boundary Commission, that no deputation in the interest of the adjacent Cheshire district attended upon them. Nor is he (the Commissioner) aware of any such meeting with the Hon. Mr. Pelham. the assistant , commissioner. The suggestions made at a previous meet- ing of the Board of Guardians, to the one at which such a deputation was named, receive confirmation in the words of the Right Hon. Commissioner—" The change of front of the Government made it very difficult to pro- pose or recommend any large alteration of county boun- daries." It. of course, remains for the several local authorities affected to seek a more equitable result than that at present arrived at.—Yours, &c., r. c..surroN. Bewsey Chambers, Sept. sth, 1888.

• WARRLNGTON STREETS. Sir,—l suppose that a stranger arriving in Warrington by the Bank Quay Station would naturally be much struck by the architectural beauties of our town. The first thing that would strike his eye (after the Patten Arms Hotel), on walking up Parker-st., would be Museum-st., a good street, though at present savouring much of the dead wall style of architecture, next Thynne-st., which will De a good street wilen cut through. But White-st. is the gem • here the traveller gets a first rate view of the back doors of the houses in Winmarleigh-st. The idea had crossed my mind that blind alleys,or as now called " Pocket-streets ' were done away within the modern style of building, but here we have one in Arpley-st., just made in all its glory. It is partly a continuation of White-st., though really a yard or two nearer to Sankey-st. If the "powers that be" have not yet named the aforesaid "Pocket-street" might I suggest (from the contiguity of the front doors of the one and the back doors of the other street) that they call it "Ashpit-view."—Yours, &c., "PERIPATETIC." September 3rd, 1888.

ST. PAUL'S CHURCH CLOCK. Sir.—l should like, through the medium of your columns, to call the attention of the proper authorities, whoever they may be, to the annoyance caused by the stoppage of St. Paul's Church clock. If these authorities cannot keep it going, it would be much more useful out of sight. The clock has been showing "half-past one" for at least a week, and, as far as I can find out, nothing has been done in the way of attempting to repair it. When one sees what may be called "a public clock" pointing to a certain time, one expects that clock to be right, and the time indicated to be correct. In going to catch a train leaving at two o'clock the other day, I looked at the clock and found it to be half-past one. Ex- pecting that was correct, I "took it easy" and lost my train. I think, most probably, that this unfortunate clock has swindled other people besides myself, and I hope, therefore, that the authorities will either keep it to the proper time, take its face down, or label it " stopped."—Yours, etc., Warrington, Sept. 15th, 1888.
BEWSEY.
