div.head: 40E1N H. SHEPPARD.
div.p: 40E1N H. SHEPPARD.

"THE TROUBLES OF A TRICYCLING TOUR." Sir,—What a lot of ignoramuses we must be, accord- ing to the showing of your correspondent "A Cyclist" However, the men refuse to accept his blame, and the ladies scorn his sympathy—the one being undeserved and the other undesired. Instead of being guilty of the sins of omission, we erred, if anything, in the opposite direction, and I can assure your aspersing correspondent that no such expedition ever set forth better equipped than we were. Instead of the ladies presenting tho ap- pearance of the ridiculous caricature which "A Cyclist" seems to have borrowed from the pages of that clever publication called "Scraps," they sat with a grace and rode with an ease that would have vied with the carriage of" A Cyclist" himself. As to the roads the Tricyclists followed the "down south" route recommended by" the Tourist's Route Map of England and Wales," published by Mr. Upcott Gill, admittedly one of the best publica- tions of its kind yet issued; and, in addition, sought the advice of local cyclists. The latter, however, only dis- played th3ir gross ignorance in their pitying remark that we "might reach Knutsford. " This we certainly did, and other places not yet included in the geography of "some experienced cyclists." Your correspondent will see from my second article that we went specially prepared in the matter of dress; nor was it quite without some preliminary riding the ladies commenced their journey. Still it was of such a character that they could truly be described as novices to the art, but as to "down-right hard work," the ladies reply: "Tell him it was not ha.,d work, and that you have the authority of the ladies for saying so." Again it was not without method that we pursued our journey, and I defy "A Cyclist," to take his meals or anything else at hotels that do not exist. So' far from being in thinly populated districts the numerous cyclists we met would have satisfied your correspondent that such was not the case, and no inhabitant was ever scared by the picture "A Cyclist" conjures up, the request for refreshment being invariably made by a deputation of one, the other five remaining in the road with the mac- hines. We refused the wine on principle, as we have done in other and far more critical occasions. I would not give a farthing for all the rank smelling liquor there is in the kingdom. In conclusion, I would just remark that what "plight to have been," was "a most enjoyable trip," and was not spoiled by want of either care or forethought. Had it been spoiled it would have been by instances over which we had no control. but "A Cyclist" will see by your next issue that altogether we had a "gay old tine," yours, &c.,
TOWNSMAN.

Warrington, September 3rd, 1888. P.S.—Since writing the above, I , have received the following from one of the ladies : ' I have just been made quite hot reading Cyclist'sblow. Flow very ignorant it makes a fellow look to write on what he knows nothing about. Evidently he thinks the subject was never thought about until the Saturday be- fore we started. Do, for pity's sake, knock him fiat, for I don't think the road could have been more studied than it was, nor do I think our correspondent could have known more about the road than thca man at Holmes Chapel. He only ought to have had alookat usto know we were not heavily clad; but there! the chap writes abroad altogether, and shows that he is not half a man if he would let his principle go for a glass of wine. Evidently, I should think from his remark that no place would be like "the Hotel" to him. I don't know how the other girls feel, but I am sure I don't want his sym- pathy.

STRIKE OF CorrroN OPERATIVES. A dispute at the Musgroves Atlas Cotton Mills, Holton, resulted on Thurs- day, in a strike affecting 1,200 operatives. The strikers say the system of weighing cotton bales acts unfairly against them. ECCLESTON FLOWER SHOW.—The seventh annual cott- agers' exhibition of flowers, fruit and vegatables, was held in a building behind the Seven Stars Inn, Eccleston, on Thursday and Friday last week Prizes, amounting to £l2 were offered, and there were about sixty exhibits, which had been tastefully arranged round the building by Mr. Leigh, the plants occupying a central place. The exhibits generally were of high class, this being especially the case in the vegatable class, in which a brass pan, two copper kettles, and a teapot were awarded for the best exhibit of celery grown within one mile of the Seven Stars Inn. The judges were Mr. J. Smetham (gardener to Mr. Nuttall, Nutirove Hall), and Mr. James Smith (gardener to Mr. Sinclair, Sutton). Mr. J. Ranson was the secretary, and Mr. W. Leigh, Treas- urer. The attendance was not so large as on previous occasions.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
BY " ARIEL:'

That the alimentary organs of the Primrose Leaguer are too delicate and aristocratic to digest Radical bread. The Frodsham Habitation had a gala day on Saturday, in which a "ham and beef tea," as the Salvationist would phrase it, held an important place in the affections of those present ; and thereby hangs a tale. Before the auspicious day, a comnaittee, presumably of "Dames," tested samples of bread, and examined tenders, and those sent in by a widow gave most satisfaction. But when it became known that the bread came from the bakehouse of a Runcorn Radical that tender was immediately set aside. Although the woman was one of the I'rimrose army, she was denied her pro- fit because she dealt with a Radical, and it would seem that Bigotry and Boycotting, each with a Big B, is not yet dead in Cheshire. Perhaps the wise dames thought that the Radical bread would be as hard of digestion as the Radical facts with which they are so constantly peppered, and to which they can only reply with a few vague platitudes. May the widow never lack a cus- tomer!

That the election of Runcorn Commissioners did not create any excitement in the town. The slits of the old members were considered unassailable, and the result proved the truth of the forecast. The battle lay between Mr. Wass and Mr. Yarwood, and the last named gentleman for the fifth time tasted the bitters of deteat. Mr. Yarwood declares that he will ne'er again champion the cause of the rate- payers, but "hope springs eternal in the human breast,' and may be when another year has passed he will again be found in the lists. That Mr. Meadowcroft, at the meeting of the Board ot Commissioners, on Wednesday, brought to light an irregularity that had occurred in regard to the proposed improvement of the Bridgewater Canal at the Sprinch. A committee had met and considered the subject, and had passed a resolution thereon, but yet no minutes were produced at the Board, nor any explanation given. Is this business- like? If circumstances had arisen that made it ad- visable that the resolution should not be confirmed, the committee, according to the mode of proceeding of such bodies, should have again met, or had the minute referred back by the Board in the ordinary way. No one would for a moment suppose that there is any antagonism against the Ship Canal Company, and they will. no doubt, be satisfied with the explanation given by the law clerk, who, by his timely interposition will, no doubt, save 4.he town a considerable sum in carrying out the sewerage project. That the opening of St. Edward's Catholic Chapel, on Sunday, was a very successful function. Church- men and Nonconformists were there at each service, in large numbers, and their presence may be taken as a tribute to the popularity Dr. Gastilda has achieved during the short period of his residence in the town.

That the Rev. Mr. Law, the new superintendent minister of the Widnes Wesleyan Circuit, has crea- ted a very favourable impression amongst his nume- rous flock. The reception meeting, on Tuesday, was a good augury of a happy and successful three years' labours in the chemical metropolis.

On the first of these sections the large amount of water collected in the cutting is on the increase, al- though the pumps are in full swing. Great headway is being made by the steam navvy at work in the field at Lower Walton which leads to the house lately occupied by Mr. Nelson Walker. A large number of men are busily engaged stripping the soil. At Stockton Heath the demolition of the houses in the way of the under- taking is being rapidly proceeded with. THELWALL. An accommodation bridge has been built across the cutting at Morris Brook for the convenience of Mr. D3.rbyshire, the tenant of the farm, the greater part of whose land lies on the other side. The new road which is to replace Thelwall-lane is being made, and several dwelling-houses, with frontages to the toad, are in course of erection. CONCERT AT THELWALL.

A concert, the first of a series to be held during the winter, was given on Tuesday evening in Morris Brook School-room, a building attached to the Mission Hall be- longing to the works. bThe proceedings commenced with a tea, and a concert followed. ACCIDENT AT LYMM. An unfortunate accident took place on Tuesdayiat the Warburton end of the Lymm section. A navvy glot into the way of the locomotive which attends on an excava- tor, and was caught, receiving severe injuries to his legs. fiv was taken by a locomotive to Thelwall Hospital.
ST. EDWARD'S CATHOLIC CHAPEL, RUNCORN.

OPENING CEREMONY BY THE BISHOP. The new chapel dedicated to St. Edward, which has been erected in Irwell-lane for the members of the Catholic faith, was opened for public worship on Sunday last. The old chapel on kill Brow had, With the lapse of years, become too small and incon- venient for the congregation that regularly wor- shipped there, and the Rev. Dr. Gasbaldi, on taking charge of the parish about six months ago, at once deter- mined on securing a more suitable and commodious edifice. The result of his labours, and the labours of several of his numerous flock, is seen in the structure that now stands beside the Presbytery. But though dig- carded for one purpose, the old chapel is not to be levelle''. with the gtotiO. Within IN wai!s th young idea will be taught how to grow, and day and Sunday school classes will be conducted there. As the congregation is by no means a rich one, the project for building was of necessity a modest one, and it was decided to try the experiment of erecting an iron structure in an atmo- sphere that is often greatly impregnated with coiroding gases, as the cost of a stone or brick structure would be greatly beyond the means obtainable. The new church, therefore, is of galvanised, corrugated iron, k best 24 Birmingham wire gauge, and is designed in the Gothic style of architecture. Seating accommodation is provided for about 750 persons, and the cost is up- wards of £7OO. The main entrance, decorated with Gothic scrolls, forms the basement of a tower 50 feet high, surrounded with a hill turret, octagonal in shape. The interior is lined throughout with well-seasoned wood, and presents a bright, cheerful, and comfortable appearance. Natural light is admitted by no less than 42 windows, glazed with Hartley's patent rolled glass, whilst artificial light is supplied by gas from seven pen- dants, having a total of 84 burners. Ventilation is secured by means of six dormer ventilators in the roof. and also through the upper portions of some of the side lights. As to heating the church, arrangements have been made for the introduction of two portable slow combustion stoves. The chapel proper measures 84 feet in length by 40 feet wide, and the roof, which is 27 feet from the floor to the apex is supported on ten iron pil- lars. The chancel is 24 feet by 18 feet, and contains the furniture from the old church. The altar had been made by Messrs. James and Sam Lea, who had performed the work in a satisfactory manner. The same workmen had also turned the candlesticks in use in the service, the designs being of a pleasing nature. The altar had been handsomely painted and decorated by Mr. David Billington, at the expense of Mr. Gregson. On the right of the chancel is Our Lady's Chapel, Ind on the left, a vestry for the boys. At the opposite end of the church is the organ chamber, 12 feet by 10, and here accom- modation has also been provided for the choir. The sitting accommodation throughout consists of modern benches of the most approved construction, and are con- venient and comfortable. The entire structure is fixed on a foundation of brick, and so arranged as to be free' from damp. Mr. Harbrow, contractor, of Bermondsey, has successfully carried out the work. The opening ceremony took place on Sunday morn- ing, when solemn High Mass was performed by thd Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, pontificially assisted by the Bishop of Shrewsbury. The following also took part in the ser- vice: The Revs. Mons. Slaughter (private Chamberlain to his Holiness Pope Leo XIII), Father Giles (Bishop's secretary), Father Thompson (Mold), and Fathers George and Therkenrath (of Ditton College). The musical por- tion of the impressive service was rendered by a choir, who had been trained by Mr. John Halford, Mr. J. Ravenscroft presiding at the organ. The sacred edifice was crowded with a congregation that included nume- rous Churchmen and Nonconformists. During the service the Bishop preached a sermon, in which he congratulated the worshippers that after long waiting, through the blessing of God and the zeal and energy of their pastor, they had at last secured so cenvenient and suitable a church for themselves. They lived in strange times, and there had never been a deeper or more honest spirit of inquiry into their religious be- lief, and they must be able to give an answer. There had been a countless number of sects sprung into exis- tence since the revolution against the Holy Catholic Church, and there were men at that moment busily imi- tating the Church of Christ, and mocking the very cere- mony of their Mass, in despite of their own authorities and of their laws, which said the Mass was a dangerous deceit, and leading people in some way to think that they belonged to the Catholic Church. But if they were examined he believed there would be found more imagi- nation than reality, and more error than truth. The Catholics had never forsworn their faith or given it up: but retained it until this day. In conclusion he desired to thank those who were Rot of their body for many kind acts of cordial consideration in helping to build their Church, and also those of their body who had helped forward that work, and he would say to the flock "Don't rest in your labours." It was an old saying, but never- h eless a true one, that "God helps those that help hemselves." Each must help to bear the burden, and ,
he hoped they would take it off the shoulders of their pastor.

in the evening another service was held, and the sacred edifice was crowded. The musical portion was rendered by the choir from St. Bedes' Chapel, Appleton. under the conducrtrship of Mr. J. Morrison. The Very Rev. Mons. Slaughter preached an eloquent sermon from the text— "We have not here a lasting city, but look forward to the one that is to come."
At the conclusion of the service the choir sang the Na- tional Anthem in Latin.

WESLEYAN RECEPTION AT WIDNES. The Rev. T. Law, formerly of Ripon, commenced his labours as superintendent minister of the Wid- nes Wesleyan circuit, on Sunday. He preached morning and evening in Victoria-road Chapel to very large congregations, and made a very geod im- pression by his eloquent discourses. On Tuesday evening a "recognition" meeting was held in Lacey- st. Schoolroom. The proceedings commenced with a tea party, about 170 persons being present. The good things were dispensed by Mesdames Robinson, S. Robinson, J. Robinson, Stead, Wendt, Lawrinson, Williams, Glover, T. Sadler, Brown, Fogg, Dainteth, Clarke (Cronton), Brimelow, and several others. Subsequently a meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. S. Robinson, who was supported by the Rev. T. Law (superintendent), Rev. J. Bryant, Messrs. Swale, T. Sadler, Stead, Robin- son, Williamson, G. Davies, Clarke, Shaw, Samuel Jack= SOR, at dR. Fogg. There was a capital audience.--The Chairman, in the name of the Widnes circuit, extended a cordial welcome to Mr. Law, and hoped that he would have a very happy and prosperous time with them. They extended to Mr. Law and Mrs Law the right hand of fellowship, promising to give him every support. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. R. Fogg, as an official of the circuit, wished Mr. Law and Mrs Law a happy time amongst the Widnes Methodists, and he hoped that at the end of three years they would be as sorry to lose Mr. Law, as they were sorry to lose their late superintendent. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Law had not come to a choice residential place, but he had come amongst a large hearted and a • sympathetic people and during the 19 years Widnes had.been a circuit, every minister had been sorry to leave, and would be delighted to come amongst them again. (Applause.)--Mr. T. S. Swale also made a speech in a humourous, yet practical vein, urging upon the congregation that Mr. Law' suc- cess depended upon the assistance they rendered him. Mr. T. Sadler, Mr. Stead (Ditton), Mr. I'. Robinson, Mr. Clark (Ditton), Mr. Williamson, Mr. P. Glover (Cronton), and Mr. W. Jackson also made speeches.—The Rev. T. Law, who was loudly applauded on rising, thanked the audience for the cordial reception he had received, and acknowledged the many kind and encouraging remarks that had been made with regard to him. He related his experiences of the various circuits in which he had so- journed, and said to judge from the speech that had been made he would spend as happy a period in Widnes as he had in any county in England. (Applause.) The meeting then concluded in the customary man- ner.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Wedne.sday morning. Mr. W. Fisher presided, and there were present Messrs. Dobson, Once, Han- 2inson, Imison, Mellor, Wiswall, Meadowcroft, .Pritchard, White, Taylor, Lake, Speakman, Lina- ker (law clerk), Marshall (secretary), Barker (sur- veyor), Dr. McDougall (medical officer).

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The Medical Officer reported that during the past month there were 29 deaths, of which four were inquest cases. Diarrhcea caused four deaths. The total deaths showed an average death rate of 19-6, and exclusive of the inquest rases of 18-2 per I,ooo.—The Surveyor said during the corresponding month last year there were 38 deaths.—The Chairman said the report was very satis- factory.

div.head: DOG FIGHT AT TIIE SLAGGHTER-HOUSES.
div.p: A DOG FIGHT AT TIIE SLAGGHTER-HOUSES.

Mr. Pritchard said before the medical officer left the room he should like to bring to the notice of the chair- man of the General Purposes Committee a certain scene that took place in the Board's slaughter-houses a short time ago, which he understood was characterised by very great cruelty, From what he had heard Dr. McDougall was the only witness. He alluded to a dog fight that took place at the slaughter-houses, and he should like to know what steps the committee had taken to bring the men guilty of such cruel practices to justice. He had also heard that some of the men who used the slaughter-houses were not of clean habits. They left offal about the place for a considerable time, and it became putrid and offensive to the neighbourhood. He further understood that the slaughter-houses remained unlocked by day and night, and that by night they were the refuge of all sorts of abandoned characters.— The Law Clerk said it would not be wise for the doctor to state whit he knew about the matter in the presence of the reporters.,—Mr. Grice said the matter had been be- fore the committee, who felt indignant that such a con- dition of -things should exist. —A long discussion took place as to whether a prosecution should be instituted or not, and it was decided that as this was the first instance the men should be warned.—Mr. Pritchard wished it to go forth that the Board would render every assistance to the police authorities in bringing these men of ferocious instincts to justice.—The Chairman *aid if another offence was committed the Board would not hesitate to prosecute.

div.head: BUILDINGS COMMITTEE.
div.p: BUILDINGS COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this committee, which were passed, on the motion of Mr. Taylor, contained a recommendation that the following plans be approved :—Mr. George Hunt, for the erection of five houses in Greenway-road (near York-st.) ; Messrs. Wilson and Newall, for the erection of three houses in Bold-st., at the corner of Stanley-st. ; Mr. John Thomason, for the erection of ten cottages in Bold-st. and Stanley-st. ; Mr. John Penning- ton, for the erection of two houses in Greenway-road, adjoining the two recently built by Mr.W. Bate; Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., for the alteration of an ad- dition to the Crown Inn, Church-st. ; Messrs. Lea and Son, for the erection of a store-room constructed of col, Tugatf.4 iron in Isfekionit,
if-INANOE.-TEE TRPROTESIENT OF WATERLOO TDOE.

The Finance bommittee recommended that any expen- diture recommended by the Library Committee must be confirmed by the Board before being discharged ; that all cheques drawn on the library fund be drawn by the Board, and that the treasurer be instructed that in future cheques on the library fund must be signed by three members of the Board; also that instructions be given to the secretary to keep the necessary books and accounts. Recommendation, that a cheque for the sum of £4l be drawn on loan account as deposit on the purchase of land at the corner of Waterloo-road for street improvements. —Mr. Imison moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Pritchard seconded the motion, and said it was the opinion of the Waterloo Bridge Committee that any im- provement to Waterloo Midge would not be complete unless they did something te widen the approaches to the bridge. As they were aware, the coal yard, weighing machine, and cottage had been purchased by the Board, and when they had taken the strip of land they required for widening the road- way, they were in hopes—they quite expected—that they would be able to dispose of the land for the amount the Board had paid for the whole. (Hear, hear.) After the improvement is made the committee were in hopes that they would be able to continue the line of the road from the foot of the brow to the branch post office, and if so the property would have to be set back to that line, and the bridge and its approaches would be then of the most complete chara6ter and a credit to the toWn.—The Chairman: A very wise course, I think.—Mr. Lake. re- ferring to the library accounts, said it did not seem fair that Mr. Marshsll should have extra tvork thrown on his shoulders, and have no extra remuneration.—Mr. Imison, as Chairman of the Finance Committee, said this change had been forced upon them by the Local Govern- mentßoard, and he pointed out that as in a short period Mr. Marshall would have some other extra work to per- form, the two things might be considered in conjunction. —The minutes were passed.
THE COUNTY couNcits.

A letter was read from Mr. John Ashton, clerk to the Runcorn Bench of Magistrates, asking the Board to ap- point a committee to arrange the representation of Run- corn on the County Council, and also to confer with the justices.—Messrs. Fisher, Speakman, and Imison were appointed a committee.

div.head: DIPROVEISiENT OF BRIDGEWATER CANAL.
div.p: THE DIPROVEISiENT OF BRIDGEWATER CANAL.

1 Mr. Meadowcroft pointed out that at a meeting of the 1 Legal and Parliamentary Committee a resolution had been passed with regard to the improvement of the navi- gation of the Bridgewater Canal at the Sprinch, but the resolution had not been placed on the agenda. As far as he understood, the committee had no objection to the proposal of Mr. Collier, the manager of the Ship Canal Company, but it was thought desirable to meet the views of the law clerk that a formal declaration should be made by the company that they were the owners of the land at the Sprinch. In his letter Mr. Collier stated that the land belonged to the company, but the law clerk thought there should be something different, and it was ' decided to recommend the Board to approve of the pro- posal subject to the law clerk's views being met.-- The Law Clerk said the reason the committee had not yet replied to the Ship Canal Company was this. He spoke to Mr. Wigg about the matter, and Mr. Wigg in- formed him they were intending to sewer their works at the furthest portion, and they had a plan in prepara- tion. He (Mr. Linaker) told Mr. Wigg what the Com- missioners had in view, and promised to send a plan as soon as it was out so that it could be seen how far that sewer would run in the line of the Commissioners' sewer, and also whether they could not have a culvert under the canal instead of a syphon. A culvert would be far more conveniant.—The Chairman remarked that they had been waiting to see if they could not act in conjunc- tion with the works, and make one tunnel do.—Mr. Meaclowcroft said that did not get over the fact that the proceedings of the committee had been entirely ignored. There were no instructions Oven the Law Clerk that it was either necessary or desirable that he should consult other persons who were really not affectedby the project of the company in any sense whatever.—The Chairman said this matter was sprung upon the Board very sud- denly by his (Mr 14Ieadowcroft's) company, and it was one of those things that required consideration.— Mr. Linaker did not think he was to blame for mention- ing the matter to Mr. Wigg. If he had not taken steps

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER

to join with him in sewering, and thus save expense he I should not have been doing his duty.—Mr. Meadowcroft thought it was an extraordinary course.—The Law Clerk said he thought it was rather rushing the Board on a matter of great importance.-Mr. Meadoweroft said it would now take another month at the earliest.—Mr. Speakman said if it were necessary a special meeting of tho Board could be held.—Mr. Meadowcroft replied that he should be sorry to call the Board together upon any matter concerning himself or the company. The town and Mr. Wigg had no connection with the land, and all the Company wanted was to take in a small strip of land that would improve the navigation, and the improve- ment to the trade of those particular works was indalcu- lable.
After some further discussion the Board went into committee to discuss other business.

div.head: ANOTHER RUNCORN PUBLICAN IN TROUBLE. THE INSPECTOR'S TEETOTALISM.
div.p: ANOTHER RUNCORN PUBLICAN IN TROUBLE. THE INSPECTOR'S TEETOTALISM.

Before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Mr. Alfred Thomas, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Phillips, landlord of the Friendship Tavern, Fry,: r-st., was charged with permitting drunkenness to take place on his premises, and also with selling drink to a drunken person. Patrick Farrell, a labourer. of Fryer-st., was charged with having been drunk in the Tavern. Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St.Helens, defended.—lnspector O'Donnell stated that about ten minutes to eleven on the night of the 4th August he went into the Friendship Tavern, accompanied by two constables. Farrell was there with a glass of beer before him, and he was drunk. There was also in the room a cripple named Kane, who made his living by playing a violin. He was very drunk, and a man was holding him on his feet whilst he placed his fiddle in his pocket. When the man released his hold Kane fell to the ground, land smashed his face in a terrible manner. His nose was broken, and his eyes were injured. The landlord was ill in the kitchen, and he called the landlady's atten- tion to the state of these men. She denied having served Kane, although he had been there all night. He had got drunk by having been supplied from one and another's mug of beer in the room. There was a pint of beer in a mug and a glass, and Farrell claimed the mug.—P.C. Brew and P.C. Harrop gave corroborative evidence, and P.S. Gosling deposed to seeing Farrell drink in the street at closing time.—Mr. Swift, in addressing the Bench for the defence, commented on the fact that the Inspector was a teetotaller, and that during his brief stay of three months he had brought about an excessive number of convictions of publicans compared with the number that had taken place previous to his advent. Above the question of whether or not there should be convictions, it was desirable that publicans, who were carrying on a trade authorised by the Legis- lature, should have confidence in the police; but there appeared to be some belief that the private opinions of the Inspector coloured or distorted his judgment. Mr. ISwift then criticised the evidence, and called the defend- ant Phillips, who said he had lived in Runcorn 28 years, and had •kept the Tavern for four months. On the Saturday night in question he was taken seriously ill, and left' the business to his wife at half-past nine. The Ifiddler was then in the taproom, and was sober. It was part of the conditions of the man's engagement to play that he should not take any drink, or he would be instantly dismissed. He never saw Farrell at all. He denied that his wife made the statement regarding the men attributed to her.— Superintendent Hollingworth It is a curious stipulation to make in a public-house that a man shall have nqdrink. -Defendant: It is the usual thing to do so. so as to conduct the house properly.—Farrell denied that he was drank. He had only had five pints since dinner time. The fid- dler fell because his crutch slipped on a wet flag—Mrs. Phillips said she never saw the fiddler take any drink, and she did not see the slightest signs of drink about him. What she told the officers was that if he was drunk the men who had been in the room must have given it to him from their pots. Farrell was served with a pint of pop and porter, and there was no appearance of drunkenness about him.—Patrick Dowd, Mary Dowd, John Dyer, and Patrick Kennedy all deposed that Farrell was sober.—The B^rich dismissed the charge of supplying drink to a drunken person, but said there was no doubt that drunkenness was permitted. As this was the defen- dant's first offence, he would only be fined 20s and costs. 20s.
DEATH OF THE REV, THOMAS CHAMBERS,
OF HALEWOOD.

The intelligence of the death of the Rev. Thomas Chambers, rector of Halewood, will be received with regret not only in clerical circles in this neighbour- hood, but throughout Lancashire, where the de- ceased gentleman was well-known and highly re- spected. Latterly Mr Chambers had been in in- different health, and accompanied by some friends went to Harrogate in the hope of the change bring- ing an improvement in his condition. Unfortunate- ly this was not realised, and his health becoming worse, he was brought to Halewood, where he died on Saturday morning. The deceased clergyman studied at Hertford College, Oxford, of which uni- versity he became 8.A., in 1850, and M.A. in 1858. He was ordained deacon in 1852 and priest in 1853 by the Right Rev. Dr. Graham, then Bishop of Chester. He was curate of Halewood and Childwall from 1852 to 1884. and was presented to the rectory of Halewood in the latter year, the patron being the Rev. Mr. Campbell, vicar of Childwall. Be continued to occupy this position up to the time of his death. In the neighbourhood of Childwall, Gateacre, and Woolton there not only reside a very large agricultural and artisan population, but also many of the merchants of Liverpool have their villas. Among all classes the late rector was esteemed for his kindly disposition, his accessibility at all times to his neighbours, whether churchmen or not, and for his affa- bility of manner was held in the highest regard. During his rectorship of Halewood, that district, like other sub- urbs of Liverpool, had undergone very considerable change, and it was Mr. Chambers's continued aim to keep his church and tho work connected with it abreast of the requirements of the altered conditions of the locality. Among all classes of his neighbours his some- what unexpected death will be a source of sincere sorrow. He WAS a Broad Churchman, and endeavoured to make the services of his church bright and attractive without carrying such matters to an extreme length. He was possessed of considerable literary attainments, and his earnest and forcible preaching, as well as his unfailing urbanity to every section of his parishioners, largely con- tributed to making his church a popular oneinthe neigh- bourhood. A warm friendship had throughout life sub- sisted between himself and the late Bishop Jacobs.on. The rev, gentleman manifested a warm interest in parochial matters and for many years had been one of the most respected members of the Prescot Union Board of Guar- dians. The deceased gentleman was never married. The living is the gift of the Rev. Canon Warr, vicar of Child- wall. It is worth £3OO a year and a house, and is the third living which Canon Warr has had to dispose of within a very brief period. The mortal remains of the late rev. gentleman were' in- terred in Halewood Parish Churchyard, on Tuesday. The body of the deceased was carried round from the vicarage by several stalwart farm parishioners, and it was received at the church-gates by the Rev. G. H. Spooner. The Rev. J. B. Bolton having read the Psalms, the Rev. J. Scott read the Lesson, the service at the grave being afterwards conducted by the Rev. C. Safford. Mr. H. Croft, organist of All Hallows Church, Allerton, played the " Dead March" in " Saul" as the body was conveyed into the sacred edifice. The coffin was covered with wreaths sent by sympathising friends, residents in the district.

div.head: RUNCORN CATUOLIC LEAGUE OF THE CROSS.
div.p: RUNCORN CATUOLIC LEAGUE OF THE CROSS.

A few months ago a Via-a-ch. of the Catholic Total AbstinenCe League of the Cross was established in Runcorn, and has met with gratifying success. Re- cently the branch has secured three rooms in Irwell- lane for the use of the members, and books, news- papers, bagatelle, draughts, chess; &c., will be provided. Advantage was taken of the presence of the Bishop of Shrewsbury at Runcorn to present his Lordship with an address, and ask him to declare the rooms open. The Bishop met the members in the church, and, having been introduced by Dr. Gastaldi, Mr.T. Wil- liams read and presented the following address ;—" To his Lordship the Right Rev. Edmund Knight, D.D., Bishop of Shrewsbury,—May it please your Lordship, we the members of the Runcorn Branch of the Catholic Total Abstinence League of the Cross, with unbounded joy take this opportunity of cordially welcoming you to this historic town, once famous for its monastic institutions; and offering to you the warmest expression of our grati- tude and admiration for the noble action you have taken in advancing the spread of Catholicity in this diocese. We have watched with deep interest how the religious movement of our people has progressed under your fos- tering care and guidance. We welcome you as the repre- sentative of our Holy Father Pope Leo XIII. to bless add open this spacious church, dedicated to the illustrious St. Edward, which through the indomitable zeal of our energetic pastor, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, to whom we owe a debt of gratitude for the persistent way in which he has laboured to bring about a scheme for the better carrying on of Christian teachina, and we sincerely hope and expect that he will receive support of all interested in the advance of such a noble work. We are not unmindful, too, of your large hearted generosity, and we rejoice exceedingly to know that your heart beats so responsive to the prayer of our respected pastor, when you so generously subscribed to- wards the building of a new school at Weston in honour of St. John the Baptist, which will no doubt foster a thorough Catholic education to scores Of children who in the past had no alternative but to attend Protestant schools We greet you to-night as an apostle of temper- ance, and value the efforts you are making in the cause of total abstinence, which has for its object the social and religious elevation of our people. We recognise in your lordship an uncompromising enemy of the vice of intem- perance, and we pray that you may long be spared to guide and direct us in our struggle with this great evil of mankind, and that as years roll on, each succeeding year will be a record of increasing success. We are also proud to be able to inform you that after „several unsuc- cessful attempts to establish e, branch of the League of I

the Cross in Runcorn we have at last succeeded, with the Rid of our worthy pastor, kid t onsidering the short space of two months we now number . about 114 mem- bers. Ifirczonatiiiiiii---Wa ask Tour lordship's blessing upon , ourselveamud otroursociety:f. and , in return we will pray ' God tha youytaylive to see the fulness of days, to rule and 11 govern t, 4ipeese 6:nrirnitted to your care ; and that your Epls2,6 pile may be crowned with such abundant fruit aslhheineuierable for ages to come in the annals of our glorlousuhurch and the- temperance movement." The address was signed on behalf of the members by Thomas4loughten,president ; James Byrne, vice-presi- dent ; and' Thotrias Williamson, secretary. The Bishop, in acktaitileidgkig the address, said he recognised that the work of the League was intimately associated with all that was-best ;in the work of the mission, because they furtherel..very much the aims of their pastor, and the goediVoik'of the congregation by taking up the cause of thinpetince. Religion must be at the head of all things, -but temperance was one of the greatest supporters pf religion. They must not, however, while, temperate themselves, be intemperate towards others; they must allow them to take their own way, and they must take theirs. When the church had to do with a man who could not take a glass of beer or wine without going in- to excess, it did not command that man to stop from drink : but advised and encouraged him, and pointed out the better way. The Bishop warned the members of the League to always take care to remember that their institution was a Catholic institution, and not a mere political one,and the success of their cause would depend to some extent upon the regularity with which they kept their duty as Catholics. In conclusion the Bishop gave the members his blessing in God's name.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

Tlng MAYOR. —lt is stated that Alderman Sutton, the Mayor, has received an invitation from the Lord Mayor of London to dinner at the Mansion House, on Wednesday, October 17th. Mn. GILBERT REENALL'S TURN-OUT. —At the Cheshire Agricultural Society's Show at Chester, on Saturday, Mr. Gilbert Greenall, of Walton Hall, ob- tained the third prize in the class for turn-outs. The value of the prize is put down at XL WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. —At this court, on Tuesday morning, before Mr. Edward Greenall, Patrick Coleman was charged with stealing a turkey from the farm of Mr. John Campkin, at Dut- ton. He was remanded to the next Daresbury Petty Sessions.

Tun REV. J. AGAR BEET.—The Rev. J. Agar Beet, who was formerly minister of the Warrington Wesleyan circuit, and is now of Richmond College, has just been appointed Fernley lecturer for 1889. This appointment has given much pleasure to his friends in Warrington and district. WARRINGTON CLERGY DAUGHTERS' SCHOOL.— The Dean of Chester has accepted the nomination as preacher for next year at the anniversary of the Warrington Clergy Daughters' School. General Sir Richard ,Wilbraham, of Rode Hall, near Stoke-upon-Trent, is the president for the year. FLOWER SHOW .6.T HOUGHTON.— The Houghton Horticultural Society had their fourth annual exhi- bition in a field on Middleton Hall Farm, lent by the president (Mr. George Comber), on Friday and Saturday., The society's district comprises Hough- ton, Middleton and Arbury, Winwick-with-Hulme, Hermitage Green, Orford, and Poulton-with-Fearn- head. There were,eight classes. On a table in the centre of the tent was a choice variety of plants, not for competition, lent by Mrs. Comber, of Middle- ton Hall, and arranged by Mr. Barber, .her gardener. Plants were lent by Mr. C. E. Arnott,, nurseryman, of Lime House, Lowton. The entries numbered .up- wards of 400, including 14 for the prizes offered' for the best cultivated cottage gardens. The judges Messrs. Edward Green (Bank Hall, Warrinv,ton), Thomas Jepson (gardener to Mr. Beamont, Orford Hall), James Hatton (of Poulton). and Mr. John Southern (of Croft.) The Edge Green Brass Band played a selection of music for dancing each after- noon. On Saturday juvenile sports took place on the show field. The tents were erected at the ex- pense of Mrs. Comber and family, and Miss Comber distributed the prizes, consisting of money, to the exhibitors on Friday evening. The total amount offered for competition was upwards of .C 35. The number of visitors, including members, subscribers, &c., during the time the exhibition was open was more than 400, besides upwards of 150 children be- longing to Winwick parish, who were admitted free on the Saturday to the juvenile sports. WESLEYA.N CHAPEL—Anniversary ser- vices in connection with Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel were conducted on Sunday, by the Rev. Geor.,e Dickenson, of Mytholmroyd, to large congregations. At the evening service the preacher took as his text the words—" Neither be partaker of other men's sins; keep thyself pure" (1 Tim. v. 22.) In the course of an interesting address he referred to th question of Sunday closing, and said that when in Liverpool he f•,rmed one of a band who were re- solved to see what the public of Liverpool felt con- cerning the opening of public-houses on the Lord's Day. They adopted a course of canvass and sent a paper to every house, obtaining the signatures of all who were willing that such houses should be closed. The minority were very few compared with the vast population of the city of Liverpool. On the completion of the work, a public meeting was hehl in St. George's Hall. The assembled congregation was informed what the voice of the Liverpool people was in connection with the closing of those houses on the Lord's Day. The question was ,one which must be approached gradually. Trenaendous in- vestments, such as the liquor traffic, could not be done away with at one blow; no Government would do it. But if they were content to let it be taken on a graduated scale they would be successful. There were many publicans who would be glad to see Sunday closing. Shaine on those men who as- serted that temperance advocates wanted to make people religious by Act of Parliament! Collections in aid of the trust funds, the total of which amoun- ted to £l7 9s Bd, were made at the close of each service. • • A CO,NTESTED 1.0.11.—At the Warrington County Court, on Saturday, before His Honour Judge Fioulkes, tne Rev. T. B. McLean, executor and heir of the late Mr. James Morris, sued John Mason, a night-watchman, living in Academy-st., for a 2s 6d, a sum alleged to have been lent by Mr. Morris to the defendant, for which an I O,U. was taken. Mr Sidney Taylor (Messrs Robert Davies, Sharp, and Kirkconnel) represented the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence.—Mr. Taylor said that it was admitted that the signature on the 1.0. U. was that of defendant, and all he could do was to put in that document and the admission, and leave the case with His Honour. He submitted, however, that if the parties thought it worth while for an 1.0. U. to be given, if the money was afterwards paid a receipt should have been given, or the paper re- turned. For the defence, Mr. Browne said that some years ago the defendant was in the habit of borrow- ing money from Mr. Morris from time to time. On one occasion he borrowed £5. Some time after Mr. Morris brought to him an 1.0. U. for .C 6 2s 6d, the borrowed money and interest, and the defendant signed it. The next day, however, he repaid the £5 in the street, and asked for a receipt, which Mr. Morris said he would give when the interest was paid. The matter was, however, never mentioned between the parties again, though they were on the best of terms, and met daily. Evidence in support of this having been given by the defendant and his wife, his Honour said that defendant could not get over the fact that the,I.O.U. was never given up. It might be that the money had been paid, but when he found the security in the hands of the creditor he ought to give great weight to it. Under the cir- cumstances he must give judgment for the plain- tiff. Mr. Browne said that considering the plaintiff had received something like £30,000 by the death of Mr. Morris. he thought he might consent to some easy mode of payment. His Honour made an order Ifor payment at the rate of 4s a month.
LATEST NEWS.

THE BISHOPRIC OF CHESTER. - The Central- News learns that Lord Salisbury has nominated to the See of Chester, Canon Jayne, vicar of Leeds, and that the rev. gentleman has accepted the nomination.. A LEAGUE SECRETARY SENT TO GAOL.—At MRCYOBI33. on Friday, Daniel O'Shea, Secretary of the Carrigrmnia Branch of the National League was sentenced to four months' imprisonment for intimidating one James Cotter.

Tim SALFORD TOWN CLERIC On Friday the late town clerk of Salford, Mr. John Graves, was declared bankrupt at the instance of a Derby lady, who is his creditor for £BOO, trust money, and his accounts will therefore now be overhauled.

_ SMALLPDX isA GAOL.—It is announced that smallpox has broken out in the prison at Leicester. On June sth George Morley was convicted of stealing goods from the premises of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and he was found suffering from the disease oti Wednesday. Tint EAST AFRICAN COMPANY.—Last night's "Gazette" contains the announcement that a charter has been granted to the Imperial British East African Comvany upon a petition to Her Majesty in Council. The objects of the company are stated to be the protection of British commercial interests in Eastern Africa in territories in- cluding the port of Momtassa granted to the company by the Sultan of Zanzibar and other African potentates. HEAVY PENALTY FOR BREACH OF THE FACTORY Am.— At Dewsbury, on Friday., Thomas Turner and Company, manufacturers, Thornhill, near Dewsbury, were mulcted in penalties amounting to £49 and costs for breaches of the Factory Act, by employing children under age and children who had not procured certificates from a school. Inspector Beaumont had visited the mill, and placed the matter before the Home Secretary, who said it was a very bad case, and proceedings were taken in 25 cases.

-- ALLEGED OBSTRUCTION BY SALVATIONISTS.—The magis- trates of Great Yarmouth were engaged for several hours, on Friday, in hearing summonses issued at the instante of the Watch Committee against thirty persons, members of the Salvation Army and Blue Ribbon Army organizations, for obstructing the public highway by holding meetings in open spaces in various parts of the town. Ultimately all the defendants agreed to suspend meetings in public streets until Saturday, the 15th inst., on the understanding that in the meantime efforts would be made to arrive at an amicable arrangement respecting the matters in dispute. TRADES UNION CoNxinuss.—The Trades Union Con- gress was resumed on Friday. On the motion of Mr M‘Lean (Edinburgh), seconded by Mr Hunter (Glas- gow), a resolution condemning the sweating system in connection with Government contracts was passed. A resolution was also adopted condemning the long hours of duty of railway men, upon whom the safety of trains depended, as being detrimental to the men so en- gaged and a source of danger to the travelling public. Some discussion took place in reference to the place of meeting for next year. Cardiff, Dundee, Liverpool, and Birmingham were proposed, but on a vote being taken Dundee was selected, 79 delegates voting for that town, and 74 for Liverpool.

CAIRO-ST. CHAPEL, WARRINGTON. THE NEW MINISTER. _ .

We understand that the pulpit at the above chapel, recently rendered vacant by the resignation of the Rev. Priestley Prime, on the ground of ill- health, has been offered to, and accepted by, the Rev. Frank Freeston, of Altrincham. The accept- ance appears to have caused great satisfaction, as the rev. gentleman, on several occasions when he has visited the chapel, has earned the admiration and esteem of the congregation. Mr. Freeston is the son of the Rev. Joseph Freeston, of Stalybridge, whose botanical and astronomical lectures are so well known in Warrington. He studied at Man- chester New College, London, and for some time he has been co-pastor with the Rev. E. Odgers, M.A., at Altrincham. It is expected that he will enter upon his ministry in about a month's time.

TITRE. Mrs. Wilkinson, the wife •of a forgeman residing in Iloyle-st., off Bewsey-rd., Warrington, was re- cently subject to an extraordinary adventure while travelling in a third-class carriage between North- with and Warrington, on the London and North- Western Railway. Her story points to a form of " outrage " against which others might do worse than, be on their guard. The matter has not been reported to the police authorities officially, but her statement is to the effect that on Tuesday evening she entered a train at Northwich, where she had been visiting some relatives, for Warrington. An- other woman, with two children, sat in the same compartment, and just as the train was about to start a respectably-dressed young "lady" entered the carriage. After a few minutes general conversation the stranger took a seat be- tween the two women, and directly afterwards the women and children, it is stated, became uncon- scious. When they recovered the young "lady" had disappeared, having apparently left the train at Greenbank Station, taking with her the contents of the purses of both women. A singular feature is the fact that the four unconscious occupants of the compartments came to their senses simultaneously. The women found their purses lying empty,entbe seat, having been "abstracted from their pockets. Mrs. Wilkinson states that her purse contained .£1 is 61d, while the other woman, who cams from Runcorn, hadin her possession about 17s. The per- petrator of the affair has not yet been found
